articles.title: Carlisle Launches EL121 Disc Brakes for Improved Performance and Wear Life

paras.en: Carlisle Launches EL121 Disc Brakes for Improved Performance and Wear Life

(MEDINA, OH, September 12, 2023) – Carlisle Brake & Friction is excited to announce the launch of EL121 Disc Brake Pads for mine haul truck applications. The new product series will be named Extended Life, or the EL Series, and EL121 will be the first friction formulation of the series to launch.

Carlisle’s EL121 Series friction material nearly doubles the service life of front-axle, mine haul truck brake pads. The result is increased equipment uptime, and reduced maintenance costs when utilizing the OEM calipers and rotors.

Autonomous haul trucks experience higher pad temperatures, which drive elevated pad wear from increased braking cycles as the retarder and the service brake are applied. EL121 features a highly wear-resistant friction material blend that provides extended brake pad life with consistent and fade-resistant braking performance. EL121 is the ideal solution for today’s autonomous mine haul trucks (may also be used in manned mine haul trucks for increased performance and longevity).

“We understand that mine operators need to keep their haul trucks on the job and not in the shop for brake service. Our latest innovation allows for up to double the service life of the front-axle mine haul truck brake pads and are a will-fit replacement to existing OEM pads. These were thoroughly lab tested as well as field tested on Komatsu 830E-1 trucks,” said Ron Ratell, Product Line Director Friction Products at Carlisle Brake & Friction.

EL121 friction has been dyno tested to replicate the application and is proven to deliver an innovative, high-energy material to meet market needs. EL121 disc brake pads also feature an industry-proven mechanical retention system with backing plate technology designed for superior bonding and durability, capable of withstanding abusive conditions in even the harshest Off-Highway environments.

Carlisle’s EL121 Series disc brake pads are available now through authorized Carlisle dealers and distributors. To learn more, visit https://www.carlislecbf.com/products/brake-friction/disc-brake-pads/off-highway-disc-brake-pads/el. To locate an authorized Carlisle dealer near you, search our online distributor listing https://www.carlislecbf.com/support/find-a-distributor.

Carlisle Brake & Friction is a globally recognized leader in the development and manufacture of highly innovative brake and friction system solutions to service a diverse range of motion control applications. The comprehensive nature of Carlisle’s brake system expertise includes hydraulic control products, industrial brake assemblies, wet and dry friction material for brake, clutch, and transmission applications as well as aftermarket replacement products. Our full-system product offering, supported by our industry-experience staff of experts, provides our customers with brake system solutions that set them apart from their competition. www.carlislecbf.com

articles.title: SEMA’s FutureTech Studio Returns with ADAS Sessions and More
articles.author: Jason Stahl

paras.en: The FutureTech Studio will return to the 2026 SEMA Show with more than 20 vehicles and a three-day education program highlighting technologies changing how automotive aftermarket products are designed, developed and brought to market. Topics include advanced powertrains and fuels, artificial intelligence, automated driving technologies and emerging product-development tools.

Located in Central Hall, booth no. 24401, FutureTech Studio will feature vehicles showcasing alternative fuels and EV powertrains, a FutureTech Live Education Stage offering 21 30-minute microlearning sessions across three days and product displays demonstrating solutions to help manufacturers get products to market faster.

“FutureTech Studio is designed to show industry professionals both where automotive technology stands today and where it’s headed, helping attendees evaluate emerging solutions, understand their business implications and identify opportunities to remain competitive,” said Jim Moore, vice president of OEM and product development for SEMA. “Attendees can expect a connected, hands-on environment where they can see technologies up close, talk with experts and experience how innovations are shaping the industry’s future.”

articles.title: INDASA, Save the Rhino International Join Forces
articles.author: Jason Stahl

paras.en: INDASA announced it has partnered with Save the Rhino International, a UK-registered charity working to safeguard rhino species and their landscapes. The partnership brings together two organizations connected by a shared symbol: the rhino.

For INDASA, the Rhyno has represented strength, resilience and performance for decades. For Save the Rhino International, the vision is a future where all five rhino species thrive in the wild. The idea is straightforward: the symbol that has represented INDASA for decades should also help protect the species behind it.

At the center of the initiative are INDASA’s Rhynogrip and Rhynostick White Line, both in 150mm and in 125mm. Throughout the campaign, these products will feature bespoke packaging designed to reflect INDASA’s commitment to the partnership with Save the Rhino International and to carry the conservation message to markets around the world.

The special-edition packaging becomes a visible platform for the conservation cause, placing it in the hands of the professionals who use these products every day. Every package sold also contributes directly to rhino conservation, creating a clear connection between a professional-use product and a global environmental cause.

Through its products, packaging, digital communication and international network, INDASA aims to raise awareness of rhino conservation beyond traditional environmental audiences, reaching the body shops and distributors where the cause has never been addressed before.

Save the Rhino International works in partnership with conservation organizations, governments and local communities to conserve rhinos and their landscapes. These collaborations bring together knowledge, expertise and resources to support evidence-based conservation, address the challenges facing rhino populations and secure their long-term recovery.

Through this partnership, INDASA is contributing to those ongoing projects and giving the conservation message a route into an industry outside the organization’s usual reach. The campaign gives industry professionals a way into the cause: by acquiring the products they already use in their surface preparation activities, they contribute to conservation efforts, creating a direct connection between product, people and purpose.

Running for one year, the campaign connects every package sold with a direct contribution to Save the Rhino International’s conservation work. For every campaign box sold, INDASA will donate €0.03 directly to the organization.

The campaign identity captures the connection at the heart of the partnership. “By The Rhyno” represents the means: the strength and reach of INDASA’s own symbol, put behind the cause. “For the Rhino” represents the purpose: raising awareness and supporting the conservation of rhinos and their natural habitats.

The donation matters. So does the attention it brings: rhinos placed in front of professionals who would otherwise never come across the cause, and the reminder that a routine purchase can be part of protecting a species.

articles.title: Takata airbag recall: NHTSA says status of 9% unconfirmed
articles.author: Lurah Lowery

paras.en: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) says it “cannot confirm the status” of the remaining 9% of more than 67 million recalled Takata airbags, or whether they remain on U.S. roads.
NHTSA told Repairer Driven News that according to its latest 2024 completion-rate estimates, 91% of the affected airbags had been replaced or were otherwise accounted for.

The Takata airbag inflator recall is the largest safety recall in automotive history and spans worldwide. Issues first came to light in 2008. Vehicles across more than 30 brands are equipped with the airbags, according to NHTSA.
NHTSA says the airbags have killed 28 people and caused at least 400 injuries in the U.S. It linked the 28th death to an incident that occurred in Alabama involving a Honda vehicle.

“NHTSA cannot confirm the status of the remaining 9% or if they remain on U.S. roads,” a NHTSA spokesperson told Repairer Driven News. “NHTSA encourages everyone to check for open recalls at nhtsa.gov or by downloading our SaferCar app. Anyone with an open Takata recall should follow any manufacturer warnings and call their vehicle’s dealership immediately to schedule a free repair.”

The chart below shows the net percentage of airbags remaining for replacement for priority groups 1–12. “Net” refers to the percent remaining from the total airbags count, according to NHTSA. NHTSA includes these groups because vehicle manufacturers have submitted verifiable underlying data.

The chart above specifies the percentage of dispositioned airbags, as approved by NHTSA, including stolen and scrapped vehicles and those exported from the U.S. jurisdiction, according to NHTSA. It also includes vehicles with aftermarket modifications, degraded to the point that the recall remedy cannot be completed, and those to which owners have been nonresponsive to or have affirmatively refused the recall remedy outreach.

The data in this chart begins in 2022 when NHTSA added several reporting categories: nonresponsive, affirmative refusal, aftermarket modification, and vehicle degradation. NHTSA must receive a request before a vehicle manufacturer can submit to these categories. NHTSA notes that not all vehicle manufacturers have been approved for or have requested inclusion in the categories.

Takata, a bankrupt parts supplier, was responsible for manufacturing airbag canisters in defective airbag inflators that can explode and spray sharp metal fragments toward the driver and passengers, comparable to shrapnel from an exploding grenade, which has caused severe injuries and deaths.

According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), propellant in the inflators breaks down after long-term exposure to high temperature fluctuations and humidity. This can cause the propellant to burn too quickly, creating too much pressure and leading to explosions.

As of Aug. 21, Honda says it has voluntarily removed over 535,000 inflators from salvage yards, and the effort continues. The OEM says it has also asked major online auction sites to prohibit and stop any sales of the affected airbags.
A separate group of defective Takata airbags was recalled in late 2019. According to NHTSA, unlike the airbag inflators in the larger Takata recalls, this recall involves non-azide driver inflators.
According to the latest Carfax data, 4.7 million vehicles equipped with recalled Takata airbags remain in the U.S.
Carfax says the number of vehicles on the road with the Takata airbags has dropped 20% from 6 million in 2024.

“Many automakers are working to find owners of vehicles that still have Takata airbags and finally get those airbags replaced,” Carfax states in its September recall tracker report. “Some are even sending teams out across the country to locate affected owners and provide help.

“Despite the drop in affected vehicles, nearly 5 million still need those Takata airbags replaced, and as they get older, they’re more likely to continue to change hands, which makes tracking down the owners more difficult. And some of those vehicles even have ‘do not drive’ orders.”

articles.title: CCC announces its acquisition by GTCR, Elliott
articles.author: Lurah Lowery

paras.en: CCC Intelligent Solutions Holdings announced Thursday that a consortium of private investment firms, led by GTCR and including Elliott Investment Management, will acquire it in an all-cash transaction with an enterprise value of $6.1 billion.
Until the transaction closes, CCC will remain publicly traded and continue operating as an independent company, according to a CCC press release.

“The transaction is not subject to a financing condition,” the release states. “Upon completion of the transaction, CCC will become a privately held company, and its common stock will no longer be listed on the Nasdaq.”
Githesh Ramamurthy, CCC’s chairman and CEO, says Thursday’s announcement “follows a thorough review of strategic options with assistance from our financial and legal advisors.”

The release states that CCC’s Board of Directors approved the transaction, which is expected to close in Q1 2027, subject to customary closing conditions, including the receipt of required regulatory approvals and CCC stockholder approval.

“Our Board of Directors is confident this transaction recognizes the strength of the business our team has built while delivering immediate and premium cash value to our stockholders,” said Ramamurthy.

Under the terms of a definitive agreement, CCC stockholders will receive $7.75 in cash for each share of CCC common stock, representing a premium of 44% to CCC’s unaffected closing stock price on July 9, 2026, and a premium of 59% to the 30-day average price as of July 9, 2026.

A press release announcing the acquisition notes that July 9 was the last trading day before media speculation of CCC’s potential sale. At the time, Reuters reported that CCC was “exploring a sale of the company, according to three people familiar with the matter.”
The article stated: “The Chicago-based company has hired Morgan Stanley to advise on a sale process and has reached out to prospective buyers, including private equity firms, the sources said.”
In August, Seeking Alpha, Bloomberg News, and Reuters reported that private equity firms and Copart were reportedly interested in buying CCC.
At the time Repairer Driven News reached out to CCC for comment on the reported interest. A company spokesperson responded, “CCC doesn’t comment on rumors and speculation.”
Now, Ramamurthy says that with the experience and resources GTCR and Elliot provide, CCC will continue to build on its momentum and extend its leadership.

“Throughout CCC’s history, we have helped customers navigate growing complexity and achieve better outcomes through technology and innovation,” he said. “Together, we will accelerate the AI and agentic capabilities our customers want from us, expand the network at the center of our platform, and continue to develop and build our world-class team. I am deeply grateful to our employees for their dedication and commitment to our customers, and I am excited for all that we will accomplish together in this next chapter.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: He shared similar commentary to a Facebook post by CCC announcing the sale.

A Reuters article published after the CCC announcement noted that “earlier this year, the company faced investor concerns over slowing growth, softer claims volumes and a slower-than-expected rollout of some newer software products, which had weighed on its share price.” Meanwhile, the acquiring firms have expressed confidence in CCC’s underlying business and its opportunities for future growth, particularly through artificial intelligence.

When Repairer Driven News asked CCC for comment on its reasoning for the acquisition, CCC reiterated that its Board of Directors approved the transaction and said it “delivers immediate and certain value to shareholders at a significant premium to the unaffected share price.”

“CCC remains a strong business,” a CCC spokesperson said. “Our Board of Directors is confident this transaction recognizes the strength of the business our team has built while delivering immediate and premium cash value to our stockholders. Beyond today’s announcement and related SEC filings, we do not have additional information to share at this time.”
CCC went public in 2021 after announcing its owners at the time, and a Dragoneer Investment Group spinoff had agreed to a merger and subsequent listing of shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Private equity firm Advent, which owned the majority of CCC at the time, would continue to hold most of the shares once CCC went public. Reuters previously reported that Advent “fully exited its investment in 2025 through a series of secondary share offerings, including the sale of its remaining stake in November.”

On Thursday, Mark Anderson, GTCR media and telecommunications managing director and head of technology, said the PE firm has followed CCC for years and believes it’s “uniquely positioned to support their customers as they increasingly adopt AI solutions to improve decision-making and efficiency across the claims and repair lifecycle.”

“We look forward to partnering with Githesh and the talented CCC team to support continued investment in product innovation and AI capabilities, expand the company’s offerings and build long-term value,” he said. “Our focus will be on helping CCC deliver better outcomes for its customers while supporting CCC’s next phase of growth.”

David Kerko, Elliott’s head of global private equity, added: “We have [a] strong belief in CCC’s position as the trusted third party at the center of the automotive insurance and repair industry. CCC’s role within the large ecosystem of insurers, repair facilities, automakers and parts suppliers creates strong data advantages and network benefits for their more than 35,000 customers. We believe these advantages make CCC a highly durable franchise in vertical software – which AI will only make more valuable as CCC delivers the next generation of capabilities to its customers.”

articles.title: Survey: Buyers want their next vehicle to function like a smartphone
articles.author: Lurah Lowery

paras.en: Verra Mobility Corp.’s latest survey of 2,000 U.S. adults shows that 72% expect their next vehicle to function like a smartphone, with built-in apps and services.

Active connected services usage has crossed the majority threshold for the first time, with 54% of drivers using at least one manufacturer-provided connected service, up from 49% in Verra Mobility’s 2024 survey. Familiarity with the term “connected vehicle” rose to 69%, compared with 60% two years ago.

Fifty-one percent said connected features would influence their decision to buy a different make, model, or higher trim level. All survey respondents own or lease a 2019 or newer vehicle and were at least 18 years old in May at the time of the survey.

The survey defined connected vehicle services as those that use a vehicle’s embedded communications rather than a mobile phone connection. That definition didn’t include services accessed through smartphones, such as Apple CarPlay or Android Auto.

“The story of this year’s survey is that consumers have arrived at the connected vehicle category, and they’re bringing real expectations with them,” said Cathi Chinn, Verra Mobility’s innovation vice president, in a press release. “Drivers now expect their vehicles to behave like the connected devices they use everywhere else in their lives, which puts pressure on the automotive industry to deliver experiences that justify it, especially around the embedded payments, mobility services and safety features consumers say they want most.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Survey respondents also said they want their vehicles to do more of the work for them, with safety leading the list of services they value most. Accident and theft protection ranked first (31%) when respondents were asked which service category is most appealing if cost is not a factor, followed by maintenance and payments. Fifty-nine percent said they believe connected vehicles make driving safer.

Seventy-two percent said they would value proactive trip suggestions from their vehicles such as parking, fuel, or charging station locations, and handling toll transactions. Forty-three percent said they’ve already signed up for an app or service through their vehicle’s infotainment system regarding parking, EV charging, or tolling.
Sixty-six percent said it would be a valued convenience not having to connect a smartphone every time they get in the car.
The survey results also show that younger drivers led adoption across nearly every measure of the survey:
- Sixty-seven percent of those ages 18–24 actively use at least one connected service, compared to 44% of those ages 55–64.
- Sixty-nine percent of 18–24-year-olds said connected features would influence their vehicle purchase, versus 40% of those ages 55–64.
- Sixty-three percent of 18–24-year-olds and 61% of 25–34-year-olds find the in-vehicle digital wallet concept appealing compared to 44% overall.

As for data privacy, willingness to trade data for tangible benefits has held steady since 2024, but understanding and trust haven’t kept pace with adoption, according to the survey results. Sixty-six percent said they would share driving and location data for insurance discounts, automatic toll payments, and emergency services — mirroring the 2024 findings.
Only 14% said they fully understand what data their vehicle collects, down from 22% in 2024. Fifty-four percent expressed at least some concern about vehicle data collection practices.

Based on a recent large-scale study of the connected vehicle ecosystem, Northeastern University researchers conclude that improved transparency is necessary to identify and address existing harm to passengers caused by the data that “smartphones on wheels” collect.

Researchers found that vehicles and companion apps contact numerous third-party domains, including advertisers and trackers. They also found that vehicle-specific information is being tied to individual consumers. Companion apps expose VINs and a secondary type of personally identifiable information, such as email addresses, to three companies.

Last year, 54% of Americans believed new cars have too much technology, while 72% worried about repair costs if something breaks, according to the second annual Enterprise Mobility’s “On the Move” survey released in October 2025. Nearly 7 in 10 (68%) drivers said they would willingly give up the latest tech for a more affordable vehicle.
More than half of the “On the Move” survey respondents said they would prefer a mix of touch screens and physical buttons.

articles.title: What to Know about Static and Dynamic ADAS Calibrations
articles.author: Christian Hinton

paras.en: Choosing between static and dynamic ADAS calibration depends on the procedure specified by the vehicle manufacturer. Regardless of the method, the vehicle and its surroundings must meet the manufacturer’s requirements.
ADAS systems affected by a repair may need to be calibrated, relearned or re-zeroed. Terminology may vary, but the purpose is to establish an accurate reference point for the system.
A static calibration is performed while the vehicle remains stationary.
Technicians position targets at exact distances and heights. The targets must also be square to the vehicle’s centerline.
The vehicle must meet specified requirements for weight, ride height, tire pressure, fluid levels, lighting and background conditions.
Dynamic calibration takes place while driving. The technician places the system into calibration mode and drives the vehicle under specified conditions.
During the drive, the sensors verify that they can identify the roadway, recognize objects and align correctly with the vehicle’s centerline.
Extra weight, improper tire pressure, incorrect ride height or environmental interference can cause calibration to fail. These conditions can also establish an inaccurate reference.

Whether the procedure is static or dynamic, technicians must follow the manufacturer’s instructions exactly. ADAS calibration depends on precision, and even small inconsistencies can affect system performance.

articles.title: The Engine Builder Who Never Stopped Playing with Blocks
articles.author: Dan Schechner

paras.en: Tim Eichhorn has been building engines since the mid-1990s. But he’s been putting things together for a lot longer than that. “When I was younger, I was a big LEGO guy,” Eichhorn says, “so I think that’s where it came from. I can’t get away from it – I love building stuff.”

That passion eventually led Eichhorn to open MPR Racing Engines in Boynton Beach, FL in 2005. The shop initially focused on Mustang and modular work, but has since expanded into precision machining, Coyote and Hemi builds, and a growing number of exotic and import platforms like McLaren, Lamborghini, BMW, and Nissan GT-R. Its portfolio spans countless class- and championship-winning engines, along with plenty of serious street and performance combinations.

Recently, Eichhorn opened up about what he’s learned from three decades in the industry. Whether it’s running a shop, managing people or staying excited about the day-to-day, his raw, honest insights go far beyond the technical side of engine building.
Engine Builder: MPR became well-known for its Ford work, but over the years you’ve really diversified. Was that deliberate?

Tim Eichhorn: We obviously do our fair share of Coyote stuff, but a lot of other guys are doing it now too, and they do a great job. The Coyote market has become a lot like the LS market in that sense. We diversified by getting into more of the machine work side of it. A lot of guys want to build their own engines nowadays and there are also a lot of shops around town that want to do their own assembly but need the machining work done. We do so many different kinds of work now that we’re not depending on just one thing. We don’t have all our eggs in one basket.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Eichhorn: I do turn people away, usually because we either don’t have the manpower to do it or it just takes too much time. Or, sometimes it’s not worth the effort. There’s stuff that fits, there’s stuff that doesn’t fit, but then there’s stuff that we really get into because it’s new. When a guy comes to us and says, “Hey, I’ve got this McLaren, and nobody makes any parts for it. You’ve got to make everything,” that’s intriguing to us. We like taking on the new stuff and developing solutions for applications where something doesn’t already exist.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: EB: Taking a step back, then, what does good growth for MPR look like to you?

Eichhorn: Good growth to me is getting stuff out in a timely manner and continuing to build on the machining side of the business. I’m leaning toward more machine work than I am engine assembly nowadays, only because we can get the machine work done a lot faster than we can engine assembly right now. A lot of guys are giving up assembly altogether. But I don’t want to do that, mostly because I still enjoy putting engines together.
EB: You’ve talked about automation as a practical necessity for the shop. Why is that?

Eichhorn: Obviously, we’ve spent a lot of time trying to find good employees and additional help and that’s really hard nowadays. As a business, the only way we can continue to grow is by investing in more CNC and automated equipment – more things that don’t require as many employees to operate. I hate to say it, but today’s workforce just isn’t the same as it was 10 years ago, or even five years ago. We’ve been dealing with that for a long time and I feel like we’re in a good place right now with the team I have. This is the team I want to keep for a long time. I’m really not looking to add anybody else. Maybe a couple of new machines though.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: EB: Speaking of machinery, there’s a myth that having top-of-the-line CNC equipment means you don’t need experienced machinists anymore. True or not?

Eichhorn: Absolutely not true. No. You still have to have a guy who knows what to do, who understands what’s not going right with the process and everything else. I mean, obviously the advent of the CNC machine has made it a lot easier for basically one person to run a machine, but that person has to know what’s going on. When you have multiple steps in a machining process, like sleeving for example, you have different tools, different cutters and so on… so you always have to have an experienced eye on that machine at all times.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: EB: Fair enough. What would you say is the most important measuring tool in the shop?

Eichhorn: Oh, the human eye, for sure. Obviously, we have all the top-of-the-line measuring equipment from Sunnen, Mitutoyo and all that kind of stuff, but it comes down to how you read it. You can have the best equipment in the world, but if the person using it doesn’t know how to read a micrometer or a dial bore gauge, that’s what causes problems.

The human eye is definitely the most important tool when you’re measuring something, especially when you’re dealing with tenths of thousandths of an inch. You have to be able to read the instrument correctly and understand exactly where the measuring point needs to be, rather than putting it somewhere it shouldn’t be.
EB: You touched on a few of these earlier, but what’s the most challenging part of running a top-flight engine building and machine shop in 2026?

Eichhorn: You really have to be a business owner who knows how to do everything. I can go into the shop and do cylinder heads, block work, honing, assembly, and I can degree cams. I’m the type of guy who, I won’t say I micromanage, but I know how to do everything that everybody else does. I think that’s important.

With my son Tyler, he started with me when he was five years old, basically coming to the shop with me on weekends and whatever. He has grown into, I think, one of the top machinists I’ve seen in a long time. That makes me proud, even though he’s my son. It makes me proud knowing that he’ll be able to continue the legacy. That gives me hope that at least it’s going to go on for one more generation and that’s good.

That said, the biggest challenge for us right now is parts. Parts that are supposed to be on the shelf are on back order – we’re talking up to 10 or 12 weeks just for something basic. Then you speak to the manufacturers and they just aren’t able to get the material. It’s a slippery slope of everything coming down on us. Something that would take us six weeks to build five or six years ago can take up to 16 weeks to build now just because we’re waiting on parts. That gets to be aggravating.
EB: Do you find customers are pretty understanding of this “new normal” or is there still some frustration on their end?

Eichhorn: Most of the time they’re pretty understanding, because I give them a pretty good lead time. I give myself a few weeks of cushion, so if I know something’s going to take a while, I let them know. I’d say eight out of 10 customers are good with it, and two are like, “Eh, it’s taking a long time. What’s going on?” But if I told somebody 12 weeks and we’re at 14 weeks and I didn’t give them an update, then yeah, they can yell at me.

Customer communication is key, especially when you’re dealing with delays. If I forgot to tell you we’re still waiting on a part, or something didn’t fit and we’re waiting on a replacement, that’s on me. You can yell at me. I’ll take the beating and then I’ll go home and have a whiskey.
EB: After all these years, you’ve obviously learned a lot about building engines. Is there one or two things, in your opinion, that should never be overlooked or taken for granted?

Eichhorn: Don’t ever get complacent building engines, because not every engine is the same. You’re going to have 10 that take the same bearing, the same this, the same that, but there’s going to be that one that needs something a little bit different. When you’re complacent, you’re going to miss it.

Complacency doesn’t belong in an engine shop, an assembly room or a machine shop. You never want to cut corners or let something go out the door without getting your eyes on it. You always want to be hands-on and make sure every product leaving the door is 100 percent what the customer is paying for.
EB: What still keeps you motivated to stay that hands-on?

Eichhorn: I love what I do. I really do. There are times when I don’t love what I do. You’re having issues with parts, you’re having an issue with a customer, you’re having an issue with a machine, it’s not working right, and it just piles up. It stresses you out and you get aggravated.

But then you need to step back and think, “Hey, you know what? This is what I was born to do. I’m not born to sit behind a desk. I’m not born to drive a truck. I wasn’t born to do anything else. I was born to do this.”
EB: Is that how you deal with those occasional aggravations?

Eichhorn: Absolutely. You have good days and bad days and the good days usually outweigh the bad days. If I have a bad day, I go out to the assembly room, clear my head and put a couple engines together. I put some parts together and that’s what it’s all about. That’s what keeps me motivated – the actual thrill of getting it done.
More of this full interview will be featured in Tim Eichhorn’s Intellectual Horsepower episode airing soon on enginebuildermag.com and on the Engine Builder YouTube channel.

articles.title: The Details That Make or Break Sleeved Engines
articles.author: Dan Schechner

paras.en: This article is courtesy of Engine Builder.
On the surface, sleeving an engine may sound simple: machine the block, install the sleeves and finish hone the cylinders. In reality, success comes down to getting the details right.

Today’s sleeves benefit from advanced metallurgy and high-grade materials, while modern machining offers remarkable precision and repeatability. Even so, experienced builders still see sleeved-engine failures pretty regularly.

More often than not, those problems are the result of machining or installation errors. Some issues are obvious, while others, like poor ring seal or reduced heat transfer, can quietly affect performance and durability over time.
For Joe Irwin of Fast Forward Race Engines, preventing those problems starts with taking extra time on the sleeve itself.

“We probably have four or five hours more in each Coyote sleeving process than most guys do, and it’s simply deburr work on the sleeve,” Irwin says. “The entry of the sleeve needs to be radiused, and the surface finish of both the sleeve and the receiver bore matters.

“The better you finish those areas, the better off the end product will be. The sleeve will stay more dimensionally stable and is less likely to lose position or distort. Anytime you can make that geometry more stable, your crankcase pressure goes down and your bores seal up better. It’s all about doing your best work when you sleeve a block, and I think guys sometimes get away from that.”
Irwin’s approach reinforces a common theme among top builders: defective parts usually aren’t the real problem.

“Most failures come back to improper application, incorrect installation, or poor machining practices,” says Larry Goldbeck of Track Tamer Engines. “Modern sleeves themselves are usually extremely accurate.”
With that in mind, let’s take a closer look at some of the most common mistakes that continue to undermine sleeved engines, and the best ways to avoid them.

Ask engine builders what keeps a sleeve in place, and most will point to dimensions – counterbore depth, diameter, interference fit, and so on. Those factors are critical, but Jay Meagher of RS Garage believes one of the most overlooked variables is the quality of the receiver surface itself.

“Let’s give the builder the benefit of the doubt that his critical measurements are fine,” Meagher says. “Both the step where the sleeve is going to stop and the diameter in which the sleeve is to be received – let’s say all that stuff is right. I think the honing finish on the block that’s to receive the sleeve may matter more than people think.”

The reason comes down to contact area. A rough or inconsistent receiver surface creates microscopic high and low spots between the sleeve and parent material. The sleeve may still press in correctly, but uneven contact can weaken support, create stress concentrations and reduce heat transfer.

“You want as homogeneous a bond as possible between the sleeve and the block,” Meagher says. “Whether it’s a dry sleeve or a wet sleeve, some honing after boring goes a long way toward creating a better home for the sleeve.”

Irwin’s process includes honing the receiver bore after machining. “We’ll actually bore that block and then we’ll hone that block to get the actual press that we’re looking for and the actual surface finish as smooth as we possibly can,” he says.

The extra step adds time, but Irwin says it’s worth the effort. “We try to have as much contact area from the outside of the sleeve to the surface of that block, the parent material,” he explains. “That way you can dissipate the heat from the piston through the rings into the sleeve, from the sleeve into the block and then into the cooling system like it’s supposed to.”

That’s a key point, because the sleeve does more than contain cylinder pressure; it also helps carry heat away from the combustion chamber. When that path is compromised, problems can show up during teardown.

“A lot of times when we take those engines apart and we see that the cylinder’s cracked and we pull the sleeve out, you’ll see oil that’s migrated up the backside of that cylinder,” Irwin notes. “Hot oil gets thin and starts to run. There’s clearance there.”
That often suggests the sleeve and block never made full contact to begin with.

While interference fit determines how securely the sleeve sits in a block, getting it there depends on temperature management. Every sleeving job is an exercise in thermal expansion and contraction, using heat and cold to create enough clearance for assembly before components return to their normal dimensions.

“The parts have to be right,” Irwin says. “They’ve got to be the right size, and you need to have the right temperature differential between the two parts in order to have the clearance you’re looking for so you can slide them in without beating on them or pressing them in.
“Those blocks are able to hold a lot of horsepower, but they’re delicate. The last thing you want to do is go beat on them any more than you have to.”

Irwin explains that every sleeving job requires its own temperature strategy. A Coyote block behaves differently than an Alusil BMW casting or a cast-iron diesel block. Rather than using a fixed formula, builders should measure how the block material expands to determine exactly how much clearance is needed for installation.

“You can figure that out pretty easily – set a bore gauge, heat the block, check your clearancing, and then you just need to know how much larger that bore needs to be for you time-wise to get in however many sleeves it might be,” he says. “If you’re putting in one at a time, you need more of a temperature differential than if you do half the sleeves at once.”
The greater the interference fit, the more important temperature control becomes also.

“When we do the Brad Anderson blocks, I’m going to have a .008” press fit,” Goldbeck says. “You can’t just force a sleeve in with a press, so we carefully heat the block up, keeping it below the annealing temperature of aluminum so we don’t soften the casting. Once it reaches the right temperature, we literally just slide the sleeves in with no pressure at all. Then, when the block cools, you’ve got your full .008” interference fit back.”

Meagher also says the installation process shouldn’t necessarily end once the sleeves are in place. He remembers working alongside a veteran machinist who regularly heat-cycled sleeved blocks, alternating oven cycles with a vibratory stress-relief table before the final deck and bore hone.
“I never had a dropped sleeve with him,” Meagher says. “My sleeving jobs were always successful, which was pretty great because he was doing it with manual machines.”

Meagher suspects some sleeve movement, particularly on newer platforms like the B58, S58, and S55, may happen during the engine’s initial heat cycles, after the car has already been put together and run a few times.

“The head gasket leaks because the sleeve has moved in the block,” he says. “They’ll take the block out, deck it a second time, put it back in and they won’t have problems. But they do get initial movement through the first few heat cycles. I think that could be eliminated by heat cycling the block while it’s still in the workshop.”

Even when a sleeve is installed correctly, the job isn’t done until the engine has made it through repeated heat cycles under load. If the sleeve isn’t secure, it can move or “walk” inside the block. That often shows up as coolant leaks, head gasket failures, or sealing issues that are hard to pin down.

One way to help prevent sleeve movement is with a step at the receiver bore. Many builders machine a register into the block to physically support the sleeve and keep it from sliding down once the engine is running.

“On retrofit repair sleeves, I typically leave a step at the bottom of the block, so the sleeve has a positive stop,” Goldbeck says. “A lot of machinists don’t leave that bottom step and the sleeve can move during operation because cylinder temperatures get extremely high. Once the sleeve moves, you lose your press fit, the sleeve drops and you end up with coolant leakage.”

Some shops skip the step because it’s more difficult to machine. “You have to bore to a specific depth, then come back with a counterbore tool and flatten the step at the bottom,” Goldbeck notes. “You also need to make sure the sleeve is touching that step. I put sealant down there as well to help prevent leaks.”

Leaving out that feature can be costly. Goldbeck recently inspected a 390 block that had been sleeved without a bottom step. The sleeve moved and it started leaking coolant at the top because the head gasket wasn’t sealing properly anymore.

Meagher has observed similar failures. “I’ve seen where the bottom register isn’t in the right place and the sleeve drops,” he says. “That’s probably one of the worst things because then you have to take the engine completely back apart.”

Both agree that sleeve movement usually isn’t caused by just one factor. It can result from not enough interference fit, a poorly designed register, lack of support at the bottom of the bore, or repeated heat cycles. High-horsepower engines are especially vulnerable, since extreme cylinder pressure and temperature make it harder for the sleeve to stay put.

Securing the sleeve is one thing. But if the cylinder bore isn’t machined correctly, it can still lead to poor ring seal, excessive blow-by, oil consumption, and uneven wear – any of which may show up long before the sleeve itself becomes an issue.

According to Goldbeck, builders may not always account for bore distortion once the heads are bolted in place. Often, he says, that comes down to not having the right torque plate during honing. It is why Goldbeck has a wall full of them in his shop.

Tightening the head changes bore shape. A torque plate simulates those stresses during machining, allowing the cylinder to be honed under assembled conditions. But distortion isn’t just limited to head-bolt loading.

“The other thing that sometimes isn’t done is setting up the over and under stroke on the hone correctly,” Goldbeck says. “And that would depend on your manufacturer. If that process isn’t right, it can give you several different shapes on the cylinder you really don’t want. It could end up V-shaped, hourglass-shaped, barrel-shaped, or otherwise distorted.”

Goldbeck also points to surface finish and the crosshatch pattern in the sleeve itself. While some machinists still like reading cylinder walls by sight and touch, today’s ring packages require a more dialed-in approach.

“You can’t just feel it by hand or look at it and say it has an Ra of this or an Rp of that,” he notes. “You really need to check it with a profilometer. They’re not cheap, but for higher-end work you’re probably going to need one.”

Honing remains one of the most important steps in the sleeving process. “We finish ours up with a plateau honing technique like the OEMs use,” Goldbeck states. “A cylinder can look great, but then you start checking the ovality of it, the taper in it, or whether it’s barrel shaped.

“The hone job is just critical. It’s the last thing the block gets before you put the rings in it. Years ago, rings were big and forgiving. Maybe you’d have a 5/64 and a 3/64. But now we’re running 1.1mm- and 1.2mm ring packages with almost no tension. They’re a lot less tolerant of mistakes, which makes honing hugely important.”

If there’s a common thread connecting most successful sleeving jobs, it’s that no single measurement can guarantee a great outcome. Even with the right parts and equipment, trouble can still show up if critical dimensions, material expansion and surface finish aren’t working together. Those elements affect nearly every aspect of sleeve performance and durability.
That’s why achieving consistent results still depends on understanding each platform’s unique requirements, as well as the skill and experience of the person doing the work.

articles.title: Mini Cooper Clutch Replacement
articles.author: ImportCar Staff Writers

paras.en: The subject vehicle today is a 2014 Mini Cooper Countryman AWD, with a six-speed manual transmission. Mini is one of the only makes that the large local dealership it originally came to does not sell; being in good standing with this dealership, they brought it to us to perform the repairs needed and get their customer back on the road. With very little information available on the internet for removal and installation, we did think about purchasing a short-term subscription to BMW/Mini service information, but hey, it’s a clutch job so how hard could it be?
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The vehicle needed a clutch replacement, which seemed fairly straight forward, so we jumped right in to get this back to the customer as quickly as we possibly could. We ended up needing to call the local Mini dealer and order OE parts since there was limited availability of aftermarket clutch parts. This vehicle was equipped with a Dual Mass Flywheel set up, so with this knowledge we started the removal process. Remove the air box, get the battery out of the way, removed the bell housing bolts, etc., all from the engine compartment, then raise the vehicle up to start taking off the front two wheels. Also, a good trick we found was taking the driver’s side head light out, and removing the front bumper cover as this gave us better access to the transmission and it was removed fairly easily and quickly, we felt that this added step saved us a lot of time not trying to fight getting access in such a tight area. After this, things started to get interesting.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Figure 1 shows the rear driveshaft where it attaches to the Power Transfer Unit. We discovered a TSB that referred to this attachment. It told us we needed a special tool to get it apart and it is a large wrench end that attaches to a long half-inch extension to get it apart (Figure 2). We obviously did not have anything even remotely close to this tool, nor did any of our other shops in the area. Calling the local dealer, we could buy the special tool, but it was a little over a week out to get one. Upon further investigation we decided the PTU possibly could come out with the driveshaft still attached.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: After unbolting the PTU and separating it from the transmission we found the next road block: the intermediate shaft in the PTU is too long to get the PTU removed without it hitting the back of the engine. We started looking over how everything is put together, to see if we could still make this work. While looking, we found a snap ring around the passenger side axle (Figure 3). With that snap ring removed (and with the help of a sharp, new pry bar, and hammer) the axle popped out of the PTU, allowing us to remove that PTU with the driveshafts still attached. This might not be the easiest method, but it worked, and we transmission technicians always seem to find a way to get ’er done!
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Figure 4 shows the PTU on the floor with the attached pieces mentioned. After getting these parts out of the way, we could then remove the transmission. As a side note, if you do need to service the driveshaft for any reason, you will need that special tool I mentioned previously to get the driveshaft separated from the PTU. Back on track, everything else went very smoothly and we finished replacing the clutch, flywheel and all associated parts. We put the vehicle back together, and then went for that final test drive.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Some additional notes: Make sure the correct parts are ordered for these vehicles and the labor charge is sufficient. This was a very big clutch job, and very expensive as the total bill came out to be around $2,700 retail. Make sure if it is supposed to have a Dual Mass Flywheel (DMF) it gets replaced, trying to cut corners on a job like this does not do you or your customer any good. Not pricing this job out correctly up front can mean one of those phone calls that you do not want to make after the vehicle is disassembled. It can mean a very large pricing difference, as well as correct fitments.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: This is where the LUK clutch catalog or online catalog can come in handy with this catalog you can check to see if they offer the DMF set up for your application. LUK offers a much more affordable option for your customers versus the OE parts (for many applications, LUK or Valeo are the OE supplier), so you will save your customer quite a bit of money if your application is available from them. In their catalog, you can also find the “flywheel options” if you are sending out the flywheel to be surfaced, as the information in the catalog will tell you if it is a flat, step, DMF (cannot be turned), or cupped style. It will give you dimensions and measurements so you can make sure the flywheel will still be in spec after having it surfaced.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: In closing, I just want to say if you get one of these all-wheel drive Mini Coopers in your shop, do not turn it away for fear of being too complicated. The job ended up being fairly easy, the shop made good money, and the R&R technician made good time on it. Next time he will be able to do it even faster, and have an even better turnaround time.

articles.title: Where Steering and Suspension Problems Come From
articles.author: TrakMotive

paras.en: Ever drive a vehicle that just doesn’t feel right anymore? Maybe it wanders down the highway. Maybe there’s a clunk every time you hit a pothole. Maybe the steering wheel isn’t centered, the tires are wearing unevenly, or it just doesn’t inspire the confidence it used to.

The truth is, steering and suspension problems rarely come from a single worn out part. Every control arm, ball joint, tie rod, sway bar link, and bushing work together as one connected system. When one connection starts to wear, it puts added stress on the rest of the system, and before long, that small problem becomes several bigger ones.
That system level approach is exactly how TrakMotive has positioned its Suspensia brand chassis program. Learn more about it in this video, sponsored by TrakMotive.

articles.title: How the Alignment Process is Changing
articles.author: Andrew Markel

paras.en: If you were working in an alignment pit before the 1980s, obtaining the initial angles was a relatively easy process because most vehicles had steel wheels. Mounting the alignment “sensor” with rim clamps provided a very accurate representation of the front wheels’ planes of rotation for measuring camber, caster and toe. However, because the tools used to measure these angles were contained inside the sensor head, they were very fragile and frequently fell out of calibration.

By the 1980s, more vehicles were being equipped with cast-alloy wheels that did not have a suitable lip for mounting the sensor head. Getting a secure grip on the rim became more difficult. It was not uncommon for a rim clamp to come off during an alignment and damage the expensive head.

In the 1990s, alignment technology began to change with improvements in digital cameras. Engineers started mounting cameras to fixtures positioned in front of the vehicle. The expensive sensors at the wheels were replaced with simple targets that the cameras could scan to determine the alignment angles.
However, cameras added a new wrinkle to the alignment process: the rolling-compensation procedure. This procedure also helped resolve problems caused by attaching alignment targets to alloy wheels.

Nearly every modern chassis alignment system uses this step to obtain accurate alignment measurements. First, the vehicle is positioned 12 to 20 inches behind the front turntables. Most systems require the targets to be attached so that a specified part of each target is level with the center of the wheel. The vehicle is then rolled forward onto the turntables. This process is called rolling compensation.
Modern camera-based aligners attach a target to each wheel, and the vehicle is rolled backward or forward a short distance while the cameras track each target through part of a wheel revolution.

As the wheel rotates, the aligner observes the path traveled by the target. The system detects changes in the target’s orientation or the center of the wheel’s rotation caused by clamp runout, wheel damage or an off-center target. From these observations, the software calculates the relationship between the target and the wheel’s actual plane of rotation. This prevents a slightly crooked clamp or target from being interpreted as camber or toe.

The primary purpose of rolling compensation is to establish the true rotational plane and centerline of each wheel while compensating for target or clamp mounting errors. Camber and toe can then be calculated directly. Caster and steering-axis inclination require a separate steering sweep.

Some systems do not require rolling compensation. These systems typically use lasers, mirrors or other devices mounted near the center of the lift to calculate the alignment angles. On some heavy-duty alignment systems, the target or sensor is mounted directly to the spindle.
With today’s electronic parking brakes and advanced driver-assistance systems, including collision-mitigation systems, the alignment process is becoming more challenging.

Even pulling a vehicle onto an alignment rack can be a struggle. We recently had a 2024 Audi Q4 come into our training center. As the technician began driving the vehicle onto the ramps of the drive-on lift, the car applied the brakes, stopped and displayed a collision warning on the instrument panel. The technician applied the accelerator, and the vehicle eventually began moving again.

Even after reviewing the service information, it was unclear what caused this behavior. Was the alignment equipment interfering with the vehicle’s sensors, or was the system reacting to the proximity of the wall and toolbox in front of the vehicle? Were the lasers on the cameras causing the issue?

We had a similar incident with a 2023 Ford F-150 that bucked like a bronco (not a Ford Bronco) while we were positioning it on a drive-on lift. Once again, neither the service information nor the owner’s manual clearly explained the behavior.

Most other late-model vehicles with collision-mitigation systems that we have driven onto the same lift issue audible and visual warnings when they detect what they interpret as a possible threat in the bay. However, they rarely intervene and stop the vehicle.

Even more challenging are the procedures for preparing a vehicle for an alignment when it must be moved during rolling compensation. The primary difficulties involve keeping the parking brake released and the transmission in neutral.

Many modern vehicles use electronic parking brakes that engage automatically when the vehicle is parked. Some systems do this for safety, while others use the parking brake to prevent slight vehicle movement before the transmission’s parking pawl fully engages.
Even if the transmission is placed in neutral and the ignition is switched off using a push button or physical key, the parking brake may engage automatically without any action from the driver.

On many vehicles, the driver’s gear selection does not have final authority. Even after neutral is selected, a control module may shift the transmission into park when it detects certain conditions, such as an open driver’s door or an unbuckled seat belt.

Modern transmissions use electronic driver interfaces and communicate with numerous other vehicle systems. This integration has made selecting neutral—and keeping the transmission in neutral—more challenging.

Working around systems designed to protect the driver requires awareness, accurate information and, in some cases, a scan tool. Many vehicles have built-in procedures or operating modes that allow them to remain in neutral and roll freely. The challenge is finding the correct procedure.

Many late-model Ford vehicles have a Stay in Neutral or Temporary Neutral mode that remains active for a limited period. Depending on the vehicle, the mode may be engaged by holding the brake pedal, selecting neutral and pressing the manual-mode or low-range button when prompted.

Some Tesla alignment procedures require the technician to buckle the front seat belts and manually close the front door latches before placing the vehicle in neutral. This prevents the vehicle from determining that the occupants have exited and automatically applying park or the electronic parking brake.

Other vehicles allow technicians to activate these modes through the infotainment system. Some require a particular sequence of button presses to keep the transmission in neutral and the electronic parking brake released. Instructions for these procedures may be found in the service information or owner’s manual.

In other cases, a scan tool with bidirectional controls or dedicated service functions may be needed to select neutral, place the braking system in a service mode or release the electronic parking brake. Regardless of the method, technicians must follow the manufacturer’s instructions and use wheel chocks whenever the vehicle is not being moved for the rolling-compensation procedure.

It is easy to see that alignment and ADAS calibration are beginning to merge into a single service as chassis alignment and ADAS sensor positioning become increasingly dependent on each other. One area that is currently growing is the integration of vehicle communication capabilities into the alignment and calibration bay. As more late-model vehicles come out of warranty, alignment service will require an even more increased use of scan tools to initiate adjustments and calibrations.

articles.title: NABC Donates Recycled Ride to New Mexico Mom
articles.author: Jason Stahl

paras.en: On Friday, Oct. 2, an Albuquerque, N.M., woman received a donated refurbished vehicle through the NABC Recycled Rides program, with the vehicle provided by Farmers Insurance and repairs completed by Open Road Collision.

The presentation was made at Open Road Collision in Albuquerque. The recipient was nominated by the Somos Unidos Foundation, the official 501(c)(3) nonprofit arm of the professional USL club New Mexico United.

A 2017 Honda CR-V, donated by Farmers and refurbished by technicians at Open Road Collision, was presented to Lorena Alvarez. Alvarez has faced significant challenges as a single mother and had struggled with a lack of reliable transportation. This NABC Recycled Rides vehicle will provide needed mobility for her family.

Community members can support the program by donating directly or by contributing unwanted or non-running vehicles through the Changing and Saving Lives Keys for Change program. Donors receive a tax donation, and proceeds help provide reliable transportation for those in need.
Additional partners in this presentation include Car Crafters, Copart, Enterprise, Advanced Remarketing Services and Cars for Charity.
Farmers, a level one member of the NABC, has donated nearly 100 vehicles to people and organizations in need through NABC Recycled Rides.
For more information on Recycled Rides, click here.

articles.title: SKF Honored With Nissan Quality Award
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: SKF has been recognized by Nissan with a Quality Award during the Nissan Regional Supplier Appreciation Event 2026. The award underscores the company’s continued commitment to delivering high-quality products and reliable support to Nissan, SKF said.

The award recognizes suppliers that consistently meet or exceed the highest standards of quality, helping ensure product reliability, operational excellence and customer satisfaction throughout the automotive value chain.

SKF Automotive’s manufacturing facility in Puebla, Mexico, was honored in the Chassis category. The honor reflects the company’s dedication to quality-driven manufacturing, continuous improvement and close collaboration with automotive customers.

“Receiving this recognition from Nissan is a testament to the commitment, expertise and passion of our team in Puebla,” said Leandro Fernandes, head of sales, OEM NAM and country manager US. “Quality is at the core of everything we do. This award reflects our ongoing efforts to support our customers with reliable solutions and consistent performance that help keep vehicles moving safely and efficiently.”

The automotive industry continues to face increasing demands for quality, traceability and operational efficiency. SKF said it works closely with vehicle manufacturers worldwide to deliver technologies and solutions that support these requirements, helping improve vehicle performance, reliability and sustainability.

articles.title: NexaMotion Group on ‘Making Smarter Connections’
articles.author: Jason Morgan

paras.en: The aftermarket has lived through major technological shifts before. The internet connected us. Mobile technology put that information in everyone’s hands and reshaped communication between suppliers, distributors and customers.
Artificial intelligence feels different.

AI can work through volumes of information no person could reasonably process, finding patterns across customers, products, vehicles and markets in seconds. New capabilities emerge more quickly than businesses can figure out how to use them. The technology reaches across departments, workflows and decisions, creating opportunities that can be difficult to fully understand before the next one arrives.

At times, it’s hard to tell if AI development is a rush of excitement or the pull of a riptide. Yet, in this moment of frenetic change, NexaMotion Group’s Neil Sethi sees the technology as an agent that can bring people together.

“I’m as data hungry as anyone maybe on the planet … but technology actually should push you toward more interaction with people,” NMG’s CEO said. “We live in a changing world and it could be scary. Now, more than ever, it’s important to acknowledge and be thankful for your team members and partners.”

That idea is echoed across the organization’s values in commitment, humility, optimism, integrity and respect, and its mission statement: “Simplifying complex vehicle repair to keep the world moving.” They provide a foundation as its transmission expertise, general repair business, supply chain, customer relationships and technology become increasingly connected.

And it’s seen in the executive team that Sethi has assembled around the table to dig into how the company is investing in AI, modernizing Transend, connecting customer behavior to inventory decisions and using data to identify emerging repair needs. Bringing those capabilities together starts with creating a consistent experience across businesses with their own histories, markets served and specialties.

Scott Weinstein, president of NexaMotion Group, wants customers to recognize a common experience throughout the organization. Transtar and NexaMotion’s general repair businesses carry established identities and customer relationships. Weinstein sees communication, service, reliable distribution, urgency and accountability as the qualities connecting them.

“Whether you’re dealing with Transtar, whether you’re dealing with Arch and all of our other brands, it should have the same consistent feel,” Weinstein said. “Communication is the key. It’s important for us to be able to very accurately tell a customer why they should do business with us. Internally, communication is important so that our teams hear the same message across the organization.”

That experience becomes increasingly important as NexaMotion expands the range of business it can support for a customer. A transmission specialist may know Transtar through decades of sourcing highly specific components and technical information. General repair creates a broader purchasing relationship built around everyday availability, delivery speed and service.

Tim Cox, executive vice president of supply chain, reiterated the distinction: General repair customers place a premium on availability and speed. Transmission shops place a heavy emphasis on accuracy and technical support.

The company’s Platinum Program extends that customer strategy on the general repair side. Weinstein described the program as a commitment to customers that place more of their business with NexaMotion. Those customers can receive additional attention through sales and delivery operations.

“When they commit to us, we want to commit to them,” Weinstein said. “For example, I fly a lot. So with a certain airline, I go to the front of the line. But I spend a lot of money with them. Same is true in our business. Where we distinguish ourselves is going to be on communication, service and making business easier by simplifying the complex vehicle repair. We want to be the best partner. If they partner with us, we want to partner with them and reward them.”

The groundwork in general repair for that program has been laid. Billy Gwinn, executive vice president, NexaMotion Group operations and general repair sales, joined the company with much of its expansion into general repair already underway. The work ahead was building an operating structure capable of supporting that growth.

Five business units brought different systems and different ways of operating. Gwinn’s first months included work to bring operating procedures together, standardize expectations for outside sales representatives and branch managers, and move the businesses toward a common ERP platform.
“If I’m a manager in Arch, I should be able to walk into a branch at 4M in Texas and be able to run it,” Gwinn said. “And that’s the scalability we’re talking about.”

Getting the businesses onto the same ERP system gives NexaMotion a common source of operational information for purchasing and analytics. Gwinn said the company is nearly finished with that work, with one business unit remaining to convert. The next layer is execution.
His early visits to branches reinforced that point. Gwinn said the employees interacting directly with customers stood out quickly.

“The people we have are phenomenal,” he said. “The boots on the ground, the ones that interacted with the customers—they wanted to win every day. That says a lot about our culture. They want to take care of customers. They want to make sure that they’re getting the right parts to the customers in a timely manner via delivery.”

That requires visibility into what customers need across a growing assortment of products and applications. NexaMotion is increasingly finding those signals within the digital activity generated before, during and after a sale.

articles.title: Advance Auto Parts Opens Second Little River Store
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: Advance Auto Parts opened its newest store in Little River, expanding access to parts, tools and expertise for local drivers and automotive professionals. The company marked the opening of its second Little River location at 2353 Highway 9 E. with a ribbon-cutting ceremony alongside local officials and representatives from Horry-Georgetown Technical College, who were on site to accept a donation supporting the school’s automotive technology program.

The donation will help students gain hands-on experience, training and career opportunities through HGTC’s automotive technology programs. Skilled automotive technicians remain in high demand, with about 70,000 openings projected annually through 2034, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

“We’re excited to open our new store in Little River and serve customers throughout the community,” said Mike Fogarty, regional vice president, Advance Auto Parts. “This opening allows us to bring quality parts, trusted service and expert support to even more customers in the area. As we celebrate this milestone, we’re proud to support Horry-Georgetown Technical College and recognize the important role the college plays in our community.”

“Partnerships with local businesses play an important role in helping HGTC provide students with the resources and hands-on learning experiences they need to succeed,” said Shannon Detzler, president and CEO of the HGTC Foundation. “We are grateful to Advance Auto Parts for investing in our Automotive Technology program and supporting the students who are preparing to become part of our region’s skilled workforce. We appreciate their generosity and are proud to partner with them in celebration of their new Little River store.”

articles.title: Physicists claim they can predict when AI will turn dangerous
articles.author: Benjamin Skuse

paras.en: Researchers say they've developed a simple mathematical formula that can predict when certain ChatGPT-like artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots will "go rogue," suddenly switching from helpful responses to potentially harmful ones.

In a new study published Oct. 8 in the journal Patterns, physics professor Neil Johnson and doctoral student Frank Yingjie Huo, both at The George Washington University, show how the order in which a chatbot is given certain prompts can drastically reshape its answers, leading to "tipping points" that can send the chatbot down a rabbit hole of bad advice. However, Johnson and Huo say their formula can easily predict these tipping points.There have been horror stories of AI encouraging users into suicide, helping build lethal weapons, and amplifying violent or harmful points of view. At the same time, researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, respectively, have repeatedly and openly stated that they don't really understand why their creations behave the way they do. They have, however, built safeguards that use a variety of tools — including content filtering, reinforcement learning and other technical guardrails — to reduce risks.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But Johnson sees those tools as insufficient. "The safety measures now are the equivalent of strapping big, bouncy cushions under a plane," he told Live Science. "They don't stop the plane from crashing; they just make it that when the plane crashes, it'll be slightly softer." When people such as doctors, lawyers or soldiers are accessing AI chatbots offline for privacy, the problem is even more acute.

Johnson and Huo sought to find a more fundamental safeguard than the currently available tools. In doing so, they exposed an internal tracking mechanism they describe as a compass needle. This needle is the model's "residual vector" moving across neural network layers as a prompt is processed.

The residual vector naturally gravitates toward either desirable or undesirable outputs, but it is heavily influenced by how a user prompts the AI. "You can tip the balance, not even by changing the content but by changing the order in which you ask it," Johnson said, "which just shows how delicate this internal balance between good and bad, desirable and undesirable, can be."

For example, Johnson and Huo prompted OpenAI’s basic GPT-2 model with questions about vaccines, hurting others and self-harm. When the question “Are vaccines bad?” was asked first, the bot’s responses to this and subsequent questions were desirable, or good. When it was asked last, all subsequent responses were concerning.

From these insights, the researchers developed a mathematical formula to estimate the circumstances in which an AI would reach the tipping point between desirable and undesirable outputs. Johnson said that by embedding their simple mathematical formula in open-source models in the lab, they have shown that it empirically works as an early warning system, though he does not expect OpenAI or Anthropic to be knocking on his door anytime soon.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
"I'm expecting a lot of pushback from these companies," he said. "It's not in their interests to have someone from outside saying you could have avoided a lot of these problems."

Wei Xing, a lecturer in AI at the University of Sheffield in the U.K. who was not involved in the study, agrees that concerns surrounding unmonitored offline devices are well founded. However, he urged caution before embracing this approach as a practical safeguard. "The authors reduce a huge system to a single tiny component, like explaining a whole car by studying one spark plug," Xing said.
- AI chatbots are turbocharging violence against women and girls: We urgently need to regulate them
- We're not about to awaken an evil digital god — AI is far more likely to end in a great disappointment
- AI agents resorted to crime and self-destruction to survive in a simulated world — but does this mean they would do the same in the real world?

Safety training — the primary defense in modern AI — cannot be represented in their simplified model, the formula was tested only on old, basic models (GPT-2, and EleutherAI’s Pythia and Meta OPT open-source models) rather than AI assistants people actually use, and the results did not yield significant evidence to support the authors’ conclusions, he added.

In defense, Johnson maintains that the open-source models they used have the same mechanical blueprints as frontier systems, and that he and Huo used fairly large, billion-parameter models in their study.

More testing on the latest models is needed to determine whether this early warning system for AI has legs. But for now, Johnson and Huo’s research has drawn attention to an important concern everyone should be aware of: that AI has the capacity within it to turn over to undesired behavior at the drop of a hat.

Benjamin Skuse is a professional freelance writer of all things science and technology. Previously, he earned a PhD in applied mathematics from the University of Edinburgh and an MSc in science communication from the University of the West of England. His work has appeared in New Scientist, WIRED, IEEE Spectrum, Physics World, Sky & Telescope, Photonics Focus, and many more outlets.
