paras.en: Watch the “Someone Out There Loves You (Live From Hoboken),” below.

articles.title: Seth Rogen Watched Curry Barker’s Next Movie, Says It’s “Even Better” Than ‘Obsession’
articles.author: James Hibberd

paras.en: For Obsession writer-director Curry Barker, rolling out a follow-up to the biggest surprise breakout of the year is a pretty daunting task — especially given Barker cast himself in the film’s lead role.
But Seth Rogen says he’s actually seen Barker’s follow-up, Anything But Ghosts, which is released next year.
And The Studio creator claims the film is not only better than Obsession, but that Barker crushes his major feature film on-camera debut.

Writing for Time magazine’s Time 100 package, Rogen described the experience of watching Obsession for the first time in a theater, then added, “I’ve seen Curry’s next film, Anything But Ghosts—and for those of you who, like me, are uncomfortable with this amount of talent in a person so young, I have bad news … it’s even better, and, to add insult to injury, he’s just as good an actor as he is a director.”

Anything But Ghosts stars Barker and his producing partner and Obsession co-star Cooper Tomlinson as two fake paranormal investigators hired by a couple (Bryce Dallas Howard and Aaron Paul) who have a real haunted house. The film was written by Barker and Tomlinson and shot before Obsession was released. Like his hit debut, Ghosts will be distributed by Focus Features.

During Barker’s interview for The Hollywood Reporter‘s cover story on the director’s wild success in June, he was in the middle of editing Ghosts and expressed concern about comparing the film to the rather high bar set by Obsession. “If I’m worried, it’s comparing it to Obsession that’s hard,” he said.

“It’s a buddy comedy, but it’s still going to be scary and messed up,” he said. “You can’t not have these feelings when your first movie is breaking box office records and you’re in your room editing your next movie thinking, ‘Oh my god, did I take this beat from Obsession?’ Thank God I have people around me to ground me and tell me that Anything But Ghosts is good and different, and that’s OK. Nobody wants the same movie twice. So people can expect it to be very different than Obsession, but my voice will still be very strong in it.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Ghosts had a production budget of $5 million — which is rather lavish when compared to the famously frugal $750,000 budget of Obsession. Obsession topped $500 million globally, and is in the awards conversation. It stands as the fifth highest-grossing horror movie of all time globally. The film will be released in May, 2027.

articles.title: Hello, Molly? The $15 Million Bird Kelly Clarkson Coveted Finally Breaks Her Silence (Exclusive)
articles.author: Hilary Lewis

paras.en: I don’t watch television. I mostly read, go to shows, see some clown. So I had only a vague idea of who Kelly Clarkson was. I knew she was on some talent show with Justin Guarini, whom I know from theater work.

On Oct. 10, Ms. Clarkson entered Art of Play, the Brooklyn curiosity shop where I live. She spent less than five minutes here and caused quite a hullabaloo. She asked a sales associate if she could purchase me, Molly, the mascot of the store and was duly informed that while that was impossible, she could contact artist Bliss Kolb to ask for a $15,000 duplicate. Bliss, of course, makes crank-driven mechanical contraptions that imitate living creatures, much like daytime talk show hosts.

The first clue that I wasn’t for sale might have been that I’m mounted on the wall. Other items not for sale in Art of Play include the light fixtures, the commode and the sign that reads, “The Art of Play,” which a number of people also inquire about, nearly all of them gay men. I’m sure Ms. Clarkson also wants an Oompa Loompa, but we don’t sell them either.

Why would a store have an item that’s not for sale? Perhaps Ms. Clarkson has never been to Brooklyn. None of the things in any of the stores here are for sale. They are like the frozen yogurt shop and doll store underneath Barbra Streisand’s house. We are all funded by our parents, some of whom are Barbra Streisand.

Ms. Clarkson posted on X that she “literally was looked at as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me. Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale. But y’all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts’ character in Pretty Woman.”

Although I have not seen Pretty Woman, or any of Garry Marshall’s work other than his excellent performance in Lost in America, I have since viewed the clip she’s referencing and find the comparison perplexing. If 1990 Julia Roberts walked in wearing a cropped white tank top attached to a blue miniskirt with a silver O-ring, I would have jumped into her purse. As the security footage uncovered by podcaster Pablo Torre shows, Ms. Clarkson wore the same dreadful outfit as every other Art of Play customer. Maybe now the owners will listen to my plea for a dress code. Then again, one of them wrote the children’s book Dragons Love Tacos, so I’m not holding my breath. Unless you don’t crank me.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: This is not the first Karen to enter Art of Play. One white woman demanded to talk to the manager about how the $1,200 applause machine wouldn’t clap for her. Another complained after asking for help solving the $185 egg-shaped puzzle, and we joshingly suggested that she “Goop it.”

The online kerfuffle had Clarkson supporters doxxing our owners and sending them death threats, causing the Retail, Wholesale and Department Store Union to issue a formal statement defending us from celebrity-fueled mobbing. America is sadly divided between people who kneel at the altar of television celebrity, and those who want to enter the secret theater in the back of a curiosity shop and see Jay Gilligan’s “Stories About Gravity” magic show.

Before you decide whose side you’re on, let me remind you of what Voltaire wrote about a little animatronic wooden duck from 1764 made by artist Jacques de Vaucanson that could eat, digest and excrete. He said, “Without … Vaucanson’s duck you would have nothing to remind you of the glory of France.” Replace “France” with “America” and “Vaucanson’s duck” with “Kelly Clarkson” and it’s really funny.

Part of why I write is that once you wind me up, I can’t stop. But also to warn other institutions about Ms. Clarkson. The Louvre might want to post extra guards around the Mona Lisa to prepare for her visit.
We have now posted an ironic price tag of $15 million because, by law, we can only do things in Brooklyn with irony. But also because we think Blake Shelton might really buy it for her.

Ms. Clarkson is now doing a residency at a hotel in Las Vegas, a place I am about as likely to visit as Manhattan. I hope she is comforted by whatever wooden toys she’s been able to acquire there, perhaps a Thomas the Tank Engine. It’s not a city for a bird with a wooden worm gear that operates a star gear and eight cams that each operate a lever that controls either one movement or a leather bellows that blows air through a brass whistle whose pitch is varied by a plunger operated by its own lever and cam.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: All of this is a media distraction from what we should really be talking about, which is Palestine. As a wooden toy bird of privilege, I feel a responsibility to use my animatronic voice in allyship with oppressed people, birds, toys, toy birds and bird toys. As another famous wooden toy once said, “There are no strings on me!” Though for $15 million, I’m willing to sing whatever you want.

articles.title: LaRoyce Hawkins Opens Up About His Final ‘Chicago P.D.’ Episode as Kevin Atwater
articles.author: Jackie Strause

paras.en: There was no indication LaRoyce Hawkins, better known to fans as Kevin Atwater, would be leaving Chicago P.D. when the 13th season concluded back in May. Then, over the Fourth of July holiday weekend came the news that he would be departing the series he has starred on since it launched, and now, that final episode has aired.

A fan-favorite and original series star ever since the show premiered with “Stepping Stone” on Jan. 8, 2014, news of Hawkins’ departure quickly became social media chatter. With no official explanation from Hawkins or NBC, speculation turned to money and cost-cutting measures across the industry. Not even until the preview of the episode that aired last week were fans made aware that the Oct. 14 episode (“Don’t Blink”) would be Atwater’s last.

The idea of Atwater leaving Chicago was floated and shot down when Karen Obilom’s Tasha Fox, a fellow officer who attended the police academy with Atwater, announced her intention to leave Chicago and join the police force in Miami in the episode of the same name last October. Fox and Atwater shared a night of passion that resulted in a pregnancy reveal in January episode “On the Way,” and an agreement that they would work on making their relationship real in “The Wicked River,” a few episodes before that season finale. At the start of season 14, the only thing that was clear in the premiere (“Demolition”) was that the baby was coming.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “Don’t Blink” starts in the hospital with the baby, a son, and Atwater and Tasha. As Atwater goes back to work dealing with a robbery, he is an attentive father, calling in during breaks and rushing to the hospital when the baby becomes sick. But he becomes deeply affected by a suspect, a father who had been absent from his son’s life. That gets Atwater thinking about what he wants not just for himself, but for his own son. His stance against the Blue Wall and systemic racism within the police force back in season eight blocked his options for promotion and a raise. In the end, he decides to relocate with Tasha and the baby from Chicago to Atlanta. And the finale in the bar, with colleagues and friends singing “He’s A Jolly Good Fellow” ends Atwater’s Chicago P.D. reign.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: It was a bittersweet moment with many agreeing that the final episode was handled well.

Last year, the Chicago-area native from Harvey spoke with The Hollywood Reporter about Atwater’s evolution and expressed his gratitude, as well as discussing the pressure of representing his hometown. He also shared the honor and privilege he felt being part of the Dick Wolf universe.

Speaking with THR now, a day before his last episode aired, he said he planned to watch the hour in real time for the first time surrounded by family. Hawkins pondered Atwater’s significance and impact.

“Because I grew up watching reruns from shows that were over way before I was born, I wasn’t unaware of the impact that you can still have for generations that you’re not necessarily a part of,” he said. “So now I’m very interested in how we will rediscover and explore Atwater.”

How Chicago P.D. tackled the pandemic is of particular significance. “By the time we remind ourselves about the pandemic period and we unpack how Atwater had to be on the front line as a cop for television, and the way that the Black man and his life seem not to matter as much [then], and to play a character that had to hold the weight of both of those, at the time, I was just ready,” he shared. “I was locked in, and I don’t think I even understood then that this is going to be a capsule of a time period that is going to [represent] a significant shift in TV. It was a significant shift in the nation.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “I’ll never forget how intentional the Dick Wolf team and the powers that be in that universe were about how we told stories after the pandemic, and I was grateful to be instrumental in how we were able to tell those stories,” he added.

Then, after watching his final episode as Atwater, Hawkins took time again to speak with THR about the episode, sharing behind the scenes gems, dishing on everything from the babies who played Atwater’s son to sharing the screen with Jason Beghe one last time, the fan reaction to his exit and stacking the show’s final scene with friends and family to say goodbye.
I was struck by the tenderness and thoughtfulness in the final episode. I don’t think we see cops presented in this light. And I really don’t think we’ve ever seen a Black cop presented like this.
I think that is something that is good to see, especially in today’s world. And when you consider all the characters that have left this show at a high level, nobody really goes out like that.
People on social media were upset when they thought Atwater got shot and might be killed off.
They had to throw that in there just to throw people off. That was crazy. Yeah, my mama was tweaking. My big sister was mad. I was like, Nah, everything is going to work out.

While the episode was really strong in showing how fatherhood can change a man, how parenthood changes a person, it also showed how this other man’s regrets as a father inspires even more responsibility and care in Atwater.

That was the part that got me. I remember when I made notes for the episode before we really got into it. After I read [the script] a few times, one of the things I said was that what I see is this father was absent in his son’s life, and how that affected his son. I see how it’s affecting him. I said, “We don’t really need the bullet. I understand the bullet because you want to be dramatic, but I don’t want it to be the bullet that [connects the dots for Atwater]. I want the case to have a handle [or impact] on me, and for my opinion to reflect, Oh I can have it all. I think I trust Tasha Fox. I think I feel like my son’s going to be amazing.” Could you tell that wasn’t a boy?
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Speaking of babies, we don’t often see fathers showing up at the hospital when the baby is sick. It was tiny things we don’t see represented, that we almost never see represented for a Black father.
That wasn’t a bad way to go. I was proud of it.
What did you feel when you were filming it?

To be honest, there were moments, especially at the beginning of filming, where I had to isolate myself because everybody knew it was my last episode. Imagine the crew and the cast, like everybody, trying to throw in their last conversations or create that last impression. That was throwing me off, because I’m trying to cook on what we got going. I learned that after the first day of shooting. When I noticed people were going to try to take those windows, I was off to the side. I’m pretty social on set, because there’s an energy I like to try to maintain. I like to hop around and engage with people, and I couldn’t really do that because I couldn’t afford to.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: It was the second episode back after a strong hiatus, and it really takes four or five episodes to get warmed up for a season like Chicago P.D. When you’re doing 20 something episodes, you don’t really get warm until episode six. So for us to still just be on [episode] two, I was trying to get my bearings back. I had to isolate myself from distractions.

But I was confident because Jesse [Lee Soffer who played Halstead until exiting in season 10] directed it, and Jesse gave me one of the best notes I’ve probably had since I’ve been on the show. He was like, “Bro, are you hyper aware of yourself? I was like, “Yeah, low key, I am.” And he was like, “You got to stop that. You can’t be so aware of yourself because sometimes I can see you editing your performance within the performance. You have to block out LaRoyce Hawkins’ thoughts and focus on the Atwater’s thoughts.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: You can’t tell me to trust myself. Directors, sometimes [are] like, “Yo, just trust yourself.” But I can trust myself too much, and I can forget there’s a world to get lost in. So it felt great shooting with Jesse directing, because every day was like a masterclass on being specific in the character thoughts. Sometimes the LaRoyce Hawkins thoughts and the character’s thoughts aren’t always aligned. So I was confident that the episode was going to be okay because I remember working hard on set on that.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Shooting it was dope, but it was also bittersweet because certain scenesm, I knew it was going to be my last scene in the bullpen. The last scene that I shot was this scene with me and Sarge [Jason Beghe who plays Sargeant Hank Voight] in his office.
How was that experience character to character with Atwater and Voight, but also actor to actor with you and Jason Beghe?

It was emotional sometimes, to be honest with you. I didn’t even realize until I looked at [the episode] that it looks like I might cry. But that’s how I felt in the moment. To be honest, it was like, Damn, dude. It was my last scene with Sarge. I love Sarge. So the conversation paralleled what was going on with the character and with myself, which was cool. Sarge saying that I can do anything, that I deserve it all, all of those moments felt like it really reflected our real relationship sometimes, and I could tell he was getting emotional sometimes, too. But we just made sure it was fun. That scene was less on paper. I’m not going to say we put humor in it, but we did find moments where it felt real. Like when [Atwater] was like, “Why didn’t you give them my name?” [And Sarge was] like, “Well, I ain’t wanna lose you.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: So there were more smiles on that day we discovered that weren’t on the page at first. [The original scene] almost felt too dramatic. It felt like a scene where I was being dismissed, and we didn’t want it to feel like that. We were able to make some adjustments. Then on the actual [last] day, I had my family and a bunch of close friends pull up. As soon as I was done shooting, a whole bunch of [folks] swarmed the set. It was like I heard trumpets and chants. Everybody marched out. It was pretty dope.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: You said that scene with Sarge was the last one you shot. How did it feel when you filmed the finale in the bar and everyone is telling Atwater, including his boy Ruzek (Patrick John Flueger), one-half of Ruzwater, how much he and you have meant?

That was a dope day. I made sure I filled that scene with homies. That’s what helped it feel so real. I had a big homie fly into Chicago from New York just to be in the background for that scene. I had one of my big homies, Raekwon [Neighbors], he owns the best daycare centers [Raekwon’s Scholastic Daycare Academy] in Cook County, back there. I just filled it with friends. I had my niece in the scene because I wanted real energy, camaraderie, togetherness and family to come through. It wasn’t the last scene we shot. I think we might have shot maybe day three or day four. So it didn’t feel like it was hard to try to conjure up that last moment type of energy because it wasn’t the last moment. I filled the space with loved ones. And that was the best part about that scene, seeing my homies behind me. Seventy-five percent of them were actually friends, and not just background extras.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: I imagine knowing that that scene was the ultimate destination helped with the other scenes because you knew where you were going.

Yeah. Even when I look at the performance, I could tell I was a little bit more locked in and a lot more specific about where I was going and coming from. The episode itself isn’t the most dynamic, but it felt grounded and I was prepared, which is what I like about my final performance. It was real. It wasn’t over the top. But I don’t think anything underwhelmed you, either. It felt pretty solid across the board.

I also like that it felt logical. It felt like, okay, my life has changed. I’m making different decisions, and what I wanted before is not what I want now, because I’m not thinking about just myself. And because I live in Atlanta and am from Chicago, I was thinking to myself, oh, it’s crazy that he’s coming to Atlanta. Especially when it was potentially Miami before.
It’s crazy because I’m actually in Atlanta right now. It’s so funny, but it’s so real.
What do you think of the ship name “Foxwater” for Tasha Fox and Kevin Atwater?

Yeah. What a lot of people don’t know is I came up with all the names. I was the one who started Burgewater [Atwater’s name merged with partner Kim Burgess, who is now married to Ruzek]. I was the first one to be like, yo, let’s just put our names together, because I felt like Atwater was just dope; you can put anything before “water” and make it sound cool. Burgewater was the first one I came up with. Foxwater was easy. I like Tasha Fox [portrayed by Karen Obilom] a lot. I think she was proud of me. She was my personal favorite love interest. I know everybody had their opinions about them all, but I think she was the best one. I think we got it right when we found her.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: I think also that Atwater and Tasha are evenly yoked. They both understand what the job is and where they both come from. Tasha Fox seems like the most compatible woman for Atwater.

Social media reacted very well to the episode itself, with many people agreeing it was beautiful. Some people did share that since Atwater is gone, they are, too; that they would try the show out next week to see what they were doing after Atwater. What are your thoughts?

I’ve been hearing a lot of that, too. And it’s hard because I love the show. I’m a fan of the show minus myself, but it’s because of myself that I’m a part of the show. So there’s a part of me that’s like, yeah, y’all ain’t gotta watch that shit no more. And then there’s a part of me that does want to see the show grow still. Actually it confirms the fact that Atwater is a true vibe [and a] part of the fabric of the show that makes it good. You don’t always know that you’re doing that.
It seems like there is potential in an Atwater show in starting over in Atlanta. Aside from Will Trent, there is no other cop show or procedural based in Atlanta.

Watching the Celeste episodes with Amanda Payton, Atwater seemed kind of dirty to me. Not telling her he was a cop when a case came up involving her and her students didn’t seem right. And then in other episodes, there were so many times when I didn’t always agree with Atwater’s actions, even though it may be part of the job.
You said you haven’t always agreed with Atwater?
Yeah, especially going back through the episodes, I just wasn’t cool with a lot of his actions.

I haven’t been either. And that was a struggle for me too as an actor. Because Atwater is a cop, sometimes the hard part for me was wrapping my mind around how a cop would think and what a cop’s opinions would be. And that didn’t always align with what LaRoyce would do. But that’s why LaRoyce isn’t Atwater. I would infuse and texturize Atwater with what made sense for LaRoyce. Whether it was empathy or some humor here, or I would drop in moments that made sense. But Atwater’s a cop, so you know his opinion would probably disagree with the average Black person based on his intentions to protect and serve.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: In the final moments of the episode when Atwater makes his decision, I thought back to when he was with the psychologist Val Soto [Natalee Louise Linez] and she told him he didn’t make time for himself. I think in this final moment with Atwater, we see him finally doing what he needed to do for himself.
He put himself first obviously because of his family. And you gotta understand Atwater lost his family once upon a time because of the job, and he wasn’t willing to do that this time.
Chicago P.D. airs on NBC Wednesday nights at 10pm ET as part of the One Chicago Block that includes Chicago Med and Chicago Fire.

articles.title: Why Trump and the GOP's billion-dollar midterm blitz isn’t working

paras.en: A billion-dollar war chest was meant to be Republicans' great equalizer heading into a bleak midterm election environment defined by economic frustration, President Donald Trump's unpopularity and fallout from the war in Iran.

From Labor Day through Oct. 14, GOP groups injected more than $740 million into congressional races that will determine control of Congress, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. That includes at least $220 million in spending from Trump-linked groups. Elon Musk has separately given another $276 million to Republican groups since July and helped boost the GOP's Senate Leadership Fund super PAC to a record quarter.

Yet with less than three weeks until the Nov. 3 Election Day, the spending blitz has barely moved the map. Democrats lead in FiftyPlusOne's polling averages across nine of the Senate's most competitive races – Alaska, Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas – little changed from before the Republican spending spree. Minnesota was expected to be solidly blue, making its tight race a concern for Democrats.
And Republican political operatives and independent election observers CNBC spoke with say the money hasn't had the effects its magnitude would be expected to in voter sentiment.

Meanwhile, the broader battlefield continues to deteriorate for Republicans. Democrats are favored to flip the House and remain competitive in the Senate, according to the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, forcing the GOP to burn millions protecting once-safe seats while abandoning former pickup targets.

"Money is an amplifier, not a magic wand," said Neil Newhouse, partner at Republican polling firm Public Opinion Strategies. "You can buy all the airtime in the world, but if the political climate is blowing 30 miles an hour in your face, ad volume alone isn't going to turn the weather around."
Republicans entered the final stretch of the midterm election with unusually deep pockets.

MAGA Inc. had nearly $416 million on hand at the end of August, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Across the broader ecosystem, major Republican organizations had roughly $1 billion available, eclipsing the $579 million available for comparable Democratic groups, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission filings.

Then came Musk — after saying he'd be less involved in this year's election. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO has given more than $276 million to Republican groups since July, including $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund Republican-boosting super PAC and more than $76 million to his own America PAC, according to figures confirmed to CNBC by an America PAC spokesperson. Musk's known federal political giving this election cycle now totals roughly $366 million, making him the largest known donor of the midterms.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And Musk is far from alone. Nine of the 10 largest individual and family donor groups this cycle are Republican-aligned, accounting for 86 cents of every dollar contributed by the top 10, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC records.

"We are watching an unprecedented concentration and scale of political influence and wealth this election cycle," said Hilary Braseth, executive director of OpenSecrets, a nonprofit, nonpartisan group that tracks campaign spending.
AdImpact projects $11.6 billion in political advertising this 2025-2026 cycle, surpassing both the 2022 midterms and the 2024 presidential election.
However, the size of Republicans’ financial advantage may overstate how much advertising that money can actually buy.

That's because much of the GOP's money, particularly spending by Trump-aligned groups, has arrived late and via super PACs, which can pay far more for airtime than candidates. Federal law entitles candidates to broadcasters' lowest unit rate during the final 60 days before a general election; outside groups get no such protection.
It's an edge for Democrats whose candidates have generally outraised their Republican counterparts.

In Dallas, for example, Democrat James Talarico's campaign spent about $2.4 million on local broadcast ads from Oct. 1 through Oct. 14, enough for the average viewer to see his ads about 48 times, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. The pro-Ken Paxton Texas PAC spent about $7.8 million for roughly 81 views per viewer – more than three times as much money for only about 70% more exposure, according to the analysis.

Airtime has become so expensive that Paxton's allies have begun buying ads during national sporting events, calculating that reaching enough Texans through a national broadcast can cost less than buying across the state's local television markets, according to the Associated Press.
"R money advantage not what it appears to be on [the] surface," Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who lost to Paxton in the primary, posted on X on Oct. 5.

Across the nine key Senate battlegrounds identified by the Cook Political Report as of Oct. 1, Republicans led broadcast TV spending in seven and outspent Democrats by 26% overall through Sept. 30, yet generated only 7% more airings.

To be sure, super PACs don't face the same pricing disadvantage on digital ads, where campaigns and outside groups compete on more equal footing. But broadcast TV still dominates political spending, with AdImpact projecting it will account for 48% of the 2026 cycle total.
But the payoff from all that spending has been harder to see in political polls.

Despite more than $113 million spent on negative advertising targeting Talarico since the Texas primary, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data, a Siena College poll released Tuesday showed Talarico leading Paxton 48% to 44%, down only slightly from his six-point lead in September.

In Michigan, after more than $87 million in attacks targeting Democrat Abdul El-Sayed this year, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data, Fox News polling from late September found El-Sayed's favorable rating among registered voters up five points from its early August survey, while Republican Mike Rogers' fell four points.

Part of the challenge is diminishing returns on ads as Election Day nears. Political advertising experts tell CNBC that as campaigns repeatedly target the same small pool of persuadable voters, each additional dollar is less likely to reach someone who has not already heard the message.

"When an undecided voter has already seen 20 negative ads today, the 21st ad doesn't persuade them. It just gets tuned out," said Michael Beckel, money in politics reform director at Issue One. "Their eyes glaze over." Issue One works to reduce the influence of money in politics and has a board that includes former Democratic and Republican elected officials.

Still, some Republicans counter that topline poll movement is the wrong barometer. They say the September cash influx helped keep vulnerable candidates competitive as the political environment deteriorated.

In Texas, Republicans spent $121.5 million on the Senate race in September, up from just $5.5 million over the previous three months, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data, while Musk's America PAC added direct mail and canvassing. Republicans involved in the race said the picture could have been far worse without that support.

"The spending hasn't put Paxton ahead, but it kept a messy race and flawed candidate from becoming an unwinnable one," said a Republican operative involved in the Texas Senate race, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly about the state of the contest.

Maine offers another test. Republicans have poured more than $50 million into the state to support incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, nearly twice Democratic spending, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings. Since early September, FiftyPlusOne's polling average has tightened modestly, from about a three-point advantage for Democrat Troy Jackson in early September to roughly two points now.
The clearest sign that the GOP's cash advantage has stalled, however, is where the money is migrating.

In April, the Senate Leadership Fund announced a record $342 million advertising program across eight states designed to protect the GOP majority and expand the map. Texas, Kansas and Nebraska were not among the states.

Since Sept. 1, the SLF and affiliated groups — according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data — have spent or committed roughly $180 million across those three states, all of which Trump carried by double digits in 2024.
"Outside groups are diverting millions into deep-red territory to build defensive moats, leaving pickup opportunities starved for cash in the final stretch," Beckel told CNBC.
But those emergency defenses have come at a cost, diverting money from races Republicans once hoped to win and forcing national groups to narrow the map elsewhere.

In North Carolina, the Senate Leadership Fund initially pledged $71 million to back Republican Michael Whatley. On Oct. 2, however, the group pulled most of its remaining ad reservations after spending about $32.8 million, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data, as Democrat Roy Cooper continued to hold a double-digit lead in FiftyPlusOne's polling average.
It's a striking retreat in a perennial battleground where Republicans have won every presidential and Senate election since 2008.
The same triage is unfolding in the House.

The Congressional Leadership Fund cut off spending this week for vulnerable GOP Reps. Thomas Kean Jr. of New Jersey and Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa following grim internal polling. The group also shelved efforts to flip Democratic-held seats represented by Reps. Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan and Greg Landsman of Ohio. The spending shifts were first reported by the New York Times.

Those four races had already absorbed about $13.7 million in Congressional Leadership Fund spending through Oct. 14, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. CLF is redirecting roughly $10 million from those races across 16 other districts, according to the Times.
The new spending includes the South Texas seat held by Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz, a district Trump carried by 18 points in 2024. De La Cruz herself won reelection by about 14 points in 2024.

articles.title: Prediction market odds on Tesla-SpaceX merger are above 50% for early 2027

paras.en: Following a Barclays note Wednesday that outlined what a merger between Tesla and SpaceX could look like, prediction market traders increased the odds of an integration above 50% for early 2027.
Odds of a merger happening before March jumped to 56% by Friday morning, up from 29%. Odds for an integration before April and May climbed to similar levels.
The contract asks, "When will Tesla and SpaceX merge?" and will be verified by news outlets and the Securities and Exchange Commission's EDGAR database.
Tesla, known for its electric vehicles, and SpaceX, a rocket and satellite company, have collaborated before. Both are controlled by Elon Musk.

On Thursday, Tesla showed off its long-delayed Roadster, which relies on SpaceX technology to make the vehicle hover. A video showcasing the Roadster's capabilities was also recorded from SpaceX's test site in Texas.
Beyond collaboration, the growing speculation of a merger comes after Musk spoke of "more and more overlap" between Tesla and SpaceX on the EV maker's latest earnings call.

Barclays now expects a merger could be announced before Tesla's annual general meeting, which must take place no later than Dec. 6, 2026. Analyst Dan Levy expects the merger may be proposed as an AI vertical integration, involving Tesla's Robotaxi and Optimus with SpaceX's Grok and Macrohard.
Terafab, the semiconductor project relying on Tesla, SpaceX and xAI, could also be a "key driver" for the merger, Levy added.
"Notably, while we suspect there would be some financial synergies, the true value would be in vertical integration," Levy said.
Earlier Friday, Evercore ISI recommended buying SpaceX shares ahead of its next scheduled earnings release, set for early November, and boosted its 12-month price target on the stock by 20% to $275.
Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

articles.title: Here's who Netflix just brought in to run content — and what it means for the streamer

paras.en: Netflix is shaking up its C-suite in an effort to fix its engagement woes.

On Thursday, the streaming giant announced that former Disney executive Peter Rice will take over as the company's chief content officer, overseeing global content organization, including scripted and unscripted series, film and live events.

Rice is replacing 10-year Netflix veteran Bela Bajaria, who most recently led the company's global content team with a focus on its live sports strategy. Bajaria was initially hired in 2016 to help the streamer launch an unscripted division as well as licensing and studio co-productions. She later transitioned to the top creative role, spearheading Netflix's $20 billion content budget.

She oversaw popular TV series like "Stranger Things," "Wednesday," "Bridgerton," "Squid Game," "Adolescence" and "Beef," as well as Netflix films like "Frankenstein" and "KPop Demon Hunters." Bajaria also helped push Netflix into live sports and events, including deals with the WWE and the NFL as well as programs like "The Roast of Tom Brady."

Prior to his stint at Disney, Rice was president of 21st Century Fox and CEO of Fox Networks Group as well as Fox's lead executive on the Hulu board. He was also the president of Fox Searchlight Pictures and helped release "Slumdog Millionaire," "Juno," "Little Miss Sunshine" and "Sideways."

The executive change follows a tumultuous period for Netflix as it faces stagnating viewership and explores avenues for growth. It comes just days after the streaming giant laid off roughly 1,000 employees, or 6% of its workforce.
In July, Netflix reported viewership increased just 2% in the first half of the year as the streamer suffers from a lack of shows with water-cooler-level hype.
Co-CEO Ted Sarandos admitted last month during the Bloomberg Screentime conference that the company is "not growing as fast as I want us to."
Those warnings, and now Bajaria's exit, have Wall Street bracing for more turbulence ahead.
"The sudden departure of Bajaria likely signals to us that user engagement may have remained soft throughout [the third quarter]," Pitz wrote.
Netflix is set to release fiscal third-quarter earnings on Tuesday.
In July, Nielsen reported that Netflix had generated 7.8% of TV viewership, while YouTube accounted for nearly double that, at 14.2%.

YouTube has been Netflix's biggest threat in the battle for viewers' time. In response, the streaming giant has sought to diversify its content in recent years, expanding into live sports, documentaries and video games in order to compete for share of consumer attention.

"If the opportunity is to recast [Netflix] into a broader content hub, the risk is missing the watercooler originals," Steven Cahall, equity analyst at Wells Fargo, wrote in a research note last month. "We see breakout hits as a must for the stock to work again."

Rice has a wealth of experience in television and film, most recently serving as the chairman of Walt Disney Television and chairman of general entertainment for the company. He managed a wide swath of channels across broadcast and streaming, including ABC, Disney Channel, Hulu and FX Networks. During his tenure, he oversaw the production of more than 300 shows, including "American Idol," "Modern Family," "Abbott Elementary," "The Bear," "Only Murders in the Building" and "Shogun."
He also headed up major sporting events such as coverage of the Super Bowl, NBA Finals and FIFA World Cup.
Under Rice's leadership, Disney earned roughly 300 Primetime Emmy nominations between 2021 and 2022. Of those nods, it won nearly 60 awards across its television networks and streaming platforms.
Meanwhile, Netflix's Emmy wins have slowed.
In 2021, it tied the record for most trophies won by an outlet in a single year with 44. This year, however, it only took home 16 prizes, its lowest Emmy haul in a decade.

With Rice, Netflix is also getting an executive with theatrical experience. After he was ousted by then-Disney CEO Bob Chapek in mid-2022, he transitioned into an independent producer role. Since 2023 he has produced films like "Saturday Night" and "28 Years Later." He's currently developing a movie adaptation of the video game "Elden Ring."

Late last year, Netflix struck a deal to buy Warner Bros. Discovery's film studio and streaming assets, only to be outbid months later by Paramount Skydance, which completed its acquisition of WBD in early October.
Some on Wall Street have speculated that the streamer may be interested in further M&A, including acquiring assets from NBCUniversal after it splits from parent company Comcast.

"[Rice's] long tenure at Fox, and then Disney after its acquisition of Fox, gives him unique insight into the consolidation of two major studios, relevant if Netflix chooses to go after another studio," Alicia Reese, senior vice president of equity research at Wedbush, wrote in a research note Thursday. "Even if it doesn't, Rice's experience fits well as Netflix pushes deeper into theatrical and builds a broader platform with varied content across the entertainment ecosystem."

articles.title: Are you addicted to your phone? What scientists say about screen time and social media

paras.en: Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.

How much time did you spend on your phone this week? It’s okay; you don’t actually have to tell me. But chances are good, like really good, that the number is higher than you’d like it to be: according to a recent survey by Pew Research Center, more than half of U.S. adults say they spend too much time on their phones. Folks under 50 are especially dissatisfied with their device usage: 64 percent of adults aged 30 to 49 think their screen use is out of hand, and 70 percent of adults aged 18 to 29 say the same.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Setting aside the survey data and just speaking personally, I think that these days, you’re either someone who actively avoids using screened devices, someone who knows they use screened devices too much or someone who’s currently in deep denial.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

There are now apps, physical phone accessories and even pared-down smartphones designed to help us curb our reflexive swiping and scrolling. But some people are taking things a step further by treating screen addiction with the same kind of programming traditionally reserved for substance abuse.

Scientific American associate editor Allison Parshall explored the new frontier of screen addiction in a feature for the latest issue of the magazine. She’s here to tell us what she’s learned about our dependence on technology—and what we can do to take back control.
Allison, thanks so much for coming on to chat. It’s always great to have you.
Allison Parshall: Thank you for having me.
Feltman: So I’d love to start by asking how you, you know, first got interested in writing this piece.

Parshall: I don’t know if you saw there were a lot of court cases to do with social media addiction earlier this year. They’re still ongoing, but, like, some of the biggest headlines were hitting. Basically Meta and Google were on trial from plaintiffs who said that their products were addictive and that they’d addicted kids, and the jury actually held them liable for that, which was a big first. So that got me interested in understanding, kind of, what’s behind these social media addiction claims because the companies claim it’s not an official addiction because there’s no diagnosis, and then, on the other side, you know, clinicians are like, “No, we’re seeing a problem.” So I kinda wanted to understand and get to the bottom of that tension.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But there was also a more personal motivation, which was that I just kept getting those, like, Sunday weekly screen time recaps, and they were always, like, way higher than I could possibly ever have fathomed. Like, I think I pushed up to seven hours a day, and that’s outside of work. So I’m doing the math, going like, “Am I on my phone literally every waking moment? That doesn’t seem possible.”
Feltman: Eight hours for work, eight hours for sleep, eight hours for what you will—is all we will phone. [Laughs.]

Parshall: All I will is phone. And then I, like, run through justifications, right? It was the winter. I was actually talking with friends most of the time; I’ve got a lot of really close long-distance friendships. A lot of it was, like, engaging creatively in things that I was very passionate about.

And then a lot of it was frankly just TikTok scrolling. So, I basically have just been kind of at war with myself and noticing a lot of my friends at war with themselves over these screen times and, like, wondering, “At what point do I say this is actually a problem? At what point does this helplessness and ambiguity I feel, like, resemble something closer to the experience of people who experience addiction to substances or to gambling and other behaviors?”
So that’s kind of where I started, with a little bit of a personal mission to figure out if I thought this was a problem or not. I can’t say I landed on a really satisfying place.

Feltman: [Laughs.] Well, it is, as you know, like, such a complex question. You know, even just speaking personally and, you know, based on the experiences of other people I know personally, because so much of it is very contextual, like you said. Like, there isn’t a distinction between online life and real life anymore. We live a lot of our lives through the channeling of these devices, so it’s like, there are many, like, good, prosocial, beneficial things one can and maybe even should do that involve staring at a screen. And then there’s the stuff that we know is just scrolling through TikTok.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: I’m curious, you know, I have some familiarity with the whole, you know, “Is it an addiction?” question, not just for screens and social media specifically but really anything that’s behavioral. And I think it feels especially complicated when it’s behavioral and involves a relatively new technology. So I’d love to hear, sort of, you know, what you’ve learned and, and what your takeaways are in terms of that whole “Is it an addiction?” question.

Parshall: I think, [the] “Is it an addiction?” question is one that I am just going to have to say: I think we’re just gonna have to live in the nuance of this forever. I don’t think we’re ever gonna have a super satisfying answer because the more you look into the history of our concept of addiction, the muddier it gets.

I think a lot of people have an understanding of, like, okay, drugs are straightforwardly addictive because they can hook your brain in a chemical way. Then when we start getting into behaviors, things get a little more squishy. Gambling, we’re like, “That’s really an addiction because it does something very specific to your brain, almost like a drug.” So, you know, that—you could put it there. Well, then you get into love and sex addiction, food addiction, and it all gets quite complicated.

But I think the thing that I realized in talking to researchers was, like, even when you go back into the history of drug addiction, we’ve had to push this line to get cocaine accepted as an addictive drug. So there’s, like, all of [these] questions of: “At what point are we going to broaden it enough?” And there’s a lot of concern among various pockets of addiction researchers and clinicians that if we make it too broad, the word loses meaning. It’s, like, a serious concern, but at the same time, you do have to let it be broad enough to encompass the problems that people are experiencing, and people are experiencing this problem of tech addiction.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Feltman: Yeah. There is so much nuance, and the focus on whether screen addiction is a real addiction or not can kind of miss the point. I mean, what do we know about why screens are so compelling to us and, so often, you know, leave us feeling worse or to make worse choices in our lives?

Parshall: Well, I mean, I think it would be helpful to start with, kind of, threading the needle on where we do want to demarcate the line of addiction, not around specific behaviors and what can and can’t be addictive but around, like, what we actually see with people that we say, “Okay, that’s where it becomes an addiction. That’s where it’s not. Hanging out with your friend for eight hours on video games, that’s where it actually becomes a problem.”

One of the researchers I talked to is Mark Griffiths, and he’s one of the people who helped develop this framework. And he was saying, you know, video game addiction, you can have someone who plays video games for seven or eight hours a day, and they are not addicted to video games. Excessive use and the length of time you spend doing something is not the marker of it. It can really dovetail with it, but it’s not the marker.

So there’s six characteristics of addiction, according to this framework, that a lot of researchers use. It needs to involve a salient behavior or a drug, so something that, kind of, is grabby to you, that causes mood modification effects, which you develop tolerance to over time, which leads to this cycle of increasing use and then withdrawal when you can’t use enough. Then those withdrawals induce craving, which induces a relapse, and that can cause conflict in your life. So those six factors are salience, mood modification, tolerance, withdrawal, relapse and conflict.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And it’s not like every single researcher agrees that you need all of these in order for things to be addictive. There’s a lot of questions specifically around withdrawals and their importance because that, kind of, comes from the drug framework and not necessarily the behavioral one. But it’s really, like, this cycle of amplification where things are getting worse and your life is deteriorating that I think is what leads people to seek help in the first place from doctors or from 12-step programs, and that leads doctors to point to that and say, “Okay, we can count that as addiction.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And for tech addiction, specifically, or social media addiction or Internet addiction or whatever grab bag of technologies you wanna use, there’s not really any great data showing the prevalence of it. Like, it seems like it’s in the low single digits, but it really depends on how wide of a net you wanna cast. People will overestimate their own addiction to technology if you give them the opportunity. People are more ready to say, “I’m addicted to this technology” and then you give them little screening tools, and they’re actually not really that addicted. Part of that is because we use this word very casually, colloquially.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Just to, like, set the groundwork here, there’s a lot of people probably who are clinically addicted to social media and technology. Whether you want to call what I’m experiencing, which is, like, periodic loss of my ability to stop scrolling TikTok even though I know it’s not good for me, and maybe, like, I’m not taking full advantage of the in-person opportunities of my life because of it, that’s a very different thing.

Feltman: So moving from this idea of “Is it addicting?” “Are people addicted?” You know, we know that the reality is, like you said, separate from people who do have clinically significant addictions to this behavior. Many of us, myself included, again, feel this compulsion to be using screens, be on social media, be on the Internet more than we know actually makes us feel good. And I feel like it’s important to stop and reflect on the fact that that is what they are designed to do. So can we talk a little bit about tech culpability here?
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Parshall: Yeah. I mean, I talked to, like, 30 people for this story. Everyone I talked to would stop in the middle of saying—whether or not they were saying, “Social media addiction’s overblown. We should just call it problematic social media use,” whether they were saying, you know, “The tech companies are driving us into the ground”—um, basically everyone stopped in the middle to say, “This is how these products are designed.” And there’s a concern with putting a lot of focus on the individual: How do they deal with social media? What are their habits? What is their, I don’t know, family genetic history of addiction and predisposition to find this really hooking?
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: There’s a concern that you’re, kind of, looking in the wrong place for the problem. And I’m very sympathetic to that. Like, I think part of the reason I can’t put this down, even though I wouldn’t say I have a lot of tendencies toward addictive things, is because it’s, like, kind of uniquely designed to hook me, and I will scroll forever. You know, you know that thing where you go back to see a video you just saw, and you scroll back up to it, and it’s, like, actually 10 videos ago? That’s what these cases are kind of resting around. These cases are really more about showing what social media companies knew based off of internal documents about the potential of their products to hook people, especially kids, and how they proceeded, kind of, regardless of those concerns.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: So there’s a lot of papers that came out both in the Facebook files—I know that The Social Reckoning movie will be out by the time listeners hear this—and through these court cases with discovery, there are cases of people internal at Meta saying explicitly, “Instagram is a drug. We’re basically pushers.” What the plaintiffs argue is a company that knew what its product could do and could have harms and didn’t do anything about it. So the company argues that, like, you know, social media addiction is not an official diagnosis, which means that it’s not something we should be resting these court cases on.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: It was interesting how hard it was to find legal experts to analyze these cases on the terms of social media addiction. It’s kind of like the word we use to talk about it, but it’s actually not the main character of these trials. The main [characters] of these trials are, like, the kids who are bringing these personal liability cases and the state’s [attorneys] general that are saying, you know, “You defrauded our consumers,” or, um, “You’ve [misled] our consumers.”

Feltman: Well, so getting back to individual action, in this idea of addiction or at least, you know, excessive, unhappy social media use. You talk to folks who are really treating this in themselves as an addiction, including with 12-step programs. Could you tell us a little bit about how this seems to be similar to, you know, treating drug or alcohol addiction and how it seems to be different?

Parshall: I talked to one woman who I met through this Internet and Technology Addicts Anonymous. And she had her own struggles with alcoholism, and she has been clean and sober for 30 years now, and from alcohol specifically.

And then, you know, when Facebook came out, she kind of realized that she was getting sucked in. And sometime in the last, I believe it was five years, she managed to start attending these basically AA meetings but for technology and get sober from that. She says that it feels like the same thing to her. Like, internally, this, like, loss of control, this [is] doing things that she doesn’t want to do and looking around at the people in her life that she feels like she’s constantly letting down and are increasingly learning to expect very little of her as, like, kind of the same kind of heartbreak.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: It seems from talking to these people who go to these 12-step programs that, for certain people, they can be really beneficial in the same way that they’re really beneficial for people who are struggling with other addictions. I mean, just from the outside looking in, it seems like a lot of that is down to community support and dedication. You get involved in these programs, and you can just go to meetings. There’s, like, a saying, “Meeting makers make it.” But also a lot of the people I talked to said, like, getting involved, volunteering, helping run the meetings, everything like that really helped pull them out.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And I think some of that is, like, it’s something to fill your life with purpose, becoming a sponsor for other people. You know, some of the addiction researchers I talked to pointed out that there’s a reason that you’re smoking all the time, or there’s a reason that you are filling all your time with TikTok. I mean, I feel that way, like, at times of life when I feel that TikTok is hardest to resist is when everything else feels like a monumental effort, and scrolling is the only thing that can, kind of, turn my brain off. The things that 12-step programs and then other forms of treatment that are more clinically evidence-based, like, you know, seeing psychologists or therapists, many of which do use 12 steps but—can help you, kind of, fill that gap or fill that hole or however you wanna think about what it is that the vice is coming into your life to replace or to fill.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And so, yeah, I think that could be done through 12-step programs. For some people, those don’t work very well ’cause they have such a heavy focus on sobriety. You can get trapped in a cycle of shame of, like, getting sober and then breaking it and then hating yourself and coming back crawling, and for some people, that just doesn’t work well. Addiction treatment in general is kind of trying to move away from the sobriety approach to a more evidence-based harm reduction. Like, okay, we’re not going to say you have to be 100 percent sober from this thing. You see this with sex and porn addiction a lot where, like, that can be a really harmful cycle.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And so the point of therapy might not necessarily be: we’re gonna cut out social media entirely. It might be: we’re going to build these guardrails around it, or we’re gonna make sure that you find a way to only stick to just a little bit. For some people, that’s also not possible, and that’s why they go for the whole sobriety thing. The researchers and clinicians and people who have been through these 12-step programs, they all kind of stress that, like, you need to have compassion with yourself and find something that works for you.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Feltman: Yeah, I know that, for me personally, relative to how much I was on social media until this point, for the last couple of years, I’ve been, like, functionally not on social media. And it’s really interesting because, every once in a while, I start to feel, you know, disconnected enough that I really want to, like, be spending some time on Instagram on my phone, and I redownload it. And the first couple times this happened, it was a real shame cycle because I was like, “Wow, I can’t do it in moderation.”

paras.en: And now I’ve really, I think, successfully reframed it as less of trying to be sober from social media and more like detoxing, where it’s like, you know, I know what it feels like when it doesn’t feel good anymore. And, like, when I really miss it in a way that feels kind of holistic and healthy and that, like, I just sort of want to be enjoying the Internet again, I redownload it. And then when I get to the point where I’m like, “Oh, no, now, now it’s poisoned my brain again,” then I get rid of it for a while.

paras.en: And I think it does, for me at least, seem to work in terms of, like, recalibrating me to stop, the decreased sensitivity to it where you’re just, like, totally desensitized and spending more and more time on there and not actually using it for the things that, like, again, are prosocial and actually feel good, like reaching out to friends and seeing cool art they’re making and stuff. But, yeah, I feel like it—what that looks like is [so] personal and context dependent that it feels really tough and unfair that, like, everybody has to figure out what that looks like for them.

paras.en: Parshall: And it’s constantly changing, too. That’s the thing that gets me. Like, I feel like I’ve navigated, I’ve, like, negotiated a good relationship, and then it changes. It’s kind of like the slippery slope doesn’t stop.
Feltman: Yeah, the algorithm changes; what’s going on in your life changes.

Parshall: I think part of that is, like, the way they’re designed to, like, kind of keep it as a slow slope. So, like, even if you start it with a good relationship, it is pretty easy to stop, and then you look up and you go, “Where am I?” And then you delete the app because you’re like, “I don’t like that I’m here.” I think your point about reframing is a really good one and one that I wanna stress that, like, if the addiction framing to you feels like it is unhelpful, it is really not necessary that you think of it as addiction.

paras.en: There’s a lot of other ways to think about it. Some researchers really like just thinking about it as a habit. And the differences between those things are a little bit hard to literally pin down. You know, a habit is like biting your nails. We don’t really say people are addicted to biting their nails, but it’s like there’s a particular cue: “I’m bored; I’m anxious.” With your phone it might be “It’s bedtime,” and you develop these habits.

And, like, you know the thing where, like, you literally can open Instagram through muscle memory or any other app that you use and start scrolling and realize you didn’t even realize that you’d chosen to do it? So, like, the researchers I talk to stress that, like, we do know how to get people to change their habits. I mean, we have more research than we do maybe on, like, tech addiction. You can shuffle around the way the apps are on the home screen. You can delete them entirely. Something I do with TikTok is: on the iPhone, it lets you remove it from your home screen but not from your phone entirely, so every time I want it, I have to search for TikTok. That doesn’t always work. Um, but it stops, it stops me from having a literal rote muscle memory on it. I might need to do that with Instagram soon, honestly. So yeah, there’s little tweaks that you can do to try to resist this thing that is probably, profit-motive-wise, going to continue to exist to want to pull you in.

That can be a really stigmatizing framework, and it can be one that, you know, I mean, especially with alcoholism, like, the, kind of, the way that people who are alcoholics talk about it often is like, “I am an alcoholic,” and for the rest of your life, you frame yourself as an alcoholic. You’re just, like, in recovery. People I talk to in 12-step programs, some of them did have that framing for tech addiction. But I would say their experience is, like, more extreme than a lot of the people that I know who use technology—in, subjectively, in their experience—too much.

When I first started this story, I was like, “How great of an arc would it be if, at the end, I can say that I managed to cut it down to three hours a day, and here’s what I did?” I did not do that. My screen time last week was higher than ever, but I was sick, in my defense.

And I think what I’ve noticed through observing these Sunday screen time notifications every week is: it really depends on the type of week I had. And there isn’t some terrible trend line for me where it’s getting worse and worse and worse and worse. It looks like this more than anything. And I think taking the advice of the researchers I talked to who said to give yourself grace ’cause you’re in kind of a screwed-up system, I’ve been trying to do that.

I’ve also been trying to listen to myself when I have that little voice in my head that’s saying, like, “You’re doing this to numb yourself,” and the things that are worth living about life in the physical world are things that take time to build. Like, you’re gonna have to go through going to, like, a deeply unpleasant social situation for a little while in order to meet the friends, to meet the friends, to meet the friends, instead of just focusing on the vicious cycle of screen time, thinking of the virtuous cycle of doing things that you’re passionate about and that can be on a screen. Trying to not have this bifurcation in my head of, like, screen time—bad. Like, noticing when I have had seven hours of screen time, being like, “Oh, actually four of those was ’cause I was reading a book I really liked, and that’s okay.” So yeah, I, I haven’t fixed myself. But I do think I’ve started to pay more attention in a way that is healthier. I would say I hope other people can, too, but I know that I’m not leading the charge on this. I’m in the muck with every single person in my life, trying to figure out what works for them. So I hope you’re able to, to make it work better for you, too.
