articles.title: How many planets could fit in the solar system?

paras.en: When I was a kid, I once watched a science-fiction flick called Journey to the Far Side of the Sun. The story’s main conceit was that scientists discover an Earth-like planet directly opposite our own in the same orbit around the sun, always hidden from our vantage point. The plot itself was somewhat silly, but the idea of a counter-Earth really stuck with me.

We know no such planet exists in real life, though; its gravitational effects on other worlds such as Mars and Venus would be obvious. Also, we’ve sent probes all through the solar system, and they’ve never spotted such a planetary arrangement.

But is this possible? Could two planets physically share the same orbit? The circumstances would have to be just right, and such a situation would be incredibly unlikely to occur. But the answer, surprisingly, is yes. In fact, many planets can technically share the same orbit! And when they do, their behavior gets pretty weird.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

The basic physics of how one object orbits another—say, a planet revolving around a star—has been known since Isaac Newton’s day. The math for such a simple system is pretty straightforward. And it’s deterministic; once you write down the equations, you can predict what the system will look like as far into the future or past as you like.

Throw in a third massive object, though, and the math gets ridiculously more complicated and difficult to solve. Under some circumstances, however, solutions exist that allow for a stable system even if two such planets interact. One of those solutions is a bit of weirdness called a horseshoe orbit, and it relies on a quirk of orbital mechanics.

Imagine that two planets orbit a star on very similar paths, but one (call it Planet 1) is just barely closer to the star than the other (Planet 2). This inner planet, being closer, will move more rapidly around the star than the outer planet. Eventually it will catch up to Planet 2. What happens next is counterintuitive: instead of smashing into each other, or one of them getting flung away on a high-speed slingshot trajectory, they will start to interact gravitationally while they are still hundreds of thousands of kilometers apart. Looking just at Planet 1 for a moment, it will be pulled ahead by Planet 2’s gravity, giving it more orbital energy.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: This is where the oddity of orbital mechanics really factors in: if you give an object more energy (say, by accelerating it), it will naturally move to a higher orbit, one with a larger radius. So as Planet 1 accelerates, it moves slightly outward from the star. But objects in larger orbits move slower. Thus, Planet 1 slows down and begins to lag behind Planet 2, widening the gap between them. As seen from Planet 2, Planet 1 will appear to approach on the inside lane, slow down, move to the outside lane and then fall away once again. It’s as if Planet 2 has repelled its sister world! In reality, both objects orbit the star in the same direction, just at different, changing speeds.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But what about Planet 2? It’s affected by Planet 1’s gravity during the encounter as well. Planet 1 pulls Planet 2 backward, stealing some of the latter’s orbital energy. That drops Planet 2 into a smaller orbit, where it speeds up and moves ahead of Planet 1. So now Planet 1 is on the outside path, and Planet 2 on the inside. They’ve swapped orbits!
Eventually they meet again, and this time the roles are reversed: they swap orbits once more, and we’re back to the original situation.

This is not just theoretical; we see this happening in the solar system. Saturn has a pair of moons called Janus and Epimetheus, which orbit the planet on paths that are only 50 kilometers different in radius, and they undergo exactly this orbit swapping every four years or so. So not only does this occur in real life, but it’s actually a stable configuration.
That means two planets can indeed share (or nearly share) the same orbit. And while they will encounter each other, they can do so safely.
But what about an arrangement with more co-orbital planets, such as, say, three? Does that work?

According to research by a team of international scientists published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS), yes, you can have more than two planets share an orbit. Astonishingly, many more can coexist!

First, the researchers used the mathematics of orbital mechanics to simulate the physics of two Earth-sized planets orbiting a sunlike star at 150 million kilometers (the real life Earth-sun distance) and showed they can persist in such horseshoe orbits for billions of years! Then the team added more and more planets to see what would happen.

When two planets meet up with each other, they swap orbits, as is already understood. But eventually one will then approach the third planet. When it does, they swap orbits and move apart. Eventually one of those two meets up with the first planet, and the whole situation repeats. This happens with every planet-on-planet encounter.

Incredibly, the scientists found this to be true if they had as many as 24 Earth-sized planets packed into a single orbit! Twenty-four! That shocked me. Still, it seems to work in the simulations; any planet can’t get very far along its path without meeting another, and when the two do so, they swap positions and continue on until the next encounter with the next planet down the line, constantly sliding around and jockeying for position.
The scientists even tried this in a simulation of our own solar system, which, they found, could support the addition of an extra couple of Earths or Venuses—or another Mercury or Mars.

Creating a system like this isn’t easy. It’s possible that a very thick ring of dust around a star could form several planets in the same orbit simultaneously, though conditions would have to be rather fine-tuned to allow that to happen. Also, planets can migrate toward and away from their host star on much grander scales as they interact gravitationally. And if enough smaller planets get tossed around by this process, they could also end up in shared orbits.

Detecting such planetary systems from Earth is possible, too. One way we find planets now is through the transit method, in which a planet passing directly in front of its star creates a mini eclipse, as seen from Earth. If several transits occur in sequence when we should only see one for that particular orbit, that would be a sign. Also, the fact that planets in this arrangement slide along their orbit and swap positions means that their positions in that orbit change, which, in turn, changes the timing of the transits. That would be detectable, too, even if all of the planets don’t actually join the transit parade.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Delightfully, the authors of the MNRAS study speculate that there is another way to form these systems: building them on purpose. Having multiple worlds all in one orbit might be handy for interplanetary travel. And while moving them around physically is a daunting task, a sufficiently technologically advanced alien civilization might feel that it’s worth the effort. If we ever were to find such a system, well, that would be interesting, wouldn’t it?
What a way to discover aliens exist! And it would really make me reassess my opinion on Journey to the Far Side of the Sun—possibly

articles.title: 5 ways to make Halloween decorations friendlier to wildlife

paras.en: Recently, a slender, yellow-striped California whipsnake, small enough to fit in a person’s hand, was brought to the California Wildlife Center in Calabasas. Its lower body was so twisted in fine strands of fake spiderwebs that it was essentially a ball, with twigs and leaves stuck in the mess.

“Had that gone on much longer, it could have started severing into its skin,” says Lauren Michaels, director of animal care at the center. Fortunately, the snake recovered and was eventually released. Not every animal is so lucky, though. Cambria Wells, the center’s education and outreach manager, recalls a hummingbird that was similarly wrapped in webbing and didn’t make it.

Every Halloween season, wildlife rehabilitation centers across the country see cases in which birds, bats, snakes, rodents, deer and other wild animals become injured or entangled in seasonal decorations.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

The good news is that you can have a spooky spectacle in front of your house and still protect wildlife. Here are five ways to make your Halloween display friendlier to the creatures that fly, slither and scurry through your yard.

Of all the Halloween decorations people display outdoors, synthetic spiderwebs are the most dangerous, according to many wildlife experts. Made of strong, stretchy plastic, the webbing’s thin, hard-to-see strands can cling to animals and become wrapped around their bodies, posing a serious entanglement hazard. Trapped animals can go hungry, suffer constriction injuries, or even dislocate their limbs as they struggle to free themselves, Wells explains.

To get the spiderweb look without the stretchy strands, the best option is a solid web decoration made from rigid plastic or metal, she advises. Rope-style webs are safer than stretchy spiderwebbing, but they can still pose an entanglement risk.

If you do use stretchy or rope webbing outdoors, Wells recommends pulling it taut against a solid surface, such as your house, rather than across an open space where an animal could fly or travel through it.

The same principle applies to other decorations. Choose solid objects over anything with netting, strings, ropes, ribbons or other materials in which an animal could become entangled. Think tombstones, solid skeletons, signs or other decorations that hold their shape and don’t have loose or dangling parts.
Popular inflatables can be a safer alternative to netting or webbing, but you should make sure their anchoring cords and power cords are secured and check regularly for damage.

In general, look for durable decorations you can reuse year after year rather than items that are designed to be thrown away after a single season to reduce the broader environmental impact of your Halloween display, Wells notes.
Turn Halloween lights off when you go to bed

“Lighting is an underappreciated form of impact on wildlife,” Wells says. Artificial light can interfere with wildlife behavior and disorient migrating birds, many of which travel during the middle of the night and the early morning at this time of year, she explains.

If you want lights as part of your decor, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service recommends opting for ones with warmer colors, such as amber, orange or red, rather than blue, white or other cooler-colored lights, whose shorter wavelengths are more disruptive to biological rhythms.
But regardless of the type of lights you use, the simplest and most effective step, Wells says, is to turn them off when you go to bed, giving wildlife darkness during the overnight hours.

Window decals, creepy figures, glowing jack-o’-lanterns and other decorations displayed on or just inside your windows can still be seen from the street without introducing loose materials into your yard that wildlife could encounter.

Pumpkins are a Halloween staple, but you should remember that they’re also food. If you want to keep wildlife from chowing down on your carefully carved jack-o’-lantern without harming any creatures, Wells says, try bringing it in in the evening or coating it with a bitter apple spray or cayenne pepper diluted with water.

When spooky season is over, you can then compost your pumpkins or dispose of them according to your local food- or yard-waste guidelines. You can also check whether a local wildlife center or animal sanctuary accepts intact, untreated pumpkins for animal feed.

Other natural materials, such as gourds, hay, and cornstalks make for festive decor, but Wells suggests choosing materials from your local area to reduce the risk of introducing invasive plants or seeds.
If you find an entangled animal, call for help
If you discover an animal caught in or injured by Halloween decorations, resist the urge to untangle and release it. Injuries may not be obvious at first, and the animal may need medical care.
Instead contact a local wildlife rehabilitation center for guidance. You can find nearby resources through Animal Help Now.

articles.title: Can math stay human in the age of AI?
articles.author: Kathryn Hulick

paras.en: “Exponentially exploding,” mathematician Thomas Bloom told me by phone, describing the flood of new results in his field. Little did he know that hours later, OpenAI was going to post 722 mathematical manuscripts an unreleased AI model had produced.

The firehose of new work lends new urgency to the question: How is AI changing mathematical discovery? In their race for headline-grabbing breakthroughs, AI companies typically do not disclose their methods and data. That competition among AI companies threatens to overwhelm human collaboration and understanding.

This tension had been playing out in miniature on a website Bloom runs that tracks progress on more than 1,000 problems originally posed and collected by Paul Erdős, one of the 20th century’s most prolific mathematicians. Here, people used to collaborate to discuss open problems, or ones for which the best solution either hasn’t been found or isn’t known to the greater math community. But increasingly, visitors were competing to close open problems with AI proofs that they often didn’t understand. Bloom, a mathematician at the University of Manchester in England, doesn’t want to spend his days refereeing AI-generated work. So, soon after we spoke, and before he knew that OpenAI would be announcing its latest results, Bloom posted that he’d no longer tag problems as open or solved, and he also closed comments.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: It’s definitely exciting that AI can tackle so many open problems so quickly. But can it help mathematicians understand the answers and build on them?

Just two days after OpenAI’s deluge of results, the peer-reviewed edition of a Google DeepMind study became public. First reported in a preprint earlier this year, it offers an inside look at how one AI system tackles open math problems. The system called AlphaProof Nexus solved 9 Erdős problems and made a number of other interesting mathematical advances, researchers report October 8 in Science.

The report includes a detailed description of how the results were obtained. Plus, human mathematicians vetted many of the proofs. That’s “quite different” from how OpenAI and Anthropic are handling their math results, Bloom says.

“The ultimate objective of any AI for math research,” says research scientist and study co-author Swarat Chaudhuri of Google DeepMind in London, should be “to advance mathematics as done by human mathematicians.”

In the recently published study Chaudhuri and his colleagues tested different configurations of their system. To tackle a collection of 353 open Erdős problems, they used multiple agents powered by the Gemini language model. These could call on AlphaProof, an AI model specially trained to do math, and the inspiration for the name of the overall system, for difficult steps. The agents also relied on Lean, math software that identifies steps that remain unproven, to check their logic. The agents shared their work, circulating promising proof attempts and discarding ones that weren’t going well.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The team also tested a simpler setup on the nine problems the full system solved. Independent Gemini agents worked through proofs using Lean’s feedback, without sharing attempts or consulting AlphaProof. That setup solved all nine, too. It was cheaper—using fewer computing resources—than the full system on easy problems and more expensive on the two toughest ones. The team did not establish whether the simpler setup would solve any of the problems the full system had missed.

The fact that the simpler setup could solve the same nine problems as the full system surprised Chaudhuri. It suggests that increasingly capable language models can tackle research mathematics with relatively simple checking tools.

But computer-checking comes with a caveat. Lean checks only the statement it’s given, as it is written in its code. And a mathematical statement may be incorrectly translated to or from Lean code. An October 6 preprint shows why this translation matters. In the paper, the researchers pinpoint mismatches between parts of OpenAI’s written Navier–Stokes proof and its Lean counterpart. The mismatches do not mean the written proof is wrong, the team writes, but they note that a valid Lean proof does not automatically validate an AI-generated math paper.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: That’s why the vetting human mathematicians did for the DeepMind publication is so important. “The human mathematician has to really think through the problem and set goals for the system,” Chaudhuri says. And even if the system failed to finish a proof, its checked steps helped mathematicians focus on the remaining gaps. “Math is ultimately a human art,” Chaudhuri says. “The system enhances the human user’s insights, and the human user is able to guide the system with new ideas.”

The mathematical results that the AlphaProof Nexus system achieved are “not really at the top level of importance,” says Bloom, who wasn’t involved with the work. But that underscores the team’s more measured approach. Google DeepMind, he says, is “trying to be more responsible with the science,” while companies like OpenAI are using math to showcase their software. OpenAI’s papers and accompanying Lean proofs were entirely AI-generated, leaving it up to the math community to work out what’s useful or useless.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: OpenAI says they worked with an independent advisory group to develop best practices on how to share their AI math results. But that group has said their advice was to not test unreleased AI models on advanced math, guidance the company clearly ignored.

The company’s fast-moving, competitive approach continues to alienate mathematicians such as Bryna Kra of Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill. She says the company made some improvements in their efforts to cite past literature. And she’s excited about AI’s potential to solve important problems in math. But there is widespread concern, she says, that AI models have accessed people’s unpublished work. “We had a healthy, collaborative, sharing culture that is being destroyed,” she says. “Now, people are wary of sharing their ideas.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Not all mathematicians feel this way about AI. The technology is “making math more accessible,” says Andrew Turner, who wonders why a small group of mathematicians should get to decide how we solve problems. Turner, who studied math and physics and is Now CTO of the company Plasma AI, based in New York City thinks “math is becoming engineering.” And doing math with machines will allow people to “answer questions previously unfathomable.”
A few days after Bloom shut down the competition on his website, Plasma AI announced a new website to track progress on Erdős problems. They will welcome AI results.

Bloom doesn’t see math as a Silicon Valley–esque move-fast-and-break-things competition. I agree, and hope that curious people will continue to explore problems they care about, with AI helping rather than taking over. At the end of his post announcing the changes to his website, Bloom wrote something that makes me tear up every time I read it. I hope everyone, even the most enthusiastic AI users, can find the time for this type of work: “Be confused, be stuck, be inspired. Find a messy proof, then find a better one,” he wrote. “Get tired, get hungry, get into a flow state. Argue, laugh, give up, drink some coffee and attack it again. Be human. Let your brain be open.”

articles.title: Artemis II results show how much science people can do at the moon
articles.author: Lisa Grossman

paras.en: Six months after the Artemis II mission sent four astronauts around the moon, the value of their closeup view is coming into focus. The first science results, released on October 7, reveal details of the moon’s array of colors, how often it gets hit by tiny rocks and lessons for squeezing as much science as possible out of future human lunar missions.

“We worked extremely hard to make sure we were able to maximize lunar science return from wherever we could in this mission,” said Artemis II flight science operations lead Kelsey Young at a virtual Lunar Surface Science Workshop meeting on October 7. “This is creating yet another tool in our toolbox as planetary scientists to understand our moon, our solar system, even our own planet.”

NASA’s Artemis II mission sent four astronauts on a 10-day journey around the moon in April — the first time humans had been anywhere near our natural satellite in more than 50 years. Astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen spent about seven hours in close proximity to the moon taking scientific observations, describing the moon’s surprising colors and textures and witnessing a solar eclipse from space.

Almost all of that event was livestreamed. But the astronauts took thousands of photos, notes and audio recordings that weren’t immediately made public. Part of the science team’s job was to digest those observations and release the data to anyone who wants to study them within six months of splashdown on April 10.

With three days to spare, the team released three reports and a massive data archive on October 7, the 67th anniversary of when the Soviet Luna 3 spacecraft took the first photograph of the farside of the moon. The results offer a rare test of what trained human observers can add to lunar research and what NASA can learn for future missions to the lunar surface.

“We’re really excited to release all of this data,” earth scientist Sara Schmidt of NASA Johnson Space flight Cener in Houston said during the meeting. After six months of hard work, “this is enabling science to happen for the next, I don’t know, 60 years, if not more.”
How astronauts learn to observe the moon
Surprisingly, the most valuable data from the mission were not the mind-blowingly gorgeous photos, but the astronauts’ verbal and written descriptions of what they were seeing.

Before launch, the astronauts had extensive training in lunar geology and science observations. They were an extension of the science team, said field geologist Cindy Evans also of NASA Johnson Space Flight Center, one of the astronauts’ instructors.
“You could hear it in their voices. They understood the language of geology,” she said.
That training was meant to help answer a question Young hears often: What can humans add that a camera can’t?

During the flyby, the astronauts worked in pairs. Two of them spoke to mission control on the ground, giving periodic updates to the science team on what they were seeing. The other two recorded themselves describing their observations and reactions and used a stylus to annotate specially made maps of the moon that had been uploaded to their tablets during flight. Those notes, doodles and recordings were not made public until now.
The idea was to give the crew high tech field notebooks, Young says.

“If you have any field experience, you know your field notebook is your best friend,” she said in the meeting. On Earth, geologists capture nuance and context in written and spoken words, as well as sketches, she said. “We wanted to provide the ability to capture that nuanced information from the crew.”
One example of this was when Koch sketched her view of the Orientale basin, detailing differences in texture and layers around the crater.
“Sketches can be so powerful,” Young says. “They’re quick and dirty and that’s exactly the right thing to do. You’re capturing that nuance really quickly before it leaves your brain.”

Some of the most unique observations came during the 54 minutes when the moon eclipsed the sun, giving the astronauts a view of the solar corona, interplanetary dust and other stars and planets. That was a favorite moment for planetary scientist Jennifer Heldmann of NASA’s Ames Research Center in California.

“That audio showed their sheer joy and amazement in what they were seeing and where they were,” Heldmann says. “They were so blown away by what they were seeing, while also taking very relevant science observations.”
But some of the most affecting moments were when words failed. When Glover and Koch saw the Earth emerge from behind the moon, for a while all they could say was “Oh my gosh!”
“I guess I should be trying to describe it, but I mean, good grief,” Glover’s tablet recorded him saying.
“No, I tried, but it’s impossible,” Koch agreed. “You might be able to fly a spaceship and talk, but if you can see that and talk, you just ain’t right.”
Astronauts spotted tiny impacts on the moon
Another thing the astronauts were able to see during the eclipse were impact flashes — tiny blips of light marking where bits of rock hit the moon.
“It’s a pinpoint of light,” Hansen said in his recorded observations. “It’s not like a meteor, you didn’t see anything else, it’s just like a bloop.”

Before launch, the science team identified and prioritized observations they hoped the crew would be able to make during the flyby. Impact flashes were at the top of the list. Seeing the flashes would give scientists a way to estimate how often the moon is struck by incoming rocks, and how large those rocks are. That’s an important thing to know for protecting future missions where astronauts will walk on the surface or build a long-term moon base.

Scientists didn’t know whether the astronauts would see any flashes at all. They saw five. The flashes were “pinpricks of light lasting less than a second, with no color associated with the flash,” Heldmann said at the meeting.

Comparing the number of flashes per minute to theoretical models of how many impacts the moon might experience, scientists determined that the incoming rocks were tiny, about 8.5 grams and just over 4.5 centimeters across — about the size of a golf ball.
“With these observations, we believe that the Artemis II crew set a record for the smallest meteorites ever optically observed to impact the moon,” Heldmann said.
The resulting craters are probably less than a meter wide, too small for cameras on NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter to see.

That’s good news for future astronauts. Artemis IV, planned for 2028, is supposed to bring astronauts to the lunar surface for the first time since Apollo. If successful, it will be a two-week mission using landers from spaceflight companies Blue Origin or SpaceX. The probability of dangerous impact during such a mission is less than 1 in 10 million, Heldmann said. For a larger moon base meant to last a decade, the probability is higher, but still low.
“Now we can start to quantify those impact probabilities, which turns out are very very low,” she says. “Crews will be very safe.”

The moon’s muted colors were another high-priority observation for the science team. Lunar hues and brightnesses can change with terrain roughness, surface temperature and mineralogy — and they’re much more discernable with human eyes than with cameras. The crew also saw how colors changed as the viewing angle and light levels changed.
“This is such a cool demonstration of the value of human eyes as scientific sensors,” said planetary scientist Ariel Deutsch, also of NASA Ames.

Combining the crew’s observations with other data going back to the 1970s let scientists connect colors to composition. Blues were associated with titanium-rich volcanic rocks. Browns reflect different iron levels. Greens are from glass formed during volcanic eruptions or asteroid impacts.
Future astronauts could use this information to create terrain maps and to find specific materials on the moon for sample collection or resources.
The crew also was enamored with the terminator, the boundary between light and dark, which revealed lunar topography in a new way.

“Even as rugged as the far side looks … man, when you look at the terminator, it is just, like, impossibly rugged,” Wiseman said during the flight. “And it reminds you that the whole farside is that way. It’s just the terminator is really bringing out the shadows and the hills and the valleys. And it is just — it’s unbelievable.”
The lighting at the terminator is similar to what future astronauts might expect at the moon’s south pole, where the sun will be low on the horizon and may cast dramatic shadows.
“We want to make sure we have a good handle on that for both science and operations and exploration,” Heldmann said.
What Artemis II taught NASA for future moon missions
With the lessons from Artemis II in hand, now it’s the next astronauts’ turn.

Some recommendations coming out of Artemis II focus on improving conditions in the spacecraft and weaving science into mission planning better. For example, due to time constraints, the astronauts’ cameras were not calibrated before flight. The team is now trying to calibrate them back on Earth, but it can’t re-create how the windows affected images because the windows were charred on the way back through Earth’s atmosphere.

Another takeaway from Artemis II is to continue to refine and train astronauts in descriptive notetaking. The audio notes will be even more important for the first landed missions, where astronauts in spacesuits will not be able to write in a notebook.
“We want to train astronauts to be field scientists, regardless of the landing site, regardless of the mission that they’re given,” Young says.
The buddy system of two astronauts at the windows, two talking to the ground, led to better science, the team concluded.

“The crew had scientific discussions and tried to understand what they were viewing,” Heldmann says. For surface missions, where time is limited and choices must be made quickly, that collaboration will be even more important.
The crew also commented on how helpful it was.

“When we actually do go down there to the surface, I know for safety reasons that we would never send someone alone, but I just want to really emphasize how important the discussion time was,” Glover said. “When we started to talk, we not only got better science discussion, we got better human connection.”

articles.title: Horned dinosaurs’ weapons evolved to handle the forces of combat
articles.author: Jake Buehler

paras.en: Triceratops’ massive skulls were built for horn-to-horn grappling. The rhino-like Centrosaurus could withstand stabbing its nose horn up and down. And the parrot-faced Psittacosaurus would have been wise to avoid a fight: Its head was ill-suited to handle blows.

New simulations using 3-D models of the heads of five different horned dinosaurs reveal what forces the skulls could withstand in battle. The results provide insight into how these dinosaurs evolved to use their face-based armory in combat, researchers report September 24 in PeerJ.
Ceratopsians — horned dinosaurs like Triceratops — have been hypothesized to use their imposing headgear as armaments for battling with other members of the species.

Fossilized facial injuries consistent with head-to-head violence have provided physical clues. “We know from many fossils that ceratopsian skulls tended to get banged up a little bit … in very particular spots on the frill or on the cheek,” says Andrew Farke, a paleontologist at Raymond M. Alf Museum of Paleontology in Claremont, California. But little else was known about how ceratopsians actually used their horns in battle.

Studying the biomechanics of the animals’ weaponized skulls could provide information on what movements and forces the dinosaurs evolved to tolerate. Such biomechanics research had previously been done on the bite stresses of theropod dinosaurs like Tyrannosaurus and on the forces felt by the club tails of armored dinosaurs, says vertebrate paleontologist Eric Austin Ames Jr.

Ames and his colleagues at the University of Bristol in England developed digital 3-D models of six skulls across five ceratopsian species spread across the group’s evolutionary tree. They simulated the combat stress experienced across the skull, varying the direction of attack and how the weaponry was used. Higher stresses in the skull meant a greater risk of mechanical failure, Ames says. The dinosaurs are more likely to have evolved to fight in a way that was well-tolerated by the skull’s mechanics.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The team found that early members of the group from about 125 million years ago — like the hornless, husky-sized Psittacosaurus — didn’t have skulls well-suited for combat of any type. The pig-sized Protoceratops had a skull that tolerated ramming fairly well. Larger, later-diverging species like Centrosaurus and the three-horned Triceratops and Spiclypeus appeared adapted to a wider range of combat styles.

Centrosaurus may have been a specialized stabber, lunging its head to jab at opponents. “When we tested [the skull] with vertical forces, it actually handled the stresses really well,” Ames says. “But when we tried side-to-side, it did not perform very well.”In contrast, Triceratops and Spiclypeus had skulls that tolerate the forces generated by interlocking horns and wrestling.

Ames thinks ceratopsians’ horns and frills probably first evolved for social and sexual display, but were soon used for full contact purposes. “Throughout their evolutionary history, their [horns’ traits] started to really explode in diversity and that coincided with different intraspecific combat styles,” he says. “This is something we see in modern herbivores.”

Much like with the antlers and horns of modern deer, buffalo or antelope, these weapons could have easily been turned on predators as well. “These adaptations are kind of like a Swiss Army knife,” Ames says. “They can be used for multiple things.”

The team created its 3-D models from surface scans of fossilized skulls. More detailed models that better simulate the complicated internal structure of these dinosaurs’ immense, bizarre skulls could provide even more insight to this prehistoric fight club, Farke says.

articles.title: There's a Surprisingly Simple Way to Remove Microplastics in Your Drinking Water
articles.author: David Nield

paras.en: Tiny fragments of plastic are making their way deep inside our bodies in concerning quantities, particularly through our food and drink.
But research suggests there is something you can actually do about it.
Scientists in China found a simple and effective means of removing them from water – and it starts with something already sitting on your stove.

Back in 2024, the team ran tests on both soft water and hard tap water (which is richer in minerals). They added nanoplastics and microplastics to the water before boiling the liquid and then filtering out any precipitates.
The tests showed that boiling and then filtering the water can make a significant difference to the plastic contaminants you might otherwise ingest.

"Tap water nano/microplastics (NMPs) escaping from centralized water treatment systems are of increasing global concern, because they pose potential health risks to humans via water consumption," the researchers explained in their published paper.
Watch the video below for a summary of the findings:
In some cases, up to 90 percent of the NMPs were removed by the boiling and filtering process, though the effectiveness varied based on the type of water.
Of course, the huge benefit is that most people can do it with what they already have in their kitchen.

"This simple boiling water strategy can 'decontaminate' NMPs from household tap water and has the potential for harmlessly alleviating human intake of NMPs through water consumption," biomedical engineer Zimin Yu from Guangzhou Medical University and colleagues explained.
A greater concentration of NMPs was removed from samples of hard tap water, which naturally forms a buildup of limescale (or calcium carbonate) as it is heated.

Commonly seen inside kitchen kettles, the chalky substance forms on the plastic's surface as changes in temperature force the calcium carbonate out of solution, effectively trapping the plastic fragments in a crust.
"Our results showed that nanoplastic precipitation efficiency increased with increasing water hardness upon boiling," the team wrote.
"For example, from 34 percent at 80 mg L−1 to 84 percent and 90 percent at 180 and 300 mg L−1 of calcium carbonate, respectively."
Even in soft water, where less calcium carbonate is dissolved, roughly a quarter of the NMPs were snagged from the water.
Any bits of lime-encrusted plastic could then be removed through a simple filter like the stainless steel mesh used to strain tea, the researchers say.
Past studies have measured fragments of polystyrene, polyethylene, polypropylene, and polyethylene terephthalate in potable tap water, which we're consuming daily in varying quantities.
To put the strategy to the ultimate test, the researchers added even more nanoplastic particles, which were effectively reduced in number.
"Drinking boiled water apparently is a viable long-term strategy for reducing global exposure to NMPs," wrote Yu and team.
"Drinking boiled water, however, is often regarded as a local tradition and prevails only in a few regions."
The scientists hope it might become a more widespread practice as plastics continue to take over the world.
Tiny pieces of plastic are an increasingly big problem. Microplastics originate from clothing, kitchen utensils, personal care products, and countless other everyday objects.
Their durability makes them persistent in the environment – including in human bodies.
Not only are many people on Earth already contaminated by microplastics, but we're also still being exposed every day, as there is minimal regulation of these insidious specks.

According to a 2025 literature review from The University of Texas at Arlington, a significant portion of our microplastic exposure may come from drinking water, as wastewater treatment plants are still not effectively removing microplastics.

Roughly 9 billion metric tons of plastic have been produced globally since plastic production began, much of which has progressively degraded into ever-smaller fragments without truly breaking down, forming a fine plastic dust that now pervades the planet.
Wastewater treatment plants actually do remove a lot of these small particles, the new review indicates, but not enough.
Related: Glass Bottles Actually Contain More Microplastics, Scientists Find
While it's still not certain exactly how damaging this plastic is to our bodies, it's clearly not the healthiest of snacks.
Plastics have already been linked to changes in the gut microbiome and the body's antibiotic resistance.

The team behind this study wants to see more research into how boiled water could keep artificial materials out of our bodies – and perhaps counter some of the alarming effects of microplastics that are emerging.

"Our results have ratified a highly feasible strategy to reduce human NMP exposure and established the foundation for further investigations with a much larger number of samples," Yu and colleagues conclude.
The research was published in Environmental Science & Technology Letters.

articles.title: Drinking 'Very' Hot Tea or Coffee Could Triple Your Risk of This Cancer, Huge Study Finds
articles.author: Peter Dockrill

paras.en: Plenty of people like to start their day with a cup of tea or coffee, but the temperature of your preferred beverage could matter a lot more than you realize.
A decade ago, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) made headlines when it classified very hot beverages at temperatures above 65 °C (149 °F) as "probably carcinogenic to humans".
That 2016 finding followed evidence that mate, a herbal drink popular in South America and often drunk at very hot temperatures, was associated with an increased risk of esophageal cancer.
Mate is typically consumed at temperatures as high as 70 °C (158 °F), but until now, the evidence for hot beverages consumed at cooler temperatures was inconclusive.

"International research has shown for some time that drinking beverages like mate at very high temperatures, as is typical in South America, is linked to increased risk of certain esophageal cancers," says nutritional epidemiologist Keren Papier from the University of Oxford.
"What was less clear was whether this also applied to the temperatures at which hot drinks are usually consumed in Western populations."
To examine the issue, Papier and fellow researchers analyzed data from two large UK cohorts, the Million Women Study and UK Biobank.
In total, the researchers incorporated data from 977,282 participants, in what they claim is the largest study to date examining the associations between hot drinks and esophageal cancer.

In both studies, participants were asked similar questions about hot drink consumption, including how hot they liked their beverages to be ('very hot', 'hot', 'warm', etc.), and how many cups of tea and coffee they consumed each day.

The researchers found that participants who preferred 'very hot' drinks had a 3.17-fold higher relative risk of developing esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) during the study period compared to people who took their drinks 'warm', after accounting for drinking frequency.
People who indicated they preferred 'hot' drinks had a 69 percent higher SCC risk than those who drank 'warm' beverages, the researchers found.

Further, the data showed that the amount of hot drinks participants consumed was also associated with cancer risk, with those consuming six or more hot drinks a day having a 71 percent increase in SCC risk compared to people who drank fewer than six hot beverages daily, after accounting for drink temperature.

The association was similar regardless of whether participants primarily drank tea or coffee, and adding milk (which was recorded in the Million Women Study) didn't appear to significantly alter the temperature-associated risks identified.

While the observational findings don't establish that hot drinks cause cancer, the researchers suggest that reducing the temperature of hot beverages even slightly could potentially prevent a substantial number of SCC cases.

"Assuming a causal association between preferred drink temperature and the risk of esophageal SCC, the estimated proportion of esophageal SCC cancers that would be prevented if individuals who consumed drinks at a very hot temperature instead consumed their drinks at a hot temperature is 14 percent," the study authors write.
"Based on national incidence rates for SCC esophageal cancers in the United Kingdom, these attributable risks translate into absolute numbers of cancers that could be prevented each year of 440."

A significant limitation with the study, however, is that the researchers didn't collect absolute temperature measurements of the beverages the participants were drinking – only their self-reported preferences of 'very hot', 'hot', 'warm', etc.

The researchers say future studies might be able to clear that up, but for now, they suggest their findings could indicate that temperature ranges below those cited in the IARC report (above 65°C) may increase cancer risk.

While their own study did not examine the biological mechanisms involved, the researchers say their findings – with similar risks seen across tea and coffee, and with milk or without – suggest that beverage temperature is the key risk factor, rather than what's in the drink.
"Animal studies support this, showing that very hot water (70° C) promotes premalignant lesions and esophageal necrosis, whereas lower-temperature beverages do not," the researchers write.
"The most likely mechanism is thermal injury, which may impair mucosal integrity and promote carcinogenic processes."
The findings are reported in the International Journal of Cancer.

articles.title: New Drug Protects People With Celiac Disease From Gluten Damage in Clinical Trial
articles.author: Carly Cassella

paras.en: For those with celiac disease, even a little bit of gluten can cause damage to the intestine.
The only available solution is a strict gluten-free diet.
Yet even when foods are carefully scrutinized, accidents can be made, and symptoms can persist in up to 40 percent of patients.
Several new pharmaceuticals are being investigated by drug companies, and one just passed a phase 2 clinical trial.
The medicine is called FB102, which admittedly doesn't sound very glamorous, but don't judge a book by its cover.
This intravenous medicine has the potential to protect the gut against accidental gluten exposure, a feat that no approved drug can currently achieve.
The company that owns the pharmaceutical, argenx SE, has now announced positive topline results from its phase 2 clinical trial.

The results are not yet peer-reviewed, but patients with celiac disease who were treated with FB102 demonstrated better preservation of the intestinal lining during gluten exposure compared to a placebo.

"These positive Phase 2 results strengthen our conviction in the potential of FB102 to address a significant unmet need for people living with celiac disease, where there are currently no approved therapies," says Luc Truyen, the chief medical officer at argenx.
The recent clinical trial enrolled 126 patients with confirmed celiac disease, who were symptom-free and who had been on a strict gluten-free diet for at least the past year.
Participants underwent a controlled, eight-week oral gluten challenge. Some were randomized to receive a placebo during this time, while others received intravenous infusions of FB102.
Neither participants nor researchers knew who was receiving what.
At day 78, researchers analyzed how much gluten-induced damage had occurred in the mucosal lining compared to at the start of the trial.
When people with celiac eat gluten, it tends to shorten the tiny projections that stick out from their intestinal walls while also deepening the grooves between them.
But FB102 seems to protect against this.
Participants in the trial who received this novel drug showed fewer signs of injury from eating gluten. They also showed a smaller inflammatory immune response in the mucosal lining.
This does not mean that FB102 will one day allow patients with celiac disease to eat gluten without care.
This drug was given under controlled conditions, and it's unclear if its protective effects work in a real-world setting.
Still, it's worth investigating further, especially as there is currently no way to protect the gut against accidental gluten exposure.

"Combined with the consistent safety profile observed across studies," says Truyen, "these findings support advancing FB102 into Phase 3 development and further exploring its broader potential across immune-mediated diseases."
The FB102 drug has been in clinical trials for several years now. It was specifically designed to target a receptor on immune cells called CD122.
This receptor responds to inflammatory messengers, and in 2009, researchers showed that if this receptor was blocked in mice with gut autoimmune issues, it led to a reversal of intestinal damage.
That led to the hypothesis that CD122 and its interaction with inflammatory signals are critical in the development and maintenance of celiac disease.
To that end, drug researchers at Forte Biosciences Inc (later acquired by argenx) developed FB102.
This drug is designed to block CD122 receptors on only some disruptive T cells, while preserving the receptor on other ones.
It shows promise in treating not just celiac disease, but other autoimmune diseases, too, like vitiligo.
This is a rare chronic autoimmune condition that causes skin to lose its pigment in patches.
Researchers suspect the drug could also work for alopecia areata.

According to the United States Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) draft guidance, a chronically administered compound like FB102 would need to show efficacy in clinical trials for at least 52 weeks, and it would need to demonstrate efficacy without a gluten challenge.
Researchers at argenx are still working up to that.

"The study builds on the Phase 1b trial, providing consistent clinical evidence that CD122 blockade can protect against gluten-induced intestinal damage and prevent emergence of patient symptoms, even under a more intense gluten challenge, validating CD122 as a promising therapeutic target in celiac disease," says Truyen.

articles.title: Yale scientists discover how stress changes the brain to make memories stronger

paras.en: Yale scientists discover how stress changes the brain to make memories stronger

- Yale scientists have uncovered how the stress hormone cortisol helps the brain turn emotional experiences into stronger, longer-lasting memories. The discovery reveals that stress can reshape communication between brain networks involved in emotion and memory, potentially explaining why certain moments are so difficult to forget.

Stress does more than influence how we feel. It can also change what we remember, particularly when an experience is emotionally intense or personally meaningful. Scientists have long known that cortisol, a hormone released during stressful situations, can strengthen emotional memories. What has been less clear is exactly how this happens inside the brain.

Researchers at Yale University have now uncovered important clues. Their study reveals that cortisol strengthens emotional memories by changing how brain networks involved in emotion and memory function and communicate with one another. The findings offer a deeper understanding of why certain experiences leave such powerful impressions while others quickly fade.

"We all experience stress, and my lab is interested in understanding how stress can be helpful," said corresponding author Elizabeth Goldfarb, an assistant professor of psychiatry at Yale School of Medicine and of psychology in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences.
The findings were published in the journal Science Advances.

Previous research involving both humans and rodents has shown that stress and cortisol can improve memory for emotional events. Scientists also know that certain brain regions, including the amygdala, play an essential role in this process. The amygdala is particularly important for processing emotions and identifying experiences that may be significant.

However, understanding precisely how cortisol strengthens memories has been challenging. Many brain regions participate in several mental functions, making it difficult to determine whether the hormone is influencing emotional responses, memory formation, or both.

"Forming memories for emotional experiences involves different processes in the brain: first, perceiving an experience as emotional or intense, and second, encoding that experience into long-term memory," said Goldfarb, who is also a member of Yale's Wu Tsai Institute, an interdisciplinary research initiative that explores cognition.
The researchers wanted to examine these processes separately to determine how cortisol affects the brain's ability to recognize emotional significance and preserve an experience as a lasting memory.
Watching the Brain Form Emotional Memories

To investigate, the Yale team conducted an experiment in which participants took a pill containing either hydrocortisone, a form of cortisol, or an inactive placebo. They then viewed a series of pictures while undergoing functional MRI (fMRI) scanning.

This imaging technique measures changes in blood flow and oxygen levels associated with brain activity, allowing researchers to identify which areas of the brain are more active during different tasks.
As participants examined the pictures, they reported their emotional reactions to each image. The following day, researchers tested how well they remembered what they had seen.

Each person completed the experiment twice, once after receiving hydrocortisone and once after receiving the placebo. The study used a double blind design, meaning neither the participants nor the experimenter knew which substance had been administered during a particular session.
This approach allowed the scientists to compare how the same person's brain responded with and without the additional cortisol.
A Five-Second Look at Brain Network Activity
One of the study's most important advances came from the way researchers analyzed the brain scans.

Scientists often study a measurement called functional connectivity, which describes how closely activity in different parts of the brain fluctuates together. When two regions show synchronized patterns of activity, it can indicate that they are participating in related processes.

Traditionally, examining these relationships requires several minutes of brain imaging data. The Yale team instead analyzed functional connectivity during individual trials lasting only around five seconds.

Using these brief snapshots, the researchers tested whether patterns of brain activity could predict two different outcomes: how emotionally intense participants found a picture and whether they would remember that picture the following day.

The approach worked for both. By identifying patterns associated with emotional intensity and memory formation separately, the scientists were able to examine how cortisol influenced each network and the interactions between them.
This gave the researchers a more detailed picture of the changing brain activity associated with emotional memory formation.
Cortisol Changes How Brain Networks Work Together
First, cortisol improved participants' ability to remember emotionally significant experiences, confirming what earlier research had suggested.
Second, and more importantly, the hormone strengthened emotional memory through distinct changes in the brain networks responsible for processing emotion and forming memories.

In networks associated with emotion, cortisol produced more consistent patterns of activity and increased their engagement. This suggests that the hormone helped the brain respond more strongly and reliably to the emotional significance of an experience.

In memory networks, cortisol had a different effect. It made their activity patterns more specialized for emotional information, suggesting that the brain was adjusting how it encoded emotionally meaningful experiences.

The hormone also increased coordination between the networks involved in emotion and memory. In other words, cortisol appeared to help these different brain systems work together more effectively when processing experiences that carried emotional weight.
Together, these findings suggest that stress strengthens emotional memories through several interacting brain mechanisms rather than through a single region or process.
Why Emotional Experiences Can Be So Memorable

The results help explain why stress does not necessarily improve memory for everything. Instead, its benefits appear to be selective, making experiences that feel particularly intense or meaningful more likely to be remembered.
The researchers believe this reflects the brain's ability to adapt to stressful situations by prioritizing information that may be important.

"Stress responses are fundamentally adaptive and can help you form strong memories -- but this is specific to experiences that you find to be emotionally intense or meaningful," Goldfarb said. "This is in part related to your brain increasing engagement of networks that track emotional intensity. So, if you are stressed out and trying to learn something new, it might help to think about exciting elements or strong feelings connected to what you are learning."

The findings also point to a potentially useful insight about learning. Connecting information to something exciting, personally important, or emotionally engaging could make it easier to remember, particularly during stressful situations.
Rather than simply disrupting memory, stress can sometimes help the brain identify which experiences deserve special attention and strengthen the networks involved in preserving them.

Other Yale researchers involved in the study include Rajita Sinha, the Foundations Fund Endowed Professor in Psychiatry and professor in the Child Study Center and of neuroscience at Yale School of Medicine (YSM), and Todd Constable, the Elizabeth Mears and House Jameson Professor of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging and professor of neurosurgery at YSM.
The research was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health.

articles.title: The uranium cubes that exposed Nazi Germany’s nuclear failure

paras.en: The uranium cubes that exposed Nazi Germanyâs nuclear failure

- Scientists investigating Nazi Germany's secret nuclear program have uncovered evidence that its final experimental reactor was nowhere near as close to working as previously claimed. Analysis of surviving uranium cubes and wartime documents reveals that Germany lacked the enormous quantities of uranium and heavy water needed to make its reactor operational.

During World War II, the United States raced to develop the atomic bomb partly out of fear that Nazi Germany might build one first. But how close did Germany actually come to achieving that goal? A new scientific investigation suggests the Nazi nuclear program was much further from success than its leading physicist claimed.

By examining surviving uranium cubes and previously documented historical evidence, researchers have uncovered major limitations in Germany's final experimental nuclear reactor. Their findings indicate that the project was not simply missing a few materials. The reactor would have required far more uranium and heavy water than Germany had available during the war.

The Manhattan Project, the secret American effort to develop nuclear weapons during World War II, was driven partly by the possibility that Nazi Germany might achieve a similar breakthrough first. Scientists knew that whoever succeeded could gain an unprecedented military advantage.

One possible route to an atomic bomb involved building a nuclear reactor capable of producing plutonium, a radioactive element that can be used in nuclear weapons. Inside a reactor, uranium atoms undergo nuclear fission, a process in which their nuclei split apart and release energy along with additional particles called neutrons. Under the right conditions, those neutrons trigger further fission reactions, creating a sustained chain reaction.
Although Nazi Germany pursued nuclear research through a program known as the Uranprojekt, historians have long debated how close its scientists came to developing a functioning reactor.

Germany's final attempt was an experimental reactor known as the B8 pile, constructed in 1945 under the direction of physicist Werner Heisenberg. The device used cubes of natural uranium suspended in heavy water, a specialized substance that played an essential role in controlling the nuclear reaction.
Why Heavy Water Was Essential to Nazi Germany's Reactor
Heavy water looks much like ordinary water, but its hydrogen atoms contain an additional neutron. This subtle difference makes it particularly useful in certain nuclear reactors.

In a reactor, heavy water serves as a neutron moderator, meaning it slows down the neutrons released during fission. Slower neutrons are more likely to trigger additional fission reactions in uranium, helping sustain the chain reaction needed for a working reactor.
For Germany, however, obtaining enough heavy water was a major obstacle.

During the war, the only European facility capable of supplying the heavy water needed by the German program was the Norsk Hydro plant in Vemork, Norway. Germany gained control of the facility after occupying Norway in April 1940.

Recognizing its importance to Germany's nuclear ambitions, Allied forces targeted the plant through sabotage and bombing operations. A major American bombing raid struck Vemork on November 16, 1943, contributing to the eventual end of heavy water production there.
Scientists Reexamine Hitler's Final Nuclear Reactor

When American forces discovered and dismantled the B8 reactor in 1945, it had never achieved criticality. In nuclear physics, criticality refers to the point at which a chain reaction becomes self-sustaining, with each generation of fission reactions producing enough neutrons to maintain the next.

Reaching this threshold is a fundamental requirement for operating a conventional nuclear reactor. Despite its name, criticality does not mean that a reactor is about to explode. It simply means the nuclear chain reaction can continue without relying on an external neutron source.

Heisenberg, who led the German reactor effort, maintained that the B8 experiment had come close to reaching this milestone. He argued that the device needed only a relatively modest increase in its uranium supply to become operational.
But a new study led by Timothy Koeth and his colleagues challenges that assessment.

The researchers examined two surviving cubes of natural uranium that had been used in the German nuclear project. They also studied historical records, technical reports, correspondence, and other archival documents to reconstruct the reactor's capabilities and determine what would have been required for it to work.
Their findings paint a very different picture of Germany's nuclear progress.
A Massive Uranium and Heavy Water Shortage

According to the researchers' calculations, the B8 reactor would have needed approximately twice as much uranium and more than twice as much heavy water as it actually contained to achieve a sustained nuclear chain reaction.

The required quantities exceeded the materials available to Germany during the war. In particular, the heavy water needed for a functioning reactor was far beyond the amount the German program could obtain from its Norwegian supply.
The researchers also examined whether German scientists could have avoided the heavy water shortage by using graphite, a form of carbon that can also slow neutrons in nuclear reactors.
This approach had worked for American scientists, who achieved the world's first controlled, sustained nuclear chain reaction using a graphite-moderated reactor in 1942.

However, the graphite available in German-controlled territory contained impurities that made it unsuitable for the same purpose. In particular, traces of boron could absorb neutrons that would otherwise help sustain the reaction, preventing the reactor from reaching criticality.
That meant Germany could not simply substitute graphite for heavy water to overcome its supply problems.
Why Nazi Germany's Nuclear Program Was Doomed
The findings suggest that Heisenberg significantly underestimated how much additional material his reactor would have required.
Rather than standing on the verge of a functioning nuclear reactor, the German scientists faced shortages they could not overcome with the resources available to them.

The research also provides a clearer explanation for why Germany's nuclear program failed to make the transition from experimental reactor designs to a working reactor capable of producing material for an atomic bomb.

Based on the designs and materials available during World War II, the researchers conclude that Nazi Germany lacked the resources necessary to make either its heavy water reactor or a graphite-based alternative operational.

More than eight decades after the war, the surviving uranium cubes have helped resolve a longstanding historical question, revealing just how far Nazi Germany remained from achieving a critical step toward building an atomic bomb.

articles.title: USC scientists discover how to create a never-ending supply of cancer-fighting cells

paras.en: USC scientists discover how to create a never-ending supply of cancer-fighting cells
Scientists have created a potentially renewable source of engineered immune cells that fight cancer, offering a promising path toward longer-lasting, ready-made immunotherapies.

- USC scientists have discovered a way to create a potentially renewable supply of genetically engineered immune cells that can attack cancer and strengthen the body's natural defenses. By growing and modifying immature immune cells rather than mature ones, researchers developed a system that can continuously produce tumor-fighting cells inside the body.

Scientists at the University of Southern California (USC) have discovered a way to produce a potentially renewable supply of cancer-fighting immune cells, opening a promising new direction for cancer treatment. By working with immature cells that can develop into powerful immune defenders, the researchers have created a system capable of generating large numbers of genetically engineered cells that recognize tumors and help activate the body's natural defenses.

The breakthrough, described in a study published in Cell, could help overcome some of the biggest obstacles facing cancer immunotherapy, including the difficulty of manufacturing enough immune cells and keeping them active in the body. In experiments involving mice, the engineered cells established themselves in bone marrow, produced new immune cells, and slowed the progression of both blood cancers and solid tumors.

The USC Stem Cell-led team focused on a type of immature immune cell called granulocyte-monocyte progenitors (GMPs). These cells normally develop into macrophages and other immune cells that protect the body from infections and participate in immune responses. The researchers found that GMPs could be grown extensively in the laboratory while retaining their ability to develop into functioning immune cells. They could also be genetically modified to recognize specific cancer markers and strengthen broader immune responses.

paras.en: "The study establishes a scalable and engineerable GMP platform for cellular immunotherapy and introduces concepts that we believe could have broad implications for both cancer immunotherapy and stem cell biology," said the paper's corresponding author Qi-Long Ying, MD, PhD, professor of stem cell biology and regenerative medicine at the Keck School of Medicine of USC.
Scientists Discover a Surprising Ability in Immune Cell Precursors
Beyond its potential applications in cancer treatment, the discovery challenges a long-standing understanding of how blood and immune cells develop.

Stem cells are known for their ability to self-renew, meaning they can repeatedly divide while maintaining their original properties. In the blood-forming system, this ability has traditionally been associated primarily with hematopoietic stem cells, which can produce all the major types of blood and immune cells.

Progenitor cells, by contrast, are further along in development and are already committed to producing a more limited range of cells. They are generally thought to have less capacity for long-term self-renewal.

The USC researchers demonstrated that GMPs can retain this ability under carefully controlled laboratory conditions. Rather than quickly maturing into other cell types, the progenitors continued multiplying while preserving their identity and their capacity to generate functional immune cells.

"The prevailing view has been that long-term self-renewal in the blood system is primarily a property of the hematopoietic stem cells that can generate any type of blood or immune cell," said Ying. "We found that, under the right conditions, GMPs can also self-renew, dividing extensively while keeping their identity and ability to produce functional immune cells. That gives us a scalable starting point for engineering cell therapies for cancer, infectious disease and potentially many other conditions."
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: This finding could be especially important for developing treatments that require large, reliable supplies of genetically engineered immune cells.
Why Macrophages Could Be Powerful Weapons Against Cancer

Macrophages are among the immune system's most versatile defenders. Their name comes from Greek words meaning "big eaters," reflecting their ability to surround and engulf bacteria, damaged cells, and other unwanted material.

They also help coordinate immune responses by sending signals that influence the behavior of other immune cells. Some macrophages can enter tumors and attack cancer cells, making them attractive candidates for cancer immunotherapy.

One particularly promising application involves solid tumors, which include cancers that form masses in organs and tissues. Existing therapies based on engineered T cells have achieved their greatest successes against certain blood cancers, but treating solid tumors has proven more difficult.
Macrophages offer a potentially different approach because they naturally migrate into tissues and can penetrate tumors. However, turning them into practical treatments presents several challenges.

Once macrophages have fully matured, they are difficult to multiply in large quantities outside the body. They are also challenging to modify genetically and can be damaged during freezing and storage, complicating the production and distribution of cell therapies.

Another problem occurs after administration. Mature macrophages often collect in organs such as the lungs and liver instead of spreading widely throughout the body. Their relatively rapid disappearance can also limit how long a treatment remains effective.
To work around these limitations, the scientists decided to begin at an earlier stage of immune cell development.
Creating a Renewable Supply of Cancer-Fighting Immune Cells

Rather than trying to manufacture large numbers of mature macrophages, first author Shi Yue, MD, of Ying's laboratory and his colleagues concentrated on GMPs, the progenitor cells that can produce macrophages.

The researchers developed a precisely defined mixture of chemicals that allowed GMPs to survive and multiply for extended periods in the laboratory. The mixture prevented the cells from prematurely developing into mature immune cells, preserving a renewable population of progenitors.

Even after extensive laboratory expansion, the GMPs maintained the molecular characteristics that defined them. Importantly, they also retained the ability to develop into functional macrophages and other related immune cells when needed.

This approach could make it possible to manufacture large numbers of engineered immune cells from a starting population that can be continually expanded, instead of repeatedly collecting and preparing mature cells.

To confirm that the method could be reproduced, collaborators in the laboratory of Ravi Majeti, MD, PhD, at Stanford University independently demonstrated that GMPs could be maintained for extended periods and genetically engineered. Their results provided additional support for the reliability of the technique and its potential use in future cell therapies.

Majeti, Director of the Institute for Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine at Stanford University, noted: "This method for the expansion and engineering of GMPs opens the door to numerous translational applications, much like T cell expansion and engineering. We have already demonstrated engineering of these cells to drive multiple potent functions, and there is a lot more to be explored."
Engineering Immune Cells to Recognize and Attack Tumors
The team next investigated whether these expandable progenitor cells could be programmed to fight cancer.

They genetically engineered GMPs to carry a chimeric antigen receptor, or CAR. This engineered receptor allows immune cells to identify a particular molecular marker on the surface of cancer cells, helping direct their activity toward tumors.

CAR technology is already an important part of cancer immunotherapy, particularly in treatments that modify a patient's T cells to recognize and attack cancer. The USC researchers explored whether a similar strategy could be applied to GMPs, allowing them to generate engineered macrophages and other immune cells.

The scientists also equipped some of the progenitor cells with an additional immune-activating signal. This modification was designed to recruit and stimulate nearby immune cells, including T cells, which can help mount a stronger attack against cancer.
The added signal offered another potentially important advantage. It remained effective even when the immune characteristics of donor cells did not match those of the recipient.

That finding raises the possibility of developing off-the-shelf treatments using cells manufactured in advance from donors. Unlike personalized cell therapies, which must be prepared separately using each patient's own cells, such products could potentially be produced in larger batches and made available to multiple patients.
Engineered Cells Slow Cancer Progression in Mice
After successfully expanding and engineering GMPs from both mice and humans, the researchers investigated their therapeutic potential in mouse experiments.

When administered to mice, the progenitor cells established themselves in the bone marrow and other locations responsible for blood cell production. These environments provided places where the GMPs could generate additional engineered macrophages and related immune cells.

This was an important difference from treatments using mature macrophages. Instead of relying solely on immune cells that may disappear relatively quickly, the progenitors could provide a continuing source of replacement cells from within the body.
The strategy may therefore help overcome the rapid clearance that has limited macrophage therapies, including approaches evaluated in recent clinical trials.
The researchers tested the engineered cells in mice with blood cancers and solid tumors. GMPs carrying CAR receptors slowed disease progression in both types of cancer.

The effects were even stronger when the progenitors carried both CAR receptors and the additional signal designed to activate other immune cells. This combination improved the treatment's ability to stimulate a broader antitumor response.

Although these findings are encouraging, the cancer-treatment results remain preclinical. Further research will be needed to establish whether engineered GMPs can be used safely and effectively in people, particularly if they are intended to persist and produce immune cells over extended periods.
Potential Applications Beyond Cancer Treatment
The scientists also explored whether their approach could help treat conditions involving defective immune defenses.

In a separate mouse experiment, they studied chronic granulomatous disease, an inherited disorder that interferes with the ability of certain immune cells to kill harmful microbes. People with this condition are particularly vulnerable to recurrent bacterial and fungal infections because their immune cells cannot eliminate some pathogens effectively.
When the researchers administered GMPs to mice with the disorder, the cells restored the animals' ability to fight bacterial infection.

This result suggests that renewable, genetically engineered immune cell progenitors might eventually have applications beyond cancer, including treatments for inherited immune deficiencies and potentially infectious diseases.
The broader lesson, according to the researchers, is that the developmental stage of an immune cell may be just as important as the genetic modifications used to turn it into a treatment.

By engineering cells before they fully mature, scientists may be able to create therapies that are easier to manufacture, more adaptable, and capable of maintaining a continuing supply of specialized immune defenders.
"Our study suggests that the future of immunotherapy may depend not only on designing better CAR receptors, but also on choosing the right developmental stage of the cell," said Ying.
The study, published in Cell, is titled "Expansion and CAR engineering of granulocyte-monocyte progenitors for cellular immunotherapy."

Along with Ying, Yue, and Majeti, the research team included Zheng Guo, Crystal Pan, Xueyuan A.
