articles.title: WHO urges vigilance after Kenya confirms second Ebola case

paras.en: WHO urges vigilance after Kenya confirms second Ebola case

The World Health Organization (WHO) continues to support Kenya’s efforts to contain Ebola after a second person tested positive for the Bundibugyo virus, the UN agency’s representative in the country said on Thursday.
The patient, a 39-year-old man, is a relative of Kenya’s first case – related to the ongoing deadly outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) – who died in hospital on 5 October.
He was among contacts who were placed in quarantine and developed symptoms on 13 October.

“I congratulate the Government for taking this important step to ensure that contacts are listed and quarantined,” WHO Representative Dr. Neema Rusibamayila Kimambo told UN News in Nairobi, a day after the Ministry of Health confirmed the new case.

“But to defeat this disease, it's not about the Government, it is not about partners It is about everybody,” she insisted. “We all have a role to play and if each one of us plays our part, then we should be able to contain the disease and stop community spread.”
Kenya’s first Ebola patient and fatality was a local man who had been living in the DRC, where the record outbreak continues to spread in the east.
He arrived in Nairobi via Uganda on 3 October and died in hospital two days later.
Dr. Kimambo commended health authorities who “cast the net very wide” to identify people who had come into contact with him – whether in the air or on the ground.
The more than 40 people included airline passengers and crew, airplane cleaners, airport workers, baggage handlers and immigration officials, as well as health personnel and family members.

Most are in quarantine, while a few low-risk contacts have self-quarantined and are being monitored. Meanwhile, every effort is being made to reach six passengers who have been difficult to locate because they have foreign phone numbers.

Even before the first case , WHO and the Kenyan Government were stepping up Ebola preparedness after the outbreak was declared in the DRC in May. Neighbouring Uganda also confronted the disease, with any outbreak officially ruled out in late August.

Teams are working across all areas, including surveillance and contact tracing. WHO has also brought in a senior incident manager who participated in the Ebola response in Uganda, as well as other experts.

“We are building on the work that we started during the preparedness phase, so case management and IPC (infection prevention and control) are critical at this time in the quarantine centres,” Dr. Kimambo said.

WHO also continues to provide assistance to Kenya in various other ways. The UN agency has donated some $70,000 worth of supplies, including IPC and laboratory items, since the first Ebola case was identified.
Additionally, more than 4,000 health workers have been trained, including for screenings at ports of entry.

While Dr. Kimambo said there still is no need to impose travel restrictions or close national borders, she underlined the importance of appropriate screening to identify travellers who may pose a health risk.
Preventing Ebola begins with understanding how the disease is transmitted, she said, which is through contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person.
She reiterated the advice to practice regular handwashing, use hand sanitizer and avoid shaking hands.

As Ebola symptoms include fever, vomiting and diarrhoea – which mimic symptoms of malaria and other diseases – she stressed the need to seek medical care quickly. In the interim, Kenyans are urged to keep calm and stay safe.

“I think one is not to over panic and be very fearful because we do not have community spread,” she said. “But two, let us be responsible. Whoever is sick, let’s make sure we go to a health facility and get care. And also, let us ensure that we take IPC measures.”

articles.title: Ukraine: Critical health supplies destroyed in ongoing Russian attacks

paras.en: Ukraine: Critical health supplies destroyed in ongoing Russian attacks

Ongoing and deadly Russian attacks across Ukraine are causing serious healthcare disruption, with more than $1.5 million-worth of medicines and supplies destroyed in four separate strikes on warehouses used by the UN there since July.

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 21 warehouses have been targeted this year, out of a total of 400 incidents, almost all involving heavy weapons which is classified as firearms, tanks, missiles, bombs and mortars.

Speaking to UN News, WHO Communications Officer Sarah Tyler described what she witnessed at hospitals and warehouses that had come under attack: “When you stand in those places, you really understand what the numbers mean.

“In just three months, four warehouses used by WHO were hit and three were destroyed…The health workers I met keep caring for patients under extraordinary pressure; protecting health care means protecting them.”

The development comes amid a large wave of large-scale attacks by Russian forces across Ukraine this week. Strikes overnight into Wednesday killed at least three people in Kyiv and left hundreds of thousands without power.
This was despite the announcement by President Trump last Friday of an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine.
Over the weekend, other Russian attacks included one in Zaporizhzhia that killed more than 20 people including four children.
Following the bombing, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) highlighted the “unimaginable loss” for families, insisting that the violence “must not become the new normal”.

WHO has verified more than 3,300 attacks on healthcare since the full-scale Russian invasion in February 2022. A total of 247 people have been killed and more than 1,090 health workers and patients have been injured, according to data compiled by the agency.

The agency underlined that the consequences of attacks extend well beyond damage to individual buildings. “When warehouses and other humanitarian installations are hit, medicines, medical equipment, laboratory reagents and other essential supplies can be lost, disrupting the support that health facilities need to treat patients,” explained Dr Ihor Perehinets, WHO Regional Emergency and Health Security Director.
He stressed that Ukraine’s health workers face “extraordinary pressure” while continuing to deliver care.
“Protecting health services means protecting the people who provide them, as well as the medical supplies, equipment and humanitarian infrastructure on which their work depends,” Dr Perehinets added.

The agency’s support in Ukraine includes emergency response, assistance with trauma care, medical supply provision, energy resilience and developing the capacity to manage chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear incidents.

WHO’s 2026 Ukraine appeal seeks $42 million to support 700,000 people. Continued funding is important to sustaining emergency health operations, maintaining access to essential services, replenishing medical supplies and strengthening preparedness.

paras.en: Martin Ho: Tottenham Women boss on summer signings, WSL start and facing Chelsea and Arsenal

Very few successes ever come easy. Whether it's title wins or top three finishes, every WSL season is becoming harder to predict - and plenty of clubs, including Tottenham, have their eyes on the prizes.

Spurs started the 2026/27 season with statement wins against Crystal Palace and Aston Villa, winning by an aggregate of 11-0 - but they came crashing back down to earth with a 6-1 defeat to London City Lionesses before the international break.

It would have offered Tottenham boss Martin Ho and his players a sharp reminder about the task they have on their hands if they want to finish in the Champions League spots this season - and it does not get any easier with Chelsea and Arsenal to come in the next two games, starting at Stamford Bridge on Sunday, live on Sky Sports.
- Transfer Centre LIVE! | WSL latest news and transfers
- WSL scores & fixtures | FREE WSL highlights
- Got Sky? Watch WSL games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream WSL games with no contract📺

But the ever-pragmatic Ho will not have forgotten that. Spurs have gone from relegation contenders to European consideration in less than 18 months under the former Brann boss, but any route to the top will not be straight forward.

Speaking exclusively to Sky Sports, he said: "You're always optimistic that it can go well, but I'm also realistic that you don't just have this long-term success. It's not linear, there's going to be ups and downs, but I know if you want long-term consistency, you're going to have to have this.

"We can't just go from being a team that's been fighting at the bottom of the table to go and challenge for the [WSL] trophy and make that successful and consistent over years to come. There's a process to that but the ambition is always to be at the top of that table.
"Since coming in, I've tried to push standards, push the expectation with staff and players to give us a platform that can give us an opportunity to progress.

"The players deserve a lot of credit for that because they take the information and run with it. They play with courage, bravery, with personality which is what I asked for and their commitment and willingness is first class.

"Maybe there were times early on when I thought it was going to take a lot longer to get to where we want to be identity-wise, but the players deserve the credit because they've enabled us to maybe accelerate a little bit quicker than what I probably thought."

Part of that has come through shrewd recruitment, particularly this summer. Spurs signed Champions League winners Victoria Pelova and Alice Sombath from Arsenal and Lyon respectively, Caitlin Dijkstra also joined from Wolfsburg in just a few of the impressive incomings.
It all follows Ho's plan of bringing in different experiences from league, European and international levels to strengthen the squad and add a steel they were perhaps missing in his first year.
"We felt like we needed certain qualities in certain positions and those players that have come in have allowed us to do that," Ho said.
"They've also been in environments where they've been competing in different ways, they'll bring those experiences here which was important for us that we have a diverse environment and culture.

"You also want to make sure you get a balance also between the youth and experience of the squad. You want to get a balance of where you feel relationships can be built and where they can be long-term on the pitch.

"Alice [Sombath] was one of those in that position where she's had such wonderful experiences at Lyon of winning titles, but also internationally, she's got really good credibility at such a young age. The opportunity to bring her in was huge for us and someone we have followed for a while.

"Then people like Victoria [Pelova], who's coming off the back of a long-term injury. She was maybe low of confidence and wasn't in a place where she felt her football could go forward. The opportunity to bring her here after having those conversations was important.
"She's been part of a winning culture and a winning environment and those environments are what we want to bring to the club, which she can share and we can lean on those experiences from her.

"But since she's come in, she's been outstanding in terms of giving her the enthusiasm again to play football, but giving her the confidence and belief she can achieve what she wants in terms of own ambitions."

On October 24, Pelova will be reunited with her former Arsenal team-mates in the north London derby at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. It is the site of Spurs' only win against the Gunners in any competition, and given their rivals' own dismal start to the season, might be sensing another.
Before that though, a resurgent Chelsea - and another insight into whether this Tottenham team have what it takes to compete against the WSL's best.

"You have to show a willingness to compete in those games first," Ho reflected. "You go in with the mindset and the objective is always to win the game, but we have to look at the process behind that first and the performance has to allow you to be in that position psychologically.

"Are they going to be tough games? 100 percent, but they're the games you want to play and I want to play in as a coach, the players want to play in. The commercial interest is big in those because they're London derbies so you have to embrace them as a player.

"But they're the ones where you will really see the character and belief of the group, they're the ones where you'll really see the development and the progress of the team, but one game doesn't tell you if you're a good team or a bad team.
"It maybe gives you some answers in terms of where we need to go and the direction we need to go in, but it doesn't define you."

After a bruising defeat nearly two weeks ago, Spurs will have a point to prove in their next two games. While they might not define them as a team, it could go some way in defining where they finish come May.

articles.title: Itauma could be one win away from another world title shot

paras.en: Moses Itauma could be one victory away from a second world title shot after a 'risky' comeback fight in January

Moses Itauma will take a "risky" comeback fight in January, says promoter Frank Warren; If Itauma wins he could then be in a position to challenge for a world title again with his conqueror Filip Hrgovic likely to make his first defence of the IBF championship in Croatia early in 2027
Moses Itauma could be one victory away from another world title shot.
Itauma, a highly regarded 21-year-old prospect, took on Filip Hrgovic for the IBF belt in August.
It was Itauma's first world championship fight. After starting very strongly, he tired, unravelled and was halted by Hrgovic in nine rounds.

Promoter Frank Warren, however, plans to bring Itauma back in a good level fight in January to set him up for another world title tilt.
"It'll be a decent fight. He's got to be in with somebody who's going to give him a test," Warren told Sky Sports.

"When you're coming off a loss any comeback fight is a risky fight. He'll be wanting to go out there with something to prove. We want to see him in with someone reasonable for the comeback fight and he wants to get back into the mix.
"He's going to have to come back and show what he's all about."

After that Itauma will be targeting a world champion. As well as promoting Itauma, Warren represents new IBF champion Hrgovic, WBC heavyweight titlist Agit Kabayel, as well as WBO champion Daniel Dubois.
"He wants to be back in the mix so he's going to be very active next year," Warren said of Itauma. "Straight in, no messing about.
"He could fight any of them. Because if he wins he'll be straight back into, I think, the top half of the rankings."

Warren added of Itauma's defeat: "Hrgovic managed to absorb the punishment. Even when [Itauma] was blowing he was still throwing shots, even when he got caught he was still trying to fight back. He did tick some other boxes as far as I was concerned."

"Everything is tracking well so far. Frank [Sanchez] is confident he'll win and is eager for his chance to become world champion.
"Hrgovic is elite and won't be an easy opponent, but I fully expect Frank to get the job done."

articles.title: ‘We’re done’: Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian oil refineries as anger at Trump mounts
articles.author: Dan De Luce

paras.en: Ukraine has resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy angrily accused the United States of betraying Kyiv with a “dangerous” withdrawal of support critical to its defense against Russia.

Ukraine held off on attacks for three days after President Donald Trump’s unilateral “energy ceasefire” announcement, but accused Russia of repeatedly attacking its power grid. Zelenskyy voiced mounting frustration over the Kremlin’s failure to abide by the truce and what he sees as U.S. attempts to pressure Kyiv, after gaps in intelligence sharing on Russian attacks and restrictions on the Starlink internet service.

Satellite internet functionality via Starshield — the military version of the SpaceX service — was being at least partially restored Thursday, according to a source in the Ukrainian Defense Ministry, who spoke on the condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the topic.
In an interview with the Financial Times published Thursday, Zelenskyy indicated his patience had already been exhausted.
“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Zelenskyy was quoted as saying.

Hours later, a fire was reported at an oil refinery in the western Ryazan region, Gov. Pavel Malkov said. The Russian Defense Ministry said Ukraine had “attempted a massive attack on the Ryazan oil refinery.”

Ukraine has been reeling from a sudden shift from Trump, who struck a diesel deal with Russia in an apparent bid to relieve pressure at the pump ahead of the midterm elections. He then demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil facilities and called for Zelenskyy to be replaced as its leader.
Trump’s “energy ceasefire” appeared to take both warring sides by surprise. He has blamed the Ukrainian campaign for fueling a rise in energy prices, despite the impact of his own war with Iran.
The moves caused frustration and confusion in Ukraine and Europe, intensifying concerns over how much of an ally the U.S. remained in the fight against Russia.

That worry was exacerbated Wednesday when Kyiv said it was facing a slowing down of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite terminals, disrupting battlefield missions and its ability to intercept Russian drones.

Ukraine was swarmed by Russian drones Wednesday and, since early Thursday, more than 850 had filled the skies over Ukraine, Zelenskyy said. “And this comes precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted,” he said, referring to the Starlink slowdown.
Musk, a staunch ally of Trump, wrote on social media that decisions on restricting the use of Starshield were up to the U.S. military and ultimately Trump.
Overnight, Musk said it was “time for Zelenskyy to go.”

The Defense Ministry source said Kyiv was still seeking clarification on the reasons for Wednesday’s throttling of the technology, on which Ukraine relies for battlefield communication, drone operations and air defense.

Questions are mounting about whether the U.S. has stopped or limited the sharing of critical military intelligence with Ukraine, after Zelenskyy said several ballistic strikes on Kyiv did not come with the usual advance warning from its partners.

European and Ukrainian officials told NBC News they believed that the moves, coming only days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia’s diesel exports and railed against Zelenskyy, were likely aimed at pressuring Kyiv into making concessions at the negotiating table amid a stalemate in peace talks.

Ukraine was concerned that the chain of events amounted to an effort to pile pressure on Kyiv and backtrack on years of U.S. promises to help fend off the Russian invasion, one of the Ukrainian officials said.

Ukraine relies heavily on U.S. intelligence and the Starshield satellite network to defend itself against Russian drone and missile attacks, and also to target Russian forces with its own drones. A reduction in intelligence assistance or satellite access could seriously undermine Ukraine’s battlefield prospects just as winter sets in, according to military experts.

Ukrainian military officials were told by their U.S. counterparts that “if you will not stop [the energy strikes], we will block intelligence,” Zelenskyy said, according to the Financial Times, although it was subsequently presented to Kyiv as a technical glitch.

The withdrawal of the intelligence and simultaneous weakening of Starlink satellite internet were “dangerous” for Ukraine, he told the newspaper, adding that fighting without the U.S. would be “very difficult.”
In a separate interview with Piers Morgan on Wednesday, Zelenskyy acknowledged he felt “betrayed” by Trump’s actions.
The White House did not immediately respond to an overnight request for comment on Zelenskyy’s accusations and the renewed Ukrainian strikes.

articles.title: Harry and Meghan cheered on first joint appearance since returning to U.K.
articles.author: Laura Saravia

paras.en: LONDON — Prince Harry and Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, were making their first royal-style public appearance together Thursday since they returned to the United Kingdom with their two children.
Harry, 42, and Meghan, 45, were visiting three charities in Nottingham, as they look to rebuild their image in Britain six years after walking away from royal life.

Nottingham, a city in central England known as the setting for the famous “Robin Hood” legend, holds a special place in the couple’s history as the place where they made their first joint public appearance after announcing their engagement in 2017.
“It’s almost a full circle moment because it looks very much like a royal engagement,” NBC News royal contributor Emily Nash said.

The events Thursday began with a visit to the Community Recording Studio, a youth and community charity in Nottingham that Harry has visited before, including just last year. They were greeted by a cheering crowd, filled largely with young children.
Harry and Meghan, who wore a long burgundy coat, stopped to take selfies, give hugs and shake hands. They also spent a few minutes talking to members of the public and the children.
The couple were also due to visit the region’s biggest food bank, Himmah, and Epic Partners, which offers disadvantaged young people mentoring programs, sports and education.
Noting that the couple will be visiting a charity Harry has a “long history with,” Nash said they were certain to “get a warm reception” given their “long connection with it.”
But they have not always received such a warm welcome since their return to the U.K. with Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5.
The couple remain locked in a public row with Buckingham Palace about their status and their lack of publicly funded police protection.

A letter sent on behalf of King Charles III to senior government and military officials confirmed Harry and Meghan remain nonworking members of the royal family. A spokesperson for the couple told NBC News they were “surprised” by the letter, though they accepted that status when they left Britain for a quieter life in Montecito, California, an affluent coastal enclave in Santa Barbara.

Their relationship with the royal family has been strained in the years since, with the couple leveling explosive allegations of racism and bullying in their Netflix documentary “Harry & Meghan” and in Harry’s memoir, “Spare.”
News of their return to the U.K. sent shock waves through the British media, and the couple have faced other complications as they settle back into British life.

“It was a bit of a bumpy road for Harry and Meghan,” Nash said. “They had to had to move their children from their school after just two days, but I’m told they’re settling in well now and Archie and Lili are very happy at their new school.”
The couple’s royal-style visit to Nottingham will renew questions about their security.
With or without it, Nash said, “this is them dipping their toe back in the water” and “nothing’s stopping them.”
“They don’t need the palace’s permission to do this,” she said.

articles.title: Donald Trump calls off planned live stream of firing squad execution
articles.author: Thomas Morgan

paras.en: Donald Trump says the Pentagon's plans to live stream a firing squad execution will not go ahead.
Nidal Hasan is set to be executed on December 3 for a deadly mass shooting in 2009 that killed 13 soldiers.
Plans to live stream the execution prompted outrage in the US and beyond, including in Australia.
US President Donald Trump says the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad will not be live streamed.
The decision came after intense backlash to the announcement that the execution would be shown online.
Hasan killed 13 US army soldiers and injured another 32 during a shooting at a Texas military base in 2009.

Australian politicians were among those critical of the decision, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese flagging that the federal government was exploring ways to prevent the stream being shown in Australia.
Mr Trump had previously indicated he approved of the live stream, but acknowledged on Thursday, local time, that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die".
In a social media post, Mr Trump said publicly airing the execution "might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan".
Hasan's execution is scheduled for December 3, according to the Pentagon.
Mr Trump said the execution could still be viewed in person by immediate families of the victims, "if they so choose".
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's announcement earlier this month that the execution would be live streamed prompted significant blowback within the US from both Republicans and Democrats.
Concerns were raised that the images could be used to fuel radicalisation.
Among those saying they would not watch the execution was Vice-President JD Vance.
“So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Mr Vance said.
In Australia, Mr Albanese said social media platforms had a moral duty to block the stream.
"I think anybody broadcasting this will damage their own reputations as well. They have a social responsibility here to do the right thing," he told the ABC's Afternoon Briefing on Tuesday.
The eSafety Commissioner, however, said the government could not prevent platforms from showing the footage.
Politicians from the Liberal Party, the Greens and One Nation all expressed opposition to the execution being live streamed online.

articles.title: Remains may be earliest evidence of ancient human speared to death
articles.author: Jacinta Bowler

paras.en: Researchers uncover Neanderthal remains they suggest show the oldest known evidence of a fatal blow with a wooden spear.
They also say the remains, known as Shanidar A, may show evidence of burial practices and familial care.
But an independent expert says, although the findings are "interesting", more research is needed to support the study's conclusions.
An oddly circular hole in a Neanderthal's shoulder bone may be the oldest known evidence of an ancient human fatally wounded with a wooden spear.
That's according to research published today in Scientific Reports.
The UK and Spanish team also found evidence of burial and caregiving behaviour in the species.
First author Emma Pomeroy, an archaeologist at the University of Cambridge, says it shows Neanderthals were even more complex than previously understood.
"We see evidence of two contrasting facets of human nature — care and violence — juxtaposed in the same individual," Dr Pomeroy said.
"We have a tendency to romanticise hunter-gatherer or pre-agriculture lifestyles as peaceful and close to the natural world … but it's not that simple."
But other experts were not convinced by the evidence outlined in the study.
Neanderthal lived with 'painful' tooth injury
The Shanidar Cave In Iraqi Kurdistan has revealed a plethora of Neanderthal remains since it was first excavated 1953.
The new study looks at recently discovered 75,000-year-old remains of a Neanderthal man in his 40s known as Shanidar A.
"Their body was placed in a very specific spot in the cave, tucked in behind a huge rock that stood between them and the cave mouth," Dr Pomeroy said.
"Over the subsequent years or decades, the remains of at least four other Neanderthal individuals were placed directly above."
Shanidar A's remains, which include a mostly complete hand, teeth and a left shoulder blade, have multiple signs of damage.
The teeth, which the team says were quite damaged, healed partially while the man was still alive.
"They must have been hit very hard in the face, which made one of their bottom front teeth split in half," Dr Pomeroy said.
"The broken edge became covered in hardened plaque showing they continued living afterwards without that part of the tooth.
"The injury would have been incredibly painful."
This, the researchers said, might indicate the man's family group provided care and support, at least in the short term.
"They likely needed some care and support from their group with drinking, communicating, eating," she said.
While Shanidar A survived the dental issues, the team suggested an unusual, smooth-edged and circular hole in his shoulder blade indicated the likely cause of his demise.
Lack of healing on the bone, and fragments found nearby suggested the injury happened about the time of death.
"It had to be something that could make a hole through a shoulder blade and all the muscle, bones and organs over the top – something like a weapon," Dr Pomeroy said.
The team hypothesised the circular hole was made with a wooden spear.
Wooden spears dating between 200,000–400,000 years old have been found in Europe.
"The diameter of the shaft near the pointed end fits well with the size of the hole in the scapula," Dr Pomeroy said.
"[But] we can never be sure because, of course, the wood has not preserved.

Sofia Samper Carro, an archaeologist at the Australian National University not involved with the discovery, said that, while some of the conclusions were "bold", the team needed more evidence to support its claims.
"I think it's a bit of a stretch with the justification they have so far,"
Dr Samper Carro agreed the circular damage to the shoulder blade was "weird" and not how bones usually break.
"Bones usually break in more kind of orthogonal … more linear fractures," she said.
However, she said, it was "very difficult" to know the cause of death, unless the weapon was also found.
"It's unusual that you get those circular shapes, but correlating that with the cause of death? I think it's a bit too much," she said.
Despite this, Dr Samper Carro said the site still had plenty to offer.
Dr Pomeroy's team is still excavating the Shanidar Cave site, examining the transition period when modern humans began to use it.
"We are investigating what Neanderthals and humans ate based on the animal bones they left behind, how they prepared plant and animal food … and a whole host of other questions," Dr Pomeroy said.
"There is so much fascinating work still to do."

articles.title: Court shown photos of Russell Brand shirtless in hotel before alleged rape
articles.author: Mazoe Ford and Riley Stuart

paras.en: The prosecution has continued to lay out its case in Russell Brand's rape trial.
In London on Thursday, the court heard evidence from one of the entertainer's six accusers.
The trial is expected to last for at least six weeks.
English entertainer Russell Brand asked a woman to take photos of him "prancing" in "horrible budgie smugglers", shortly before he raped her, a London court has heard.
Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing.
Brand, 51, is standing trial in Southwark Crown Court accused of several sexual offences relating to six women over a 10-year period from 1999.
He has been charged with three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one count of indecent assault. He pleaded not guilty to all.
The trial began this week and on Thursday, local time, the court heard evidence from a woman given the pseudonym Ms A, who claims Brand raped her at a political conference in 1999.
Pictures she took of Brand in her hotel room on the night the actor and comedian's alleged assault were shown to the jury.
Ms A told the court she had met Brand, who was performing but not yet famous, on the sidelines of the Labour Party's conference in Bournemouth.
She told the court they got talking about politics and discussed the potential to collaborate on a creative project.
Ms A told the court she invited him to continue speaking in her hotel room and did not initially fear for her safety because she thought Brand was gay.
"I blame myself for inviting him back to my room … that was my office. That was my workspace," she told the court, through tears. "He violated that space."
Brand was aged 24 at the time of the alleged assault, and is now 51.
The court was on Thursday played video of an interview police conducted with Ms A in September 2023 in which she outlined her accusations.
In the video, Ms A told a detective when she and Brand arrived at her hotel room, she suggested he make a cup of tea while she went to the bathroom.
She told the detective that when she emerged, Brand had undressed and was in his underwear.
"He was prancing around, I remember him prancing around being silly and asking me to take pictures of him," Ms A told the detective.
In the video played to the court Ms A told the detective Brand was "jumping up and down and being silly like an ostrich kicking his legs up".
She said he then pushed her on to the bed and raped her, which she described in detail.
Later in the day, some of the pictures Ms A said Brand asked her to take were shown to the jury.
Brand's barrister Ian Winter KC challenged Ms A's memory of the alleged assault during his cross-examination.
"You fell under his spell," he said to Ms A. "He's a very attractive young man. He's brilliant. He is very charismatic ... you wanted to spend more time with him."
"I thought he was a gay man, somebody who was intellectual and somebody who was friendly," she said.
Ms A told the court she had no idea why Brand had asked her to take photos of him wearing his "horrible budgie smugglers".
In the video played to the court, Ms A wiped away tears as she described how she felt "guilty" and "dirty" after the alleged assault, but that Brand had acted like "nothing was wrong".

She also said she did not tell police about the alleged assault until 2023 because she did not think she would be believed, but decided to after she saw a documentary airing allegations of misconduct about Brand.

articles.title: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian refineries, as Zelenskyy expresses frustration with U.S.

paras.en: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian refineries, as Zelenskyy expresses frustration with U.S.
Refinery owned by Russian oil giant Rosneft hit with Ukraine drone attack

Ukraine has resumed its attacks on Russian refineries with a strike at an installation in the Ryazan region, the regional governor said Thursday, after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy voiced his anger at the withdrawal of U.S. intelligence.

Since U.S. President Donald Trump's surprise announcement of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had refrained from attacking Russian refineries, which the U.S. leader had blamed for raising diesel prices on global markets.

But Zelenskyy had expressed increasing frustration with Russia's continued attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, which on Wednesday had left 600,000 people without power, he said. He warned that Ukraine would not suspend its own attacks indefinitely if Russia did not reciprocate and also criticized what he said was Trump's favouritism toward Russia.
In an interview with the Financial Times published on Thursday, he said Ukraine's patience had run out. "The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We're done."
- Starlink restrictions would hamper Ukraine's war effort. But the country can adapt, experts say
- 12 U.S. senators, including 6 Republicans, tell Trump to drop diesel deal with Russia
Pavel Malkov, the governor of Russia's Ryazan region, said in a post on Telegram that a major Ukrainian drone attack on the area had sparked a fire at an oil refinery.
"The material damage is now being assessed. Emergency services are working at the scene," he said.

The Ryazan refinery is owned by Russian oil giant Rosneft and feeds Moscow with fuel. It has been attacked several times by drones in recent months. The refinery accounts for almost five per cent of Russia's total oil refining throughput.
President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that the recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries had not caused significant damage and vowed that Moscow would respond, Interfax reported.
"They hit here and there. Nothing particularly significant. Nevertheless they are carrying on," Putin said.
In his interview, Zelenskyy criticized Washington's eagerness to strike business deals with Moscow and Trump's apparent admiration for Russia's Vladimir Putin.

Trump on Saturday called for Ukraine to replace Zelenskyy and railed against Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, one day after announcing a diesel supply deal with Russia, aiming to lower fuel prices that have soared since the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began in February.

Despite Ukraine's suspension of refinery attacks for three days, Ukrainian officials complained that they had not received any U.S. early-warning alerts in recent days for incoming Russian ballistic missiles.

They also said the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications service had been slowed across the country, hampering front-line operations and medium-range strikes against Russian military sites.
Musk said Wednesday in a post on X that Starshield — the military version of Starlink — was owned and controlled by the U.S. government, which decided on any limits on speed.
- Director Alex Gibney on terrifying Musk documentary: 'It's not a funeral; it's a warning'
- How high inflation is hurting Trump's Republicans in U.S. midterm campaign
Zelenskyy has said that Ukrainian military officials were warned by their U.S. counterparts that Washington would block intelligence unless they halted strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
In the FT interview, Zelenskyy said the suspension was presented to Kyiv as a technical glitch, but he dismissed that possibility, calling it a matter of "will."
Europe does not have a ready-made alternative to Starlink that Ukrainian soldiers could attach to their drones, although European governments and companies are working on long-term options.

Asked whether Ukraine would be open to halting energy strikes as a way of repairing relations with the White House, Zelenskyy told the newspaper he could only agree if in return he was given more U.S.-made Patriot interceptors, calling it the "minimum" that would be acceptable.

Trump has had a contentious relationship with Ukraine's president, dating back to 2019 when he was impeached by the Democrat-led U.S. House of Representatives for pressuring Zelenskyy for a political favour in exchange for military aid for Ukraine. Trump was acquitted in the U.S. Senate.
Trump has also been highly critical of the amount of military and humanitarian aid given to Ukraine by Joe Biden's presidential administration after Russia's 2022 invasion.
Ukraine's air force said 580 Russian drones attacked the country overnight, with 536 shot down.

The central Ukrainian region of Kirovohrad was hit by the largest Russian attack on its territory during the war, killing three people and wounding another six overnight, the local governor said Thursday.
Firefighters work at the site of an enterprise hit by a Russian drone strike on Thursday in Kropyvnytskyi. (State Emergency Service of Ukraine/Reuters)
The region, a relatively infrequent target of bombardment, was hit by more than 360 drones, local governor Andriy Raikovych wrote on Telegram.

Russia also hit Ukraine's Naftogaz gas-extraction facility in the central Poltava region overnight, the company said. It said in a statement on Telegram that the attack suspended the operations, damaged equipment and caused a fire.

Ukraine's military said Thursday it had damaged six Russian Su-34M military aircraft in an overnight strike on the Borisoglebsk airfield in Russia's Voronezh region. The Su-34M is a large fighter-bomber, costing tens of millions of dollars apiece and frequently used by Russia to drop devastating glide bombs onto Ukrainian cities near the front line.
Reuters could not independently verify the battlefield reports.

At sea, rescuers were searching Thursday for seven missing crew from one of two chemical tankers that caught fire overnight just outside Romanian territorial waters in the Black Sea, after Russian drones strayed into national airspace, Romanian officials said.

The incidents follow drone strikes on at least five other cargo ships near the coasts of Romania and neighbouring fellow NATO member Bulgaria over the past 10 days. At least 23 sailors were lost from those strikes, which took place just outside NATO's territorial waters.

articles.title: IN PHOTOS | Heavy rain floods homes, streets in Istanbul, killing 3

paras.en: IN PHOTOS | Heavy rain floods homes, streets in Istanbul, killing 3
Turkish weather agency has predicted more showers in coming days
A heavy downpour has shut down Istanbul, flooded roads and homes, and killed at least three people, officials said Thursday.
The heavy rain on Wednesday flooded homes and businesses, and inundated roads and underpasses, stranding vehicles and causing traffic chaos in Turkey's largest city.
Here, a car owner searches for his vehicle swept away by a flood in Istanbul's Ayazağa district.
The Istanbul governor's office on Thursday reported three deaths in the city and said four other people were reported missing.

A 14-year-old was electrocuted after stepping in a puddle at a park in the city's Fatih district, and a 34-year-old slipped on a sidewalk in the Sariyer district and hit their head, according to local media reports. The governor's office said the body of a third victim was discovered near another park in the Kagithane district.
Below, vehicles lie scattered in the aftermath of the rainfall in Istanbul.

A woman walks across a ladder positioned over floodwaters in Istanbul. Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi said that more than 2,700 people who were stranded by the floods were safely evacuated throughout the city.
A drone view shows partially submerged trucks on a flooded street in Istanbul.
A creek overflows after heavy rainfall in Istanbul, in this screengrab from a social media video verified by Reuters.
Turkey's weather agency has predicted more showers for Istanbul and the surrounding area in the coming days.

articles.title: Pentagon will not livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter: Trump

paras.en: Pentagon will not livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter: Trump
U.S. president made the announcement on social media

U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that the Pentagon will no longer livestream the firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan after the announcement faced bipartisan criticism and Vice-President JD Vance said he wouldn't watch it.
Trump said on social media that publicly airing the execution "might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan."
But, he continued, "any very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device."
The Pentagon has said Hasan's execution is scheduled for Dec. 3. Trump said the execution can be viewed in person by immediate families of the victims, "if they so choose."

The announcement earlier this month from Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth that Hasan's execution would be public — and subsequent confirmation from the Pentagon that it would be livestreamed — prompted significant blowback from both Republicans and Democrats, with many pointing out that the images could be used to fuel radicalization.

It also came as capital punishment already faced renewed scrutiny after Christa Pike, convicted of murder in the 1990s, survived an execution attempt by Tennessee that left her badly injured and requiring hospitalization.
The Pentagon on Thursday declined to elaborate beyond Trump's statement.
- Vance, Republican lawmakers and religious leaders oppose Pentagon plan to livestream an execution
- The U.S. plans to livestream an execution. Here's how that compares to global practice
Hegseth had said the broadcasting of the execution was needed to ensure that people understand that "there's serious consequences for these types of things."
When asked how the public execution comported with his Christian faith earlier this month, Vance said "I don't know that that's actually going to happen."
"So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance said.
But he continued: "Now, that said, I mean, look, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."

Vance is Catholic, and the church has long opposed capital punishment. The head of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops had condemned the Trump administration's decision to livestream Hasan's execution, with Archbishop Paul S. Coakley saying the move was a "barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered."
Other top Republicans, including House Speaker Mike Johnson, in Louisiana, voiced similar sentiments.
For his part, the U.S. president has defended his decision to approve the use of a firing squad, but had for days distanced himself from Hegseth's announcement that it would be public.
"Well, they're making a determination about that," Trump said Friday when asked about the livestream.

As for Hasan and the method of execution, Trump said then: "He will be killed. He will be, through firing squad. I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes. And I think the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."

The cancellation comes less than three weeks before elections to determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress, as voters increasingly register disapproval of Trump's policies in opinion polls.
Sen. John Curtis, a Republican representing Utah, called the cancellation "the right move" in a statement.
Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others on Nov. 5, 2009, at a military base in Fort Hood, Texas.

An Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, Hasan walked into a medical building on Nov. 5, 2009, where soldiers were waiting in long lines to receive immunizations and medical clearance for deployment.
He shouted "Allahu akbar" — Arabic for "God is great!" — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He also shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.

Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defence during his 2013 trial. Hasan was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement, and he now uses a wheelchair.
Hasan could seek a lengthy delay of his execution, but it's not clear whether or not he will. An attorney representing Hasan could not immediately be reached for comment by Reuters.

The U.S. military hasn't executed a service member by firing squad since the Second World War. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.
This undated photo provided by the Bell County Sheriff's Department shows former Army psychiatrist Maj. Nidal Hasan. (Bell County Sheriff's Department/The Associated Press)

articles.title: Romania: 2 ships on fire in Black Sea, 7 crew missing

paras.en: Romanian authorities have launched search and rescue operations in the Black Sea in a bid to find seven missing crew from a chemical tanker that caught fire overnight to Thursday.
Another vessel, also a chemical tanker, was also set on fire in the same region some hours earlier, but all its crew is said to be safe.
The fires occurred after Russian drones strayed into Romanian airspace, though Romanian officials have so far not explicitly said the unmanned aircraft caused the blazes.

However, there have been drone strikes on at least five other cargo ships off the coasts of Romanian and neighboring Bulgaria — both NATO members — in the past 10 days, with at least 23 sailors lost in those incidents.
Romanian President Nicusor Dan met with NATO chief Mark Rutte to address the situation.

"This is unacceptable and it has to stop. Lives, global trade, and critical infrastructure are at stake," Dan wrote on X after a meeting with NATO chief Mark Rutte to discuss a recent spate of such attacks.
"NATO has strengthened our posture along the eastern flank including with increasing counter-drone capabilities," Rutte said regarding the incident.
He said the military alliance would "continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defense posture as needed."
What do we know about the ship fires in the Black Sea?
Both ships were anchored near the mouth of the Sulina Canal leading to the Black Sea out of the Danube River when they caught fire.
Romania's naval authority said it launched its search and rescue operation after receiving an emergency alert from the San Marino-flagged tanker Wine Trader.
Five of the 12 crew members were said to be safe, while seven were missing.
"Whether it was struck by a drone or not, an investigation is currently underway," Defense Minister Radu Miruta told the Digi24 television channel.
"This is a matter of significant gravity, given that such incidents are occurring in Romanian territorial waters," he said.
The other fire, which broke out earlier, occurred onboard the Comoros-flagged chemical and oil tanker Yara J.
Ships often use the canal as a place to anchor in the case of delays caused by weather or congestion.

Romania, which shares a 614-kilometer (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube, has reported repeated breaches of its airspace by Russian drones over the past four years during Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor.
The Danube and its ports are now frequently used by Ukrainian vessels as Ukraine's Black Sea ports come under attack from Russian forces.
Ukrainian ships are also choosing routes in the Black Sea close to the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania.
This comes as shipping in the Black Sea has come under increasing attacks in recent months that have drastically reduced grain transports from both Ukraine and Russia, both major cereal exporters.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Thursday that the EU, of which both his country and Romania are members, will discuss a proposed moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea at its ongoing summit in Brussels.
Bulgaria summoned the Russian ambassador over the sinking of a ship off the country's coast on Tuesday following a drone attack.

articles.title: EU summit to focus on China, Ukraine and bloc budget

paras.en: European Union leaders are meeting in Brussels on Thursday for two days of talks that will focus on some of the major economic challenges facing the bloc, including competition from China.
The summit is sure to include some heated debate over the bloc's budget for the years 2028 to 2034, with the usual divisive negotiations between net contributors and net recipients.
On Friday, leaders are set to discuss further support for Ukraine as it faces a full-scale Russian invasion, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy due to attend.
The leaders are expected to discuss ways to remedy the bloc's massive trade deficit with China, which reached €360 billion ($400.4 billion) last year and is set to exceed that level this year.
The meeting comes less than a week after the bloc's executive body, the European Commission, reached an agreement with Beijing to curb imports of hybrid cars from China.
The EU has accused China of unfair economic practices, saying its state subsidies for its industries are creating an unlevel playing field.
Industry groups say the surge in imports from China is leading to an increasing number of factory closures in the bloc.
Ahead of the meeting, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron called for new EU measures to counter any actions leading to market distortion.
The leaders will, however, also be looking at soaring energy prices within the bloc as another factor weighing on its competitiveness.
The bloc's next seven-year budget from 2028 to 2034 is also set to be another controversial issue on the agenda, ahead of a special summit set for November to try to reach agreement.
Discussions on the budget, which requires unanimous approval, are often intense, with divisions between wealthier states and those that rely on EU cohesion funds.

"We are in very, very difficult negotiations regarding the future finances of the European Union," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has been leading the appeals for a leaner budget, said on arrival in Brussels.
"We must significantly reduce the common budget compared with the commission’s proposals. No member state of the European Union can afford this," said Merz.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson also said the proposals currently on the table were "simply not acceptable."

Italy's Giorgia Meloni is among the most vocal defenders of maintaining the traditional funds like cohesion payments, she told parliament on Wednesday that she saw "no contradiction between old policies and new priorities."
The talks at the summit are not expected to bring any breakthrough, but leaders are hoping to reach a compromise by the end of the year.
Pressure to finalize the budget is growing ahead of elections next year in several member states that could make it even more difficult to reach a deal acceptable to all.
The EU leaders are expected to turn their attention to the situation in Ukraine on Friday, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy invited to join the meeting.
"All of us in Europe want this war to end," Zelenskyy wrote after arriving. "And for that to happen, strong signals are needed — more real pressure on Russia and more defense support for Ukraine."
He is likely to urge the bloc to up its support for Kyiv as Russia intensifies its strikes ahead of winter, killing dozens of civilians.

European aid is taking on ever more importance as the US under President Donald Trump continues its ambivalent path with regard to the conflict, as reflected in a recent deal securing Russian diesel imports despite international sanctions.
Trump has also called for Zelenskyy to be replaced as Ukrainian leader.
Edited by: Natalie Muller and Wesley Dockery

articles.title: Can Kenya preserve the democratic space Raila Odinga fought for?

paras.en: AsKenya marks the first anniversary of Raila Odinga's death on Thursday, the former prime minister remains a towering figure. For many, he symbolizes the struggle for multiparty democracyand constitutional reforms. For others, his political alliances raise questions about compromise, opposition politics and the direction of the movement he built.

The question is not only how Kenya remembers Odinga — but whether the principles he championed can survive. "I want his legacy to live beyond the party," 20-year-old Nairobi resident Beatrice Chebet told DW.
Chebet said Odinga wanted a Kenya grounded in peace, democracy, constitutionalism and the rule of law. She said younger generations must carry those aspirations forward.

Odinga had a lasting effect on the experiences and political journey of younger Kenyans, Chebet said. "Some of us were Gen Zs," she said. "We did not know any form of multipartyism without reading Raila.”

Odinga's influence was shaped by decades of opposition politics, detentions and campaigns for democratic change. His role in the disputed 2007 presidential election placed him at the center of one of Kenya's most consequential political crises. The postelection violence killed more than 1,100 people and displaced hundreds of thousands.

A power-sharing agreement brokered with international mediation led by Kofi Annan, the former secretary-general of the United Nations, made Odinga prime minister in a coalition government with President Mwai Kibaki. The settlement also established a reform agenda, including constitutional change. Kenya adopted a new constitution in 2010, introducing a devolved system of government.

The security and intelligence strategist Byron Adera said Odinga's impact extended beyond electoral politics. "Raila was an institution that rocked institutions, bringing about lasting and very impactful institutional reforms for the betterment of Kenya," Adera told DW. He identifies constitutional reform and efforts to bring competing political interests together as important parts of Odinga's legacy.

Reconciliation also became one of the most contested aspects of Odinga's career. His "handshakes" of reconciliation with Kibaki in 2008 and President Uhuru Kenyatta in 2018 and cooperation with President William Ruto in 2024 illustrated his willingness to pursue political agreements with former rivals.

Supporters saw dialogue as a way to reduce tensions and advance national interests; critics questioned what such arrangements meant for an independent opposition. Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has strongly criticized the political rapprochement between President William Ruto and the late Raila Odinga.

In May, Gachagua called the handshake process "nonsense" and said it had eroded Kenya's democracy by weakening the opposition's ability to hold the government accountable. His position offers a contrasting view of the alliances that shaped Odinga's later political years.
The debate over Odinga's legacy is especially pressing within the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM), the party he helped found and led for years.

Edwin Sifuna, a potential presidential candidate in the 2027 election, who describes Odinga as both his leader and friend, said the ODM's identity and direction had changed fundamentally. "We run the risk of losing our core support, people who believed in the ideals of ODM, because we were always the party of the people," Sifuna told DW.

Sifuna said Odinga's influence on national politics and public debate was greatly missed. His remarks point to a central challenge for ODM: whether it can preserve its identity and connection with ordinary Kenyans while navigating a changing political landscape. However, in a bid to keep the Odinga name in politics, Winnie Odinga, daughter of Raila Odinga, declared that she will run for Senator of Nairobi County in the 2027 election.

Chebet said Odinga's legacy would be measured by whether future generations continue to defend the principles associated with his political journey. Adera, meanwhile, emphasizes the lasting importance of institutional reform and building bridges.

Their perspectives highlight the tension at the heart of Odinga's legacy: a leader remembered for expanding democratic possibilities, but whose political compromises remain debatable. A year after his death, Odinga's influence is still visible in Kenya's political arguments, party divisions and public calls for democratic accountability.

The lasting test will be whether Kenya's institutions, political parties and younger generation can carry those principles forward — and whether the democratic space Odinga helped shape can endure beyond the man himself.

articles.title: Israeli ad-tech firm helped place spyware on Al Jazeera devices

paras.en: Israeli advertising technology company Discover-Tech helped place spyware on dozens of devices used by Al Jazeera and other companies, a Citizen Lab investigation prompted by Al Jazeera’s initial internal probe has confirmed.
Al Jazeera Media Network on Thursday said it “condemns the targeting of devices belonging to several of its employees with spyware” and pledged to continue to “protect its employees and systems”.
The network said targeting journalists is an “assault on press freedom and the public’s right to knowledge” and called for those responsible to be held accountable.

Spyware from Candiru, an Israeli spyware firm blacklisted by the United States government in 2021 for its malicious cyber activities, was planted on these devices, using what Citizen Lab described as the first-known instance of “zero-click” targeted advertising.
Al Jazeera journalists were among the millions whose devices were targeted – including several who reported on sensitive subjects.

Al Jazeera’s in-house technology team first discovered unusual patterns on devices used by some journalists in 2024. The pattern continued into 2025. Al Jazeera reached out to Citizen Lab for a more detailed investigation into its suspicions that spyware was responsible for the activity.

“Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera collected during the attack period provides a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed,” the University of Toronto-based team said in its report published Thursday.
Al Jazeera said that the cooperation “contributed to verifying these attacks and publicly documenting them”.
Candiru’s spyware has previously been used to carry out surveillance on at least 100 journalists, dissidents and others in several countries.

articles.title: UK Green member behind anti-Zionism motion ‘receives death threats’

paras.en: London, United Kingdom – The British-Palestinian woman behind the Zionism is racism motion, passed by the Green Party of England and Wales earlier this month, says she has received death and rape threats since the vote.

In an interview with Al Jazeera on Thursday, Green member Lubna Speitan, an artist and activist, said she has received dozens of threatening social media messages and emails, which she has reported to the police.
“These threats were anticipated,” said Speitan, who believes they are a form of “intimidation” from pro-Israel agitators.
While “no one wants to be on the receiving end of death threats”, she said it is “necessary to confront these evils”.

The Greens passed the motion by 1,022 votes to 813 at their party conference in Brighton, but it has been criticised by virtually all other British political parties and has brought turmoil to the Greens.
Several of its left-wing MPs have criticised the move, and on Thursday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham ruled out partnering with the party, calling the motion “wrong” and “anti-Semitic”.

The motion defines Zionism, the belief that Jews have a historic claim to Palestine, as a form of racism, predicated on the dispossession and ethnic cleansing of Palestinians. Palestinians made up more than 90 percent of the population in 1917, when Britain declared its support for a Jewish state in the country.

The motion supports Palestinians’ right to self-determination and calls for the establishment of a single democratic state in historic Palestine for Muslims and Jews. It also says that anti-Zionism should not be equated with anti-Semitism.
Fifty-six members of Speitan’s family have been killed since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza three years ago.

“Zionism is defined clearly as an ethnonationalist settler-colonial project. The motion also recognises, correctly, that not all Jews are Zionists and not all Zionists are Jews,” she said. “It targets an ideology: Zionism.”
She added that she has been “personally smeared” by media outlets.

Recent headlines in the British press have claimed she was “friends” with an “al-Qaeda terrorist”, as she reportedly offered to testify in defence of Minh Quang Pham, a UK citizen who had planned an attack at Heathrow Airport.
“This tactic of guilt by association will not be dignified with a response,” Speitan said of the reports.
The Green Party of England and Wales told Al Jazeera that Speitan holds no party positions “other than being a member”.

“The Green Party takes all allegations of this nature seriously. Where members have expressed views that do not fit in with the party’s values, we have internal processes to investigate, and an investigation is under way,” it said.
Media watchdog NewsCord, which reviewed coverage of the motion, concluded that opponents of the resolution received 10 times more coverage than its supporters.

The Green Party is not the first Western political institution to classify Zionism as a form of racism. In 1975, the United Nations General Assembly passed a resolution declaring that Zionism was a racist ideology. Seventy-two countries voted in favour of the motion, while 35 opposed it and 32 abstained. The resolution was later repealed in 1991.

articles.title: Albania’s PM dismisses calls to resign as student protests spread

paras.en: Albania’s prime minister has dismissed calls for his resignation as thousands of protesters clash with riot police in the capital for the third day in a row, leaving government buildings damaged.

“My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward,” Prime Minister Edi Rama said in a written statement to the Reuters news agency, following protester demands for him to resign.
“The alternative would be a betrayal of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on European Union membership,” Rama added on Thursday.

This comes as riot police used water cannons and tear gas against crowds of protesters in the capital, Tirana. Demonstrators have accused officials of corruption and neglecting education, expressing anger about the sale of parts of Albania’s southern coastline to a luxury resort development backed by United States President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.

Tirana’s streets were littered with burnt-out rubbish bins, shattered bus stops and broken traffic lights. In the capital’s central Skanderbeg Square, police hit fleeing protesters with batons as tourists looked on.
Thursday’s protests also spread to several smaller cities as students joined university boycotts.
Rama, whose government denies corruption, said he would be ready to discuss rising education costs but rejected the calls to resign.

“Perhaps some forces, at home and abroad, do not want Albania to succeed as a forerunner for EU membership. But I will not allow violence to derail Albania’s European future,” Rama said in his statement to Reuters.
Rama earlier posted a video on his Facebook page showing him touring the burnt-out remains of an office at a university campus in Tirana.
“Until yesterday, this was the office of the College of Europe, the school of a united Europe,” he said in the video, his first public comments since the protests began.
“Everyone is responsible before the law, and everyone who has had a hand in this chaos will certainly pay.”
The prime minister was due to meet his party’s parliamentary group early on Thursday, when protesters circulated an “ultimatum” demanding his resignation by 1pm (11:00 GMT).
But even before the deadline passed, protesters had already begun clashing with police, building makeshift barriers and setting fire to bins.
‘Our prime minister is the meaning of the word corruption’
A student who gave her name as Kiara told Reuters the cost of living, poor job prospects and alleged corruption were the main issues for protesters.

“Our prime minister is the meaning of the word corruption. You can only find work in your field if you know a guy who knows a guy,” she said, her face covered by a mask, like many on the streets on Thursday.
The protesters demanded Rama’s resignation, saying no one had listened to their concerns during a summer of largely peaceful protests over the luxury resort development linked to Kushner.
Police said 65 people were arrested during Wednesday’s protests, suspected of “attacking police officers, institutions, public and private property”.
The Health Ministry said in a statement that hospitals in Tirana treated 89 people on Wednesday, including 61 police officers.
Four officers and two protesters remained hospitalised, with a demonstrator and two officers expected to undergo surgery.
“Attacking institutions, destroying public property and threatening public safety have nothing to do with the legitimate demands of students,” Rama said.

articles.title: Greetings from Mexico City, where a bullfighting ban doesn't stop this matador training
articles.author: Eyder Peralta

paras.en: Greetings from Mexico City, where a bullfighting ban doesn't stop this matador training

They practice in the middle of Mexico City's big urban park. With a pair of real horns, one of them plays the bull by gliding toward the fuchsia bullfighting cape. They're practicing to kill, but as the sunlight filters through the trees and the bullfighter dodges with grace, his hips to one side, his arms perfectly perpendicular, it looks incongruently beautiful.
"It's the ballet of death," José Luis Herros explains. But the movement from the bull looks too slow, too graceful, I tell him.
"That's the way bulls move," he says. When their head is down and it's ready to gore you with its horns, he explains, it comes at you slowly.
"The whole point of bullfighting is to face fear and death with the intelligence that we supposedly have," he says. "The bull has two daggers, we have this piece of cloth."
The people who gather here are real bullfighters. Mexico City has banned killing bulls so they travel outside the capital city for their sport.

As soon as I showed interest, they showed me the scars from moments that took them to the edge of death. "One bull tore my chest in half," Luis Conrado (in the sweater) told me. "But I kept fighting and I cut off an ear."
Again, I thought, the beauty of this scene was incongruous with the frank talk of death.

articles.title: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian oil refineries, officials say, after brief truce
articles.author: The Associated Press

paras.en: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian oil refineries, officials say, after brief truce

KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian drones attacked a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region early Thursday, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that a brief truce spurned by Moscow was over amid deepening tensions with Washington.

The drone strike started a fire at the refinery about 300 kilometers (180 miles) southeast of Moscow, Russia's Defense Ministry and Ryazan Gov. Pavel Malkov said. Russia's Astra online news outlet posted what it said was a photograph of the blaze.
A senior Ukrainian official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak publicly confirmed that Ukraine had hit the refinery.
Zelenskyy complains about U.S. behavior in recent days
The strike could further complicate Kyiv's relations with U.S. President Donald Trump, which have soured again in recent days.

Zelenskyy was outraged by Russia's continuing aerial bombardment of his country's energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump's demand on Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks. The Ukrainian government said that it was heeding the ceasefire.

Zelenskyy complained that, despite going along with Trump's demand for a truce, Ukraine in recent days was denied the usual Western intelligence on Russian ballistic missile strikes and limits were placed on its use of U.S.-made Starlink communication terminals.

The Ukrainian leader said that his patience had run out. He said in an interview with the Financial Times published Thursday that Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries would resume. "We're done," he was quoted as saying.
Trump made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, despite international efforts to sanction Russia for its invasion and diplomatically isolate Putin.

Zelenskyy slammed the agreement, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than 4½ years ago. U.S. efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress.

Zelenskyy said in an interview late Wednesday with Piers Morgan on the British journalist's YouTube show that he felt betrayed by Trump's deal with Putin, the energy ceasefire announcement and the Starlink operational issues.

"Really, yes, between us," Zelenskyy told Morgan when asked if he felt betrayed by the American president. "Our country has to survive, and we count on our real partners, strategic partners, the United States and President Trump."
He said that the U.S. behavior "was really strange and what was not like between partners but that they switch off Starlink, so some actually crazy steps between us."
Starlink speed limits affect Ukraine's ability to defend itself
In the same interview, Zelenskyy said that "we are losing a strong partner" in the United States.
He said that "it's painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side. But we are OK that he's in the middle."
Zelenskyy said someone is pushing Trump into a stance that is "not the right side of history."
The Starlink speed limits choked Ukrainian efforts to defend itself and hit back against Russia, Kyiv officials said.
Elon Musk noted on X that the military version of Starlink is controlled by the U.S. military and Trump.
The absence of Western intelligence leaves Ukraine more vulnerable to Russian ballistic missiles. Trump has said the U.S. hasn't stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
Russian strike in Ukraine kills 3 civilians

Three people were killed and six others injured after the Kirovohrad region of central Ukraine came under a Russian drone attack lasting more than 10 hours, Ukraine's Emergency Services said Thursday.

Zelenskyy said on X that between midnight and Thursday morning Russia launched more than 850 drones at Ukraine, adding that the barrage came "precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted."
Russian aerial attacks hit 15 Ukrainian regions, he said.

"It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine," Zelenskyy said. "It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war and guarantee security."
Ukrainian air defenses stopped 536 Russian drones during a large-scale overnight attack, the Ukrainian Air Force said, but impacts were recorded at 31 locations.
Russia's Defense Ministry said that air defenses downed 166 Ukrainian drones overnight. It said that its forces hit two vessels carrying military cargo.

articles.title: Social Security benefits to get a boost. And, Hasan Piker defends his rhetoric
articles.author: Brittney Melton

paras.en: Social Security benefits to get a boost. And, Hasan Piker defends his rhetoric

Consumer prices in September were 3.7% higher than they were a year ago, according to a Labor Department report. A spike in energy prices linked to the U.S. war with Iran drove up the cost of living. Excluding energy and food prices, core inflation reached 2.6% in September, up from August. The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% increase in benefits for next year after the release of the inflation report. This annual cost-of-living adjustment is based on prices from July, August and September. Some recipients say the increase is not enough.

paras.en: - 🎧 Social Security may run out of money to make full payments to retirees as soon as 2032. NPR's Planet Money examines possible solutions.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced he will resume attacks on Russian oil refineries, despite President Trump's request to refrain from doing so. Zelenskyy told the Financial Times that he had ordered commanders to stand down earlier this week, but wouldn't anymore. But Ukraine's ability to conduct these long-range attacks may be limited, as it has seen sudden crippling restrictions to Starshield, the satellite communications system provided by the U.S.

- 🎧 The U.S. is seemingly trying to limit Ukraine's ability to fight Russia, though that has not been announced outright, NPR's Greg Myre tells Up First. Ukraine's defense ministry said today that operations are back to normal. The country relies on the Starshield system for offensive and defensive drones to protect against Russian strikes. Elon Musk, who developed the system for the U.S. government and military, says the U.S. government sets its speed and usage limits.

A man shot and wounded by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in New York last week says he didn't know the men who shot him were ICE agents until after he woke up in the hospital. A new petition filed in Brooklyn federal court says the agents — many of them masked — didn't identify themselves before approaching Oscar Belgal's vehicle with their firearms drawn. The filing contradicts the Trump administration's version of events.
